A Prussian letter in a numerical nomenclator, intercepted and copied at The Hague (DECODE R1957), listed with no decipherment. Its clear opening, its length and the positions of six repeated code groups identify it as no. 5263 of the Politische Correspondenz (1882), printed from the King’s minute; the text is taken from that print. WAINUT later rebuilt the King’s cabinet code from six other letters and tested it blind on this one. The ministerial letter of the same day (R1955) is in another code and has its own page. 16 140 47 169 4310 = … le roi de Sardaigne 1064 = Vienne · 3042 = dessein · 545 = avec · 87 = encore Berlin → London, intercepted at The Hague · numerical nomenclator · 28 December 1751 Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 from Frederick II Go to the full text ↓ The Hague, Koninklijk Huisarchief, archive of Prince William V, inv. 198 · two pages, French, 550 code groups between a clear opening and a clear date line · DECODE R1957, “non-decrypted” (no decipherment on the record) · catalogue item 215 The Dutch opened the Prussian King’s post to London and copied the ciphered letters. The King’s minute of this one was printed in Berlin in 1882. The text here is taken from that print, matched to the Hague copy by its clear opening, its length and the positions of repeated code groups. The code itself was not rebuilt. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 19 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method · R1957 text, the printed concept matched to the Hague copy (Bourdeau): read from existing decipherment (complete) · The King-to-Michell cabinet code of 1751 (WAINUT): key recovered based on plaintext from external sources (partial) · On the map With WAINUT (solution) · Also credited · Politische Correspondenz Friedrichs des Grossen (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Read from existing decipherment · complete (R1957, text from the 1882 print); cabinet key partial (69.5% of R1957’s groups) The letter Frederick II to his London resident Louis Michell, Berlin, 28 December 1751: a secret order to find out whether London knew of an Austro-Russian plan to make Prince Charles of Lorraine the next King of Poland, and to report to the King alone. Where Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 198; DECODE R1957, listed with no decipherment. A second letter of that day, R1955, is the ministerial one. The cipher A Prussian nomenclator of numbers: 550 groups for 438 words of print. R1955 uses a different code, the one of Michell’s own reports to the King. How it was read The clear opening is word for word no. 5263 in vol. 8 of the Politische Correspondenz Friedrichs des Grossen (1882). Repeated groups fall where the print’s repeated words do: 1064 is Vienne at all four places, 4310 Sardaigne at all three. What it says The King accepts that Sardinia will join the Austro-Spanish treaty at Madrid and suspects Vienna’s Italian neutrality clears the ground for the Polish plan. Still open The cabinet code is rebuilt for 179 values; R1955 is deciphered in part, 95 of 360 groups (26.4%), and is not in print. The extended key has not been tested on a held-out letter. Their match of R1957 with no. 5263 was made independently of ours. Reviewed and re-run here on 12 October 2026.
michell1751.html#letter

Louis Michell was the Prussian secretary of legation in London, in charge of the mission there. The King wrote to him through two channels. One was the departement des affaires étrangères under Podewils, with ministerial rescripts. The other was the Immediaterlass , the King writing directly. Both went by post through the Dutch Republic, where the Stadtholder’s cabinet opened and copied them. The copies of both 28 December letters survive among the papers of William V (inv. 198), and DECODE catalogued them as R1955 and R1957. R1957 is two pages. The heading Au S r Michel à Londres and the opening clause are in clear, then 550 numbers separated by points, then A Berlin ce 28 décembre 1751 and (signé) Féderic . The copyist underlined a few groups with one to three strokes and wrote two corrections above the line. DECODE shows the two pages in reverse order: its P2 is the first page. The first page of the copy: the clear opening, then the code, from 1555 1550 ( et suis ) onward. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 198, first page (image P2), via DECODE R1957.
michell1751.html#match

Volume 8 of the Politische Correspondenz prints several letters of the King dated Berlin, 28 December 1751. No. 5263, “Au secrétaire Michell à Londres”, begins “J’ai reçu votre dépêche du 14 de ce mois”, the clear opening of the Hague copy. The other Hague letter of that day opens “Toutes vos dépêches m’ont été bien rendues et la dernière est du 14 e de ce mois” and uses a different code, with half-groups such as 150½ and 660½. That is the letter DECODE’s note calls “a letter of the same date with different length”. After the opening, the print has 438 words and the cipher 550 groups, a ratio of 1.26. That is usual for a nomenclator that has code words for common words and names and spells the rest in syllables. The main test is order. For every group that occurs three times or more and every word of the print with the same count, the relative positions were compared ( anchors.py ). Six pairs line up across every occurrence, with the largest gap at most 4.3 % of the text: Group Word Occurrences Largest gap 87 encore 3 0.017 1064 Vienne 4 0.022 545 avec 3 0.024 4364 faire 6 0.039 4310 Sardaigne 3 0.039 3042 dessein (corrected: sur ; see §04) 3 0.043 Local context agrees. …que le roi de Sardaigne entre comme partie contractante… sits at the start as 16 140 47 169 4310, giving 169 = de (the commonest group, 11 times) and 47 = roi (both corrected by the rebuilt key, §04: 169 is que , 47 probably affaire ). 3279 47 recurs twice later, where the print has le roi d’Angleterre . The first two groups, 1555 1550, stand for et suis . A different text would not put these six words in this order at these places.
michell1751.html#reading

The text below is as printed from the minute. The letter sent may differ in small points of wording. J’ai reçu votre dépêche du 14 de ce mois et suis également que vous du sentiment que l’affaire que le roi de Sardaigne entre comme partie contractante dans le traité qui se négocie à Madrid entre les cours de l’Espagne et de Vienne, ne manquera pas, quoique je sois persuadé que le général Wall prédise bien juste là-dessus. Comme je viens d’être informé en secret d’un projet que les cours de Vienne et de Pétersbourg ont formé, pour faire succéder à la couronne de Pologne le prince Charles de Lorraine, quand elle viendra à vaquer, je présume que c’est dans cette vue que la cour de Vienne a tâché de faire son traité de neutralité pour ses possessions en Italie avec l’Espagne et le roi de Sardaigne, afin d’avoir les bras libres de ce côté-là à poursuivre son dessein sur la Pologne. Ainsi mon intention est que vous devez employer tous vos soins et votre savoir-faire pour approfondir au possible si la cour de Londres est informée de ce dessein-là, ou si peut-être celle de Vienne s’est entendue là-dessus en particulier avec celle de Russie, sans en communiquer avec le roi d’Angleterre, ce que j’ai cependant de la peine à croire; tout au contraire je présume presque que c’est peut-être de l’avis du dernier que la Reine-Impératrice s’est prêtée à faire de nouvelles cessions au roi de Sardaigne, en lui faisant entrevoir que ce serait dans le dessein sur la Pologne qu’elle se verrait indemnisée de ces cessions. […] Au surplus, marquez-moi encore si vous croyez que le système pacifique d’à présent du ministère d’Angleterre se soutiendra encore et pour combien de temps […]. Faites-moi votre rapport là-dessus, mais observez qu’il faut que vous ne le fassiez sur tout ce que dessus qu’à moi seul immédiatement, sans en faire des doubles au département des affaires étrangères. […] Frederick agrees that Sardinia will join the Austro-Spanish treaty being negotiated at Madrid. He has learned in secret that Vienna and St Petersburg mean to make Prince Charles of Lorraine the next King of Poland, and he reads Austria’s Italian neutrality as clearing the ground for it. Michell is to find out whether London knows of the plan. The King suspects that Maria Theresa’s new cessions to Sardinia were made on George II’s advice, with Poland as her compensation. Michell is also to judge how long the English ministry’s peaceful course will last if George II lives a few more years. His report is to go to the King alone, not to the department. Last, he is to say whether George II grieved for the Queen of Denmark, who died on 19 December, and whether the Duke of Cumberland’s dangerous illness had troubled him. The order to report to the King alone explains why two letters went to Michell that day. It also shows that the ministerial channel was not the one Frederick trusted with this, though the Dutch copied both.
michell1751.html#cabinet

Six more letters from the King to Michell in the same code, of November and December 1751, survive in Dutch copies in the Nationaal Archief (1.10.29, Fagel, inv. 5177). Their minutes are printed as nos. 5169, 5197, 5208, 5227, 5231 and 5253. WAINUT aligned the six with the print and got a key of 72 values, then fixed it by a SHA-256 hash before transcribing R1957. Decoded with that key alone, R1957 gives 168 whole words. Their longest common subsequence with no. 5263 is 123 words. When the same words are shuffled 500 times, the mean is 58.9 and the highest is 65. Twelve other letters to Michell score at shuffle level. We re-ran the test on our own OCR of the print and got 121 against the same 58.9 and 65. Whether the test was blind rests on WAINUT’s frozen hash, which matches the key file in the pull request. The commits that put the key before the transcription are in their private history, which is not public. With R1957 added, the key has 179 values and gives a value to 381 of R1957’s 548 groups (69.5%). The extended key has not been tested on a letter held out from it. The key corrects two of our anchors. 3042 is sur , not dessein : dessein is 700, and 700 3042 stands for dessein sur before la Pologne , which is why 3042 matched dessein by position. 169 is que , not de . 1900 is Pologne and 4366 is le . WAINUT’s transcription also showed that ours had read the copyist’s theta-shaped 8 as 0 in 27 groups. These are now corrected in ct.txt . The ministerial letter of the same day, R1955, is not in the cabinet code (the key gives values to only 2.8–5.6% of its groups). It is in Michell’s envoy code, a different cipher, with its own page .

167 of R1957’s 548 groups have no value in the extended key; most are one-off syllables of spelled words and names. The extended key needs a held-out letter. The print follows the minute. Small differences in the letter as sent show only where the extended key gives values.

Opened and dated, not yet transcribed; the writer is unidentified. 1328 · 3192 · 3105 · 1564 · 2337 · 1523 · 3597 · 3143 ? · ? · ? · ? · ? · ? · ? · ? Germany → Axel Oxenstierna · code numbers inside clear Swedish · June 1633 · surveyed, not solved Swedish letters to Oxenstierna, June 1633 to Axel Oxenstierna Four reports to the Swedish chancellor, mostly in clear Swedish with the names and places in code numbers, part glossed at the time; they have only been opened and dated. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 18 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letters Four Swedish letters to Axel Oxenstierna (“Höghwälborne Herre, gunstige patron”), dated 8/18 June and 27 June 1633 on the leaves. The writer is not yet identified. Where Riksarkivet, Stockholm, Oxenstierna collection E 708; DECODE R4338–R4341, “Oxenstiernska_samlingen_E_708-1” to “-4”, dated 1646, with no decipherment recorded. Formerly part of catalogue item 207. The cipher Two-digit letter codes, four-digit codes for names and places, and letter pairs (rr, mm, aa, tt). Some groups have their meaning written above them in a hand of the time. Whether all four letters use one code is not known. How it was tried Not yet: the letters were opened on 21 September 2026, dated and set aside. Still open Everything: the codes, the glosses, the writer, and a key the archive’s key list names for 1633 but which was not found among the key records fetched. These letters were filed on this site until 14 October 2026 with ten other Riksarkivet records of catalogue item 207. They are different ciphers, each with its own page: the archbishop of Bremen’s letters of 1631 (deciphered), R4282 (deciphered by George Lasry), R4284 , R4306 (deciphered in part by George Lasry) and Rusdorff’s letters of 1628 .
oxenstierna1633.html#letters

The lower part of the letter of 8/18 June 1633: four-digit codes inside the clear Swedish, several with a gloss written above. Image: Riksarkivet, Stockholm, Oxenstiernska samlingen E 708, letter of 8/18 June 1633, f. 20, via DECODE R4338. The first letter, headed “8/18 Juni 1633” and foliated 20, seems from its clear words to deal with money, contributions and garrisons (Berlin, Hamburg and Wolgast are named in clear); it has not been studied closely. The code numbers stand mostly for names and places, and the glosses of the time cover part of them. DECODE’s date of 1646 is wrong for these leaves. The archive’s list of keys names one for “Oxenstierna and Lars Nilsson Tungel (1633)”. Tungel was a Swedish diplomat in Germany in these years and is a candidate for the writer, but that is not checked, and the key was not among the seventy key records fetched from the same boxes.

Eleven numeric despatches of Rákóczi’s envoy at the Porte, five of them filed under other senders, decrypted with the Hungarian syllabic nomenclator issued to him (DECODE R580), which DECODE had not linked to them: 99.7% of 16,698 groups. A twelfth letter, in a graphic-sign alphabet, has its own page. 203 · 39 · 52 · 194 · 135 · 52 · 135 · 219 le·gy·en pa·ti·en·ti·a — “legyen patientia” 257 Fényes Porta · 277 Vezér · 219|229 A · 192 ge Constantinople → Ferenc Rákóczi II · Hungarian syllabic nomenclator · 1706–1710 János Pápai to Ferenc Rákóczi II, 1706–1710 to Francis II Rákóczi Go to the full text ↓ Eleven despatches of János Pápai to Rákóczi, MNL OL G15 (DECODE R740–R823), catalogued as not or partly decrypted, five of them under other senders. The key table issued to Pápai survives as DECODE R580; applied unchanged, it decrypts 99.7% of the groups in the eleven numeric letters. Ten of them build sentences, but seven of those (R741, R757, R765, R793, R794, R796, R823) read at 88.9–91.4% of their words, under the 95% a complete reading needs; the short cipher passage of R740 is decoded, not read. A twelfth letter, R731, uses a separate alphabet of graphic signs and has its own page . Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (99% of the cipher) Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (99% of the cipher) The letters Twelve despatches of János Pápai, Ferenc Rákóczi II’s envoy at the Ottoman Porte, 1706–1710, in Hungarian with some Latin. Where Hungarian National Archives key; DECODE R580 (the key), with letters R795, R796, R793, R794, R805, R823, R765, R784, R757, R741, R740 and R731. The cipher A Hungarian syllabic nomenclator with values 10–322: two homophones per letter, syllables, and names. Groups above 322 are nulls. How it was read Pápai’s own key, R580, applied unchanged: first on R805 (336 of 336 groups), then on the rest. A second pass brings the numeric letters to 16,641 of 16,698 groups (99.7%). What it says Imperial troops crossing Ottoman ground, audiences with the Vezír, the French ambassador failing to bring the Porte to war, Muscovy, and money. Still open R731 (Belgrade, 1710) hides six short passages in a graphic alphabet, about 330 signs, and no Hungarian came out. 57 digit fragments fit no key value.

DECODE R580 (G15 Caps. C Fasc. 43/39) is a Hungarian syllabic nomenclator with values from 10 to 322: Letters, two homophones each: A 219|229, B 209|239, E 179|269, N 100|304, T 79|309, Z 60|312. The same pattern covers ö, ü and the digraphs ny, ly, gy, ty, cz, sz, nk and rt. Syllables in columns by final digit: 11 ab , 21 ad … 192 ge , 245 va … 236 üz . Names: 246 Király , 256 Fejedelem , 257 Fényes Porta , 267 Török Császár , 277 Vezér , 287 Bassa , 297 Bécs . Countries run from 17 to 207; towns, rivers and months from 18 to 298. The letters have no word division and no nulls. DECODE had R805 as “partially decrypted” from a few interlinear syllables. The first test of the key on R805 gave 336 of 336 groups as running Hungarian, and the other letters followed without any change to the key.
papai1706.html#what-the-letters-say

The key gives continuous text without word division. The quotations below are from the word-divided readings of 23 October 2026 ( texts/R*_reading.md , with English beside them), in the figures’ spelling; for R805 and R795, which have no word-divided reading file yet, word breaks and accents are editorial. Every value is grade H (a direct table value). R805, 1 May 1706. The Porte should refuse the Germans passage across Ottoman ground: az németnek szabados általmenetelt ne engedgye … az Aradi Bassának ordere nélkül meg ne engedgye az németnek Szeged felé való általmenetelt . The envoys have also spoken to the Vezír about Muscovy. R823, 19 Dec 1706. An audience in the presence of the Imperial internuncio, reported partly in Latin: presentia autem vestra non est ingrata Portae . The hereditary-kingship argument follows: imperator: hereditarii reges sunt Angliae, Daniae, Sveciae, et tamen legibus subsunt , with the envoys’ answer that Hungary will not give up its old laws. R765, 5 Jan 1707. Submission to the Prince’s will and the state of Poland. On the Prince’s order the envoys went to the French ambassador: A Francia Ország oratorhoz elmentünk . R795, R796, R793, R794, January–March 1706 (added 21 Sept 2026). Catalogued as two ciphertexts of “Constantinople envoys”, partly deciphered interlinear at the time; they are four despatches of Pápai, decrypted with his key. The check of 23 October 2026 first found R793 and R796 garbled in places; their figures were then re-transcribed on the DECODE images. The decoder had dropped every figure line that also carried an interlinear tag (eight lines of R793), and the transcriber had left out a line of each letter, repeated half a line of R796 and slipped about thirty groups. Corrected and decoded again, both now build sentences beside the transcriber’s copy of the interlinear decipherment; a name on p. 1 of R793, part of its Black Sea passage and the closing lines of R796 stay open, where the figures agree with the image and no key value carries them. R795, signed Constancz die prima Januarii Ezer het szaz hat, Pápai János , written with Ferenc Horváth, reports the Prince’s discretion money handed to the Vezír’s Kiaya, the Tatar Khan, the Pasha of Temesvár and a new route for letters through Moldavia. R796 (20 February) answers the Prince’s letter from the Tisza: the Germans spread false news, the confederates are scorned, the Muscovite envoy is at the Porte and nothing is resolved on the propositions. R793 (March) reports secret talks with the Porte’s chancellor on the Muscovite quarrel, the King of Sweden and a Hungarian confederation with the Porte certis conditionibus , and the Prince’s manifesto translated and given to the Vezír. R794 (undated) concerns recruiting horse in Wallachia and the French King’s money, which the ambassador will not pay without the King’s order. In R795 every group above 322 is a null. R784, 1707 (added 21 Sept 2026). Catalogued as “unknown sender to Rákóczi”. Unsigned and undated, but in Pápai’s key, which decrypts it unchanged. A Francia Ország oratori jelentette [?mirtt], hogy semmi ratitiökkal nem inducálhattya Fényes Portát az hadakozásra : the French ambassador reported that no arguments could bring the Porte to war. The grandees of the last war have sworn to see that the Sultan resolves on it, and the whole Turkish nation leans that way. France means to turn Turkey wholly against the Germans ( ezt a Török Országot egészen a német ellen fordítsa ), from which Hungary would draw harm rather than profit. The ambassador has written the same to the Tatar Khan, and if Muscovy and Poland do not second it, the Germans will overrun Hungary. A note on p. 2 in another hand asks the Prince to keep the letter secret and decipher it himself ( … titokban tartani s maga decifrálni ). R757, 16 May 1708. A message from the Muscovite ambassador, and Pápai explains why he cannot send money from Constantinople. R740, 2 Jan 1710. The Kiaya’s answer, which is the only enciphered passage: legyen patientiával, ne siessen, várakozzék … ha a Fényes Porta szívére nem veszi … ne kellyen illyen haszontalan költeni s alkalmatlankodni F[elsé]gdnek a Fényes Portán . That is, the Prince should be patient and stop spending money and effort at the Porte to no purpose. The passage is only 168 groups and its middle does not build (half its sentences hold): the transcription agrees with the image, the slips are the writer’s, and no other text of it is known, so R740 is decoded, not read (check of 23 October 2026). R741, 8 May 1710. A visit to the Defterdar. The Pasha of Belgrade’s letter had concerned only the merchants’ business.

Translation R796_en.md # R796 — English (János Pápai to Ferenc Rákóczi II, Constantinople, 20 February 1706) Same holes as R796_reading.md. Modern spelling; codes as names. Gracious lord! I received with due obedience on the eleventh of this month Your Highness's letter sent undated from by the Tisza. […] From the letters with it Your Highness can understand at length how matters have gone so far. As for the false news spread by the Germans, since we have not neglected our duty either, we have carried it out: not only did the Turk not believe it, but even the confederates despised it, knowing besides that they are wont to multiply the scant [?truth] of their affairs with many lies. We did not fail to plead for those trapped in Moldavia; but since it prejudices the articles of the armistice, I see they are reluctant to give a firman to the voivode about it; nevertheless I shall not cease to [press] this request further, or at least that an order be given to the voivode through the Moldavian kapukehaya here, whose [260] I have written to his principal; only let Your Highness meanwhile keep in correspondence with that voivode. I know he protects those exiles anyway; it will be all the better if Your Highness writes to the serdar of Babadag, who was pasha of Belgrade, since they were moved from there and sent to Babadag, and he commands Moldavia. The coming in of the Transylvanian [envoys?] they do not [?…]; [only] in the present state of things do they admit them, since the Turk regards Transylvania as [his own]. We did not fail to press the Sublime Porte with [the treaties?] of peace, and we press it still; but it must be admitted that the German never frightened this nation as much as on the occasion of the last war; that is why it is so reluctant, and does not willingly wish to prejudice the armistice. Besides, neither the Vizier nor the Turkish Emperor are [martial?] men, but [take] such good news for their pleasure […]; if Your Highness writes to the Vizier's chancellor and to the mufti too, [about] the standing of the armistice. Nevertheless let Your Highness not think that the Sublime Porte will give him help, since by its nature it hates [the idea] against itself for the future too, and does not wish to settle on the proposals submitted. Until now it has been good […], but there is no resolution; […] only hope too […]. And I remain Your Highness's humble servant, János Pápai. Constantinople, one thousand [seven] hundred and six, twentieth of February. [P.S.] [The kapukehaya?] sent to Albania with Mr Ferenc Horváth […] would remain to go; whoever does not stay here […]. [I humbly ask?] Your Highness to put it down not to my sloth that I cannot report often, but to the lack of a sure opportunity. [Though?] we find [?…] a disposition towards us, we do not cease [to carry out] Your Highness's orders, but so far we have not been able to bring our affairs begun to effect. In recent days we approached the Sublime Porte with [new writings], which we presented in two parts: one on the Muscovite business, but very secretly, through the chancellor and the mufti, so that, as was necessary, his co-religionist should not notice; upon which […], having arrived, reported on the settlement of the frontier disputed between the Muscovites and the Sublime Porte, on the frontier by the Tana [Azov]: it has not been settled, […] the envoy; the peace with the Muscovite Tsar has not been fully ratified. [It is time] for the Sublime Porte to take a hand, since with the Sublime Porte on one side and the King of Sweden on the other, if he attacks, Poland could not hold out; the Roman Emperor's affairs being such that he could not act against our Sublime Porte with all his strength; indeed, if the Roman Emperor wanted to attempt something, his war with the French and the Hungarians [would prevent it]; and if our Sublime Porte allies itself with the Hungarians, the King of Sweden being an ally of the Hungarians, Prince Rákóczi will bring it about that he allies himself with the Sublime Porte on certain conditions. The Muscovite, under colour of the peace, already [holds?] the Astrakhanians, the Circassians, the Mingrelians […] of the Sublime Porte; among the [Kakhetians?] he has already sent two hundred priests, armed […], he leaves that mouth [of the river] there, which [threatens] the Sublime Porte, there being harbour enough in Circassia and Mingrelia on the Black Sea, directly against Constantinople on one side, and on the other in that […] Black Sea […] with Moldavia, the Roman Emperor [and] the confederates' gatherings too. When they understood this, the Vizier, informed of the withdrawal without its being noticed, so moderated his views on all this; they presented it in writing. Here the Vizier soon called me and asked me: do you think the Hungarians would ally themselves with the Swede? In this with them […], but I believe they too have an interest in it. Meanwhile the chancellor explained our project on this to the Vizier: that both Your Highness and the Transylvanian King, through Your Highness's mediation, wish to ally with the Sublime Porte, the other with other reasons, which demonstrated the harm to the Sublime Porte that would follow from the confederation to be made in Poland. This had to be [delivered] with the manifesto, which we gave to the Vizier already translated. The envoy himself is persuading the Vizier. We hope for the desired answer in a few days; if these two writings of mine do not move them, after that we see nothing else. They would gladly be friends with us, as [appears] from the chancellor's words, except that the German too [is] much despised […], all the more since the German has now retaken Transylvania. Those who are in Moldavia, about them [the envoy] wrote to the voivode; he is waiting meanwhile until the firman goes off. The Vizier too inclines towards us; we shall obtain it through the envoy, even if it prejudices the pacification. About money: the envoy gives not a penny. And I remain Your Highness's humble servant, János Pápai. Constantinople, the sixteenth of March, one thousand seven hundred and six. [200] […] János Pápai. [P.S.] The propositions must [?…] all in Wallachia, [?…] only that they allow the recruiting here, which [?…] the recruiting of four thousand horse costs us a great deal, since beforehand thirty thalers' discretion must go to its officers separately, [?and] to the [?common soldiers]. But since Your Highness has enough cavalry besides, foot is more needed. When we hand the Vizier our memorial about Muscovy, we make no specification either of horse or of foot, but only asked permission to recruit; and if Your Highness wants more foot, it will be easy, horse or foot. [?…] to make a disposition about money quickly, since the ambassador will not have it; without it we get nowhere in the recruiting. As I humbly report to my gracious lord, so that I may inform Your Highness of the matters in hand: when some days ago I wanted to send my servant off with the Moldavian couriers, I had already sent to the lodgings for some boyar, seized for his tax; my servant too has had to wait here until now. [?…] Yesterday, very secretly, early in the morning, he sent his son, who is now interpreter at the Vizier's gate, summoning me; he wished, [?…] the order being, first to meet the Vizier's kiaya [?…] very secretly, [?…] without pomp, since he so wished, and I asked him to obtain an audience with the Vizier; he much obliges Your Highness's [7] too, so that when, having taken leave of the Vizier, I went towards evening to the ambassador, I asked: the affairs are now starting, money is needed for the discretion and for recruiting Turks [?through] the Albanians; to which he answered: [?…] the money due from the King for Your Highness is assigned to it, [?but without] his order [?he cannot] give cash, and without it he cannot give his own, having spent more than ten thousand thalers of his own not for the promotion of Hungarian affairs, and the King has not refunded even that; and we cannot want him to make himself a debtor and a beggar; though what he spends for Your Highness is surely refunded, without the King's order he cannot give, [?not] up to three thousand thalers [?…], from which the discretion is not even covered. [?…] through lack of money a damaging confusion falls on our affairs. [?…] Kassa [?…] serve; he had to be summoned to him by the [?Vizier's] order; he [?said] I should put in writing the matters relating to the propositions and take them to him, so that he may have them turned into Turkish [?…] tomorrow [?…] to him. The Latin passages are translated with the rest. ## Translation The ambassador of Muscovy sent me word thus: those Hungarians have not been [to me], I have not seen them, but if they make themselves known I shall hear them and give them an answer or not; it is in my power. I cannot send money from here, since by the religion of this Sublime Porte the canon is that whoever comes here is admitted [?…]. Before the ambassador of Muscovy and through a request at the Sublime Porte we also called Mr Hentér, but he did not come; doing our duty, we went to his request. [?…] said: I shall tell you the resolution of the Sublime Porte [?…] you are joined with Mr Hentér: [?…] the steward of the court had resolved to admit you three to his presence, but he put off that intention; yet [?…] to the Porte [?…] the kiaya will resolve; we shall let you know. This present steward of the court is a prudent man, more so than the former; Hentér brought those [?…] together with your propositions; he went through them from head to foot and examined them. From the start we asked: [?…] safe conduct? He answered: yes, but not [?…]. We answered: yes, but with arms. He answered: yes, and not [?…]. Going to the kiaya, the chancellor was present too; kissing his robe, we congratulated him on his new office; he seated us with respect [3000]. Then he asked Mr Hentér: did [?…] Your Majesty and the Estates [?…] come? He answered: yes; when the Prince was inaugurated to the Principality, he took the country's homage to His Majesty, and His Majesty too swore to the Estates. He asked him: whether the Prince now [?…] the seat at Pozsony [?…] outside others' realm? We answered: Sibiu is not the seat of the Princes but [Gyula]fehérvár, where His Majesty's general actually is; the Estates of the country are in His Majesty's loyalty [?…] on Rabutin's entry, those of Sibiu and Brașov [?…] obeyed the German; notwithstanding that, the Estates of the whole country are in His Majesty's loyalty. Mr Hentér briefly proposed the wish of Your Majesty and the Estates about the admission of the [?…] envoys. The kiaya answered: the letter he brought from the Prince and the Estates of the country [?…] refer to you, that we should credit your words; [?…] as we now understood, that solemn envoys might come. I ask this: does the Prince hold all Transylvania? Mr Hentér: I cannot say so, for the German holds Brașov, Sibiu, Făgăraș. We said: if [?…] we may speak more fully in this matter, the Sublime Porte well knows that when Bocskai, Gábor Bethlen and other princes [3000] afterwards turned to the Sublime Porte, before they held all Transylvania and those towns, the Sublime Porte [?…] their wishes and protected them. The [?…] kiaya answered: the Sublime Porte held Buda, [?…] our faith [?…] the canon; we hold that [?…] we accept envoys from the Prince; a Prince [?…] [160] outside another's co-possession, for a principality consists in the country being [?…] in his jurisdiction as absolute [?dominion]; to such envoys we must give their due honour and send [?…] with pomp; but in the [present] state of the country we could not give the honour to the envoys of the prince. Pozsony is far; [let him correspond] by the Prince's order, either by word or letter, with the Pasha of Belgrade; Poland [?…] are close to one another; let him keep the Sublime Porte constantly informed [?…] the head [?…] of Kassa [?correspond] with the Pasha of Belgrade; [?…] until God turns [?affairs] to the better, and both we and the Prince will have a better way of talking with the Pasha of Belgrade. Wherever the Prince [?…] the Prince's trusted man is, there too, if you propose anything, we shall listen. In so great a matter we must proceed by degrees; it will be better for the Prince too. Mr Hentér was sent back [?…] a firman is given, I take it myself before the Vizier, I procure the answer. He answered: we know that, but we do not speak, since until further disposition for the two of us the Prince requires us to stay here; we have recourse with that, let him admit [us]; yes, tell me, I report it to the Vizier; once [?…] they will give an answer by letter [?…]. There will be a firman for safe conduct [?…]; are you content with this resolution of the Porte? God will soon give better. The secret treaty: but since he ordered us to suspend Your Majesty's intention, we kept silent. Explanation: the kiaya seemed to attach [us] to himself, so that this should not change any more. [?…] the Vizier [?…] may judge from which the Sublime Porte finds difficulty; accordingly he moderates the Transylvanian operations, likewise the operations with the Pasha of Belgrade, further on. Through the kiaya's favourites too he [?invited] us to a secret colloquy with the kiaya, so that [?…] the kiaya's answer: he is not an absolute Prince as long as he does not hold it entirely; [?…] they do not acknowledge such; now they could say nothing else about the admission of the envoys to the Sublime Porte. [?…] your affair, for it has got on its feet; you have not [?…] in vain so far. But in the letter of the Pasha of Belgrade there was nothing else but that [?…] the merchants have so far paid [?…]; therefore [?…] the order. In his letters he wrote only of the merchants' affairs, but he sends his post after me, which will catch me up on the way, and through it he recommends Your Majesty's affairs to the Grand Vizier. But not here either, for the defterdar, when he had read it, said: this letter was indeed written about the merchants' affairs, but to the end that from Buda [?…] the pasha's report [?…] here from the Prince, who [?…] Your Majesty's letter; I am not now in such a position, in my office, that I could serve the Prince. That is the office of the Vizier's kiaya; though you are not now the Grand Vizier's kiaya, you are still an intimate of the Vizier, the Pasha [?writes], so that we should carry on the affairs before the Vizier through you. The Vizier [?asked] about the coming of the Prince's man here, and then too he communicated the matter only with you. The Vizier with his own hand [?…] to the Pasha that he should send me [?…]; but what business have you with the Vizier? The Prince wants help; [?…] can help go up to him? We do not see [?…] secret [?…]: if now from Bender some thousands of Albanians [were sent by] the Vizier into Moldavia towards Câmpulung, under colour of watching the Polish borders, under colour of that watch they could seep little by little into Máramaros, into his realm; it could be done without any noise; those troops would not have to pass through another country, [?…] from Bender to Moldavia, from there along the Máramaros borders, beyond Câmpulung into Máramaros. This cannot be without injury to the peace, for they would go as deserters, making tumult among one another, as Albanians and Bosnians have deserted to us before. [?…] it would collide with breaking the peace. [?…] Belgrade [?…] would dispute it, at least with this you could [?…] the Turks killed at Kecskemét and elsewhere, and then with such help the peace with the Roman Emperor could be better restored with us, and we too surviving, Turkey would be strengthened by our neighbourhood against the Roman Emperor. [?…] the Sublime Porte, since through the Porte's protection it established [?…] the enemy [?…] from the country, makes it safe [?…] towards Hungary too in time; you will have such a neighbour as you will not easily manage: avoid the enemy, if only we avoid him and do not [?…] against him; [?…] he makes such a circle [?…]. What advice he gives: that I should go to the chief kiaya and through him make myself known to the Vizier. Even then he had shut the doors and told his servants to watch that no one came in. [?…] some days for the man of the Pasha of Belgrade; if he comes, good, I shall hand Your Majesty's letter to the Vizier; but if I see I hope for nothing, I shall keep silent about new proposals in general terms. I ask that his requests so far [?…] Your Majesty, that it may help our affairs. After that, if nothing comes, I shall go back, and so I shall see out April; [?…] he speaks of our affairs too so badly and coldly, as if he were no well-wisher of our nation. Probably. They are not emended to Merecki, serejski or Dąbrowski. A cautiously word-divided reading, retaining the source’s irregular forms: Pan starosta serecki iest tu. Pytałam się ieżeli ma co postanowionego. Ni ma nic. Iedzie ⟨dzie⟩ do Lublina. To tesz prawda że był u dominikanow wtenczas iakeś tańcował z nią w polu. Powiedał mi Stabrowski. ‘The starosta serecki is here. I asked whether he has anything settled. He has nothing. He is going to Lublin. It is also true that he was with the Dominicans at the time when you danced with her in the field. Stabrowski told me.’ ⟨dzie⟩ marks a syllable the writer enciphered twice (M): the figures run 21 25 30 16 21 25 30 16 21 25 30 35 , iedziedziedo , evenly spaced with no cancellation, so the second dzie is taken as a slip of the pen; the alternative is the dialect form dzie for gdzie , ‘somewhere’. serecki is clear on the image ( 36 25 37 25 29 20 21 , the 20 retouched in darker ink); the starostwo it names is not identified. Other irregularities are not silently repaired. The division iakeś tańcował , ‘when you danced’, replaces iak estancował (corrected 30 September 2026; the letter values, grade I, are unchanged). It follows the writer’s own grouping: on the image the figures 21 27 20 25 36 ( iakes ) close a line as one group, and 19 27 34 29 35 17 27 32 ( tancowal ) open the next as one group, followed by a stop. A line end alone would not settle it, since the writer also breaks words across lines ( udomini|kanow , powi|edal ). But jakeś tańcował is ordinary Polish, the ending -eś of the second person placed on jak , while the earlier division needs a word estancował that Polish does not have, and a lodging verb such as stancować would need a second s that the figures do not give. The change makes Dunin, the addressee, the one who danced with her, and turns the clause into a date for his visit to the Dominicans; the earlier gloss, his staying with a woman, is withdrawn. On the image the first figure of the last group is 36 (s), not 39 (p) as first transcribed: its second digit closes at the foot like the 6 of starosta , while the 9 of 39 in polu on the same line ends in a tail. The transcription was corrected on 30 September 2026, and the name reads Stabrowski , an existing surname, instead of p. Tabrowski . On 2 October 2026 the values R2242, the sibling letter, gives for its graphic word signs were tried at every occurrence (five adopted, six ruled out), and Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken gave the writer and the date. The writer calls William V “mon père” and asks that the cipher be shown to “mon frère”, so he is one of the Stadholder’s two sons. The addressee is an officer managing the rassemblement , the Dutch troops who followed the House of Orange into Germany in British pay after the French conquest of January 1795. Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken (vol. II, 1795–1798; searched in full text on 2 October 2026) does not print R1892 but fixes its setting. No. 724, of 7 October 1795, is Prince Frederick writing to General Dundas from Nienburg , where he commanded the rassemblement, and the writer of the Dutch postscript would much rather have stayed at “Nam..nburg”, Nienburg (M). On 26 November 1795 the Princess writes that her younger son has arrived in England, “c’est aussi pour le rassemblement qu’il est venu” (p. 893). The writer is therefore Prince Frederick , in England, and “mon frère” is the Hereditary Prince. No. 734 (the Hereditary Prince to William V, 25–27 December 1795) reports that Henry Dundas’s new orders of 8 December had decided against the rassemblement; troops not taking British service were to go to Nassau. Page 1 still anticipates that decision (“au cas que le général Dundas vous déclarât … que les troupes devroient se laisser embarquer”), so it was written before the orders reached the continent: late November or early December 1795 . DECODE’s “1 January 1795”, before the flight of the House of Orange, cannot be the date of the letter. “To William V” in the record reflects where the letter is kept, not its addressee.

Fetched the record and its two images, and the key records R2240 and R2233, from DECODE with a session login. Turned and cut the photocopies into strips; two transcription passes (one per page) wrote each column as a TOP+BOTTOM token, clear words in brackets and signs by name: 1,039 pairs on page 1, 790 on page 2. Page 2’s pairs, split at every sign and clear word, went to a simulated-annealing solver scoring Dutch quadgrams from the shared corpus, with a one-to-one key (swap moves). A many-to-one first run collapsed onto e and n and was discarded. The one-to-one run gave hetrassemblementtezamentehouden and officieren at once. The same square applied unchanged to page 1 gave French text; four values were adjusted from it (54 = q, 14 = x, 13 = y, 12 = z in French).

Translation p1_en.md # R1892 page 1: English Translation of `p1_reading.md` (23 Oct 2026), same holes. ## Translation Written in cipher in the letter of […] dated […] December. My father is charging Nagel to go again to the ministers to insist on some answer to the various representations made to them concerning the matter of the rassemblement; I venture to flatter myself that at last, [if it] is ended, one will come. But as it might happen in the meantime that General Dundas declares to you […] that he will stop the pay, or else that the troops must let themselves be embarked, you would have to subscribe to it and limit yourself solely to trying to obtain leave to give a gratification to those who would not submit, in case you were […] obliged to this. I ask you, however, to make known to the troops on what footing they will enter the service of His Britannic Majesty, and for that purpose you may give them a paper roughly like the one that was meant to be given to them at the first [moment] when there was question of their embarkation. You can find this paper among [my] papers, and you can make in it the changes you judge fitting in present circumstances. Be so good as not to put on the account for […] the expense of my lodging, [not wishing] […] to be under the least obligation, but to pay it from the money of mine that you hold. Nevers was being urged to come to court, where everyone wanted him, the ligueurs included. Paris talked of asking the King, as a sign that he pardoned the city, to let it choose among four names. Only the curés of Saint-André (Christophe Aubry) and Saint-Benoît (Jean Boucher) were still inciting the people. The new municipality was steered by rumour, and La Chapelle-Marteau reported everything decided at the Hôtel de Ville to Guise’s council. With 33, “de Bray”, Pierre d’Épinac archbishop of Lyon and the président de Neuilly in attendance, that council undid whatever it disliked. When Guise wanted the Arsenal’s artillery for Corbeil, the échevin Cotteblanche refused without the King’s permission. The League municipality was raising loans through the notaries on the guarantee of Neuilly, Claude Marcel, the prévôt and the échevins. Count Guido Rangone (1485–1539), a condottiere from Modena in French service, spent the winter of 1529–30 in Venice after the defeat at Landriano. He wrote to the Grand Master, Anne de Montmorency, in Italian, mostly in clear: news of the Peace of Bologna, the Duke of Urbino, the Turkish envoy, the Swiss and Grisons going home. Twice he switched to cipher. 24 December 1529 , Français 3082 f. 42r, no. 19 (Gallica view 65). Five lines of cipher after the passage on Ravenna and Cervia, which Venice was handing back to the Pope. Copy: Clairambault 330 f. 206, headed “Vol. 143 fol. 42”. 10 January 1530 , Français 3070 f. 81r, no. 40 (DECODE R4249). Seven lines of cipher after “adesso lo dirò più brevemente che io potrò. Mons.r”, broken by the clear words “vida V. Ex. che tratti sono questi”. Autograph signature “S.re Guido Rangone Co.”. Copy: Clairambault 331 f. 15, headed “Vol. 134 fol. 81”. Neither copy has a decipherment. Four other Rangone letters from Venice in 1529–30 (Français 3012 no. 44, 3013 no. 19, 3034 no. 18, 2980 no. 44) were checked and are in clear. The ciphered letter of Joachin de Vaux from Ferrara, March 1529, in Français 3012 uses a different sign set. Français 3070 f. 81r: the seven cipher lines of 10 January 1530, with the clear words “vida V. Ex. che tratti sono questi” in line 5. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3070 f. 81r, via Gallica and DECODE R4249.

A homophonic simple substitution without word division. Vowels have two to eight signs each (e: ω, P, ∞ and two stars; a: ɪ, ʃ, Ȥ; o: 8 and ϙ), consonants one to three (n: K, ᏕᏏ, ㅌ; l: ≈, ξ, ✡). One sign is a null: it stands inside the name Fre·goso . No code signs for names were found. This is the ordinary Italian design of the 1520s, with more homophones than the ciphers of Visconti or Bizozola from the same campaigns. The key is in targets/rangone1530/key.json . Three pairs of look-alike signs turned out to be different signs and had to be separated: a capital Θ (t) against the narrow θ (i), a “∋” with a leading dash (u) against the plain one (i), and two blotted stars.

Io vi scrissi ultimamente Ill.mo S.re uno certo caso acaduto mi et non li dissi più oltra per alhora; adesso lo dirò più brevemente che io potrò. Mons.r ’l fa instantia [a m]e de ven[i]re al servicio loro, o[?] le mie … malissimo satisfato di lui; ha mandato a dirlo al [s]ignore Cesare e farli grande oferte. Vida V. Ex. che tratti sono questi, essendo seguito la [?]icon[p]uorano a[t]tenderui. Hora lassamo andare questi mei particulari … “My Lord, he urges [me] to come into their service … is very ill satisfied with him; he has sent to tell it to Signor Cesare and to make him great offers. See, Your Excellency, what treatment this is, it having followed [?] …” In January 1530 the Venetian Senate appointed Cesare Fregoso military governor of Verona with 2,500 ducats a year ( Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani , “Fregoso, Cesare”). He had married Rangone’s sister Costanza that autumn. The cipher is Rangone’s complaint that the Republic was courting his brother-in-law while it treated him badly, the “certo caso” of his previous letter. In October 1530 the French in turn dismissed Rangone over his protests at a cut in his pension.
rangone1530.html#how-it-was-broken

Both originals and both copies were transcribed sign by sign ( cipher.txt ): 264 signs, flat top frequencies, so homophonic. Simulated annealing of the sign-to-letter map against the it-cinquecento five-gram model, with a letter-frequency penalty. Short runs gave pseudo-Italian and no two runs agreed. The clear text of the same letter scores −1.72 per five-gram, the runs −2.3. The search had failed; the model was adequate. An incremental annealer, 40 restarts of two million moves each. One restart reached −1.97 and gave real words and the name Fregoso. Every perturbed restart from that key went back to it. A sensitivity table: 35 signs are fixed by the text with margins of 6 to 85 log units; the others occur once or twice. Corrections from the words: б = h ( ha mandato , e harà , ho una ), the tailed sign = f ( oferte ), D = b ( ben disposte ), the null, and the three split pairs. Word-aware scoring of the remaining signs, singly and in pairs, under a spaced language model. No value won by more than noise, so they stay open.

An initial-letter code of Charles V’s court: each word is its initial and a number. It hides most of a letter to “Garbino” from Madrid, 11 April 1528 (BnF fr. 3022 no. 20), and the letters of Hieronimo Ranzo, Gattinara’s kinsman (fr. 2988, fr. 3019; DECODE R1894). This project transcribed about 3,900 groups but recovered only function words. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 September 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (72% of the cipher) With George Lasry (solution) and Paolo Rosson (earlier solution, verification) and Norbert Biermann (transcription) ciphertext-only Summary. No. 20 of français 3022 is a letter to “Garbino” , Madrid, 11 April 1528, in the code of Hieronimo Ranzo, a kinsman of the Chancellor Gattinara. The same code is used in Ranzo’s signed letters in fr. 2988 and fr. 3019 (DECODE R1894). All 1,315 groups of no. 20 were transcribed here, with about 2,600 more from Ranzo’s own letters, but this project’s solver recovered only function words. Two independent decipherments came on 6 October 2026: Paolo Rosson’s, with Claude, built on this project’s transcription ( section 03 measures it), and George Lasry’s , with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, from Norbert Biermann’s transcription of five letters ( section 04 ). Outcome: key recovered from ciphertext-only, by George Lasry and, independently, by Paolo Rosson; partial. Measured per letter with Lasry’s key first and Rosson’s second ( section 04 ): Ranzo’s two letters in fr. 2988 give sense for 96.2 % and 97.0 % of their groups, over the 95 % line, and fr. 20506 is a copy of the second; no. 20 reads 94.4 %, fr. 4050 87.7 %, fr. 6638 89.0 %; 92.9 % of 6,428 groups in all. In letter 4 (fr. 4050) runs of open codes break most sentences of the middle, so it counts as decoded, not read; in the four letters that read, 4,606 of the 6,428 groups give sense (71.7 %, reading audit, 22 October 2026). On 23 October 2026 letter 4 (Madrid, 10 March 1528) was joined into words by hand from Biermann’s transcription with Lasry’s key, Rosson’s key (which confirms nine of Lasry’s tentative values there and gives three more: e173 express , s72 sara , d46 debia ) and the code list’s rough alphabetical order ( texts/letter4_reading.md , English letter4_en.md ). With 39 code values resting on sense and list position only, about 70 tentative values seen once or twice and 47 code types still open, and one run of eleven codes (f. 79r l. 27 to f. 79v l. 2) that does not build, it stays decoded, not read; the partial reading is kept.

f. 44r, no. 20: “R. de […] S. r da poi de haverni scripto per piu l[ette]re”, the dates of letters received (23 November, 3 and 28 December, 4 February), then the code. Every group is a small letter with a number above it. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3022 f. 44r, via Gallica (btv1b90601558, view 86). No. 20 is an Italian letter, dated at Madrid on 11 April 1528, endorsed on the back to “Garbino”. It alternates clear and code. The clear passages report that the Chancellor was ill with gout, that fifty galleys were being fitted out, that a million ducats had been raised in Castile and 500,000 more were expected from the Cortes of Aragon, and that the Empress was in the seventh month and the prince would be sworn heir. The coded passages, about two thirds of the letter, are what it was sent for. Bound after the letter are papers of Garbino’s network, not keys to this letter. On f. 48 is a jargon, with more on f. 49: cover letters signed “Antonio de Cosenza” to “Andrea Romano in Valencia”, news disguised as the price of grain, and a list of cover names. On f. 49v the Emperor is “Joan Jacobo”, del Vasto “portolano de Gergenti”, Garbino himself “antonio petra”. On f. 50 is an “Aditione nel zifra”, an addition to a code key. The “Aditione” is not the key to this letter. It belongs to another code of the same design, an initial letter with a number, and is shown here only to illustrate how such a code is built. Checked against the transcriptions: of its 113 groups, only one (g217, once) occurs anywhere in the 3,912 groups of no. 20 and Ranzo’s letters, and its numbers overlap those the letters already use (it starts the b list at 157; the letters run to b215). No value in the decipherments below was taken from it as a key. f. 50, the “Aditione nel zifra”, an addition to another code of the same design, shown for illustration; it is not the key to no. 20 or to Ranzo’s letters: apresso a 327 , al garbino a 330 , Defensione d 308 , havendo h 106 , perilche p 400 . Syllables ( ar , are , an , exne ) have groups too. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3022 f. 50, via Gallica (btv1b90601558). In a code of this design each group is the initial of the word with a number; in the illustrative addition apresso is a 327 , Cartagenia c 327 , soa santità s 395 , and common syllables get groups of their own. The letter to Garbino follows the same design with its own lists: its groups run to a323, b215, c325, p383, s387. The same code is used in the signed letters of Hieronimo Ranzo in BnF fr. 2988 ff. 2 and 9–10 and fr. 3019 f. 73. Ranzo was a Vercelli nobleman at Charles V’s court, of the family of Gattinara’s mother. Norbert Biermann discussed the addition sheet alongside Ranzo’s code in a 2017 Cipherbrain thread; it is of the same design but, as above, not the same key. The Garbino letter is very likely Ranzo’s. The letter is bound in français 3022 among imperial papers of 1527–28 that reached French hands, next to letters of the Marquis del Vasto; those are in different ciphers and have their own page .

The catalogue says “no decipherment noted”, and the obvious place for a French decipherment was checked first. The eighteenth-century Clairambault copies were searched. Clairambault 327 ff. 279–280 copies no. 20 as “Lettre non signée écrite au seigneur Garbino du 11 d’avril 1528 … partie en chiffre, partie non”, with the cipher copied and nothing deciphered. Clairambault 314 f. 337 copies the addition sheet. Neither carries a decipherment, and none turned up in the neighbouring français volumes. Cipherbrain (Klaus Schmeh, 2016, with comments by Norbert Biermann and Thomas in 2017) found no known nomenclator for Ranzo’s code.

On 14 October 2026 a Cryptoole alert led to Paolo Rosson’s page “The Venetian? cipher with superscript digits of 1528” (Cryptoole IT1520-1, listed solved on 6 October 2026 with George Lasry). Working with Claude, from this project’s transcription of no. 20 and of Ranzo’s letters in fr. 2988, he built a key table of 779 values (117 sure, 595 probable, 67 guesses). Numbers 0–5 are nulls, 6–9 spell single letters, 10 and above index a list of stems under the initial. He estimates about 85 % of tokens right, and checked the transcription against the images, finding that in fr. 2988 57 “g” are s and 63 “t” are r (two hands). No palaeographer has checked the reading. His key and corrections were applied here to the existing transcriptions ( measure_rosson.py ). The fit is not independent, since the key was built on them. The decoded text is coherent Italian of 1528. On the last page of Ranzo’s letter, for example, the writer says that fornari has left for Italy with Julian to carry a sum of money for exchange payments to the army; earlier in the same letter he tells the addressee to address letters through Hieronimo Ranzo and to mention nothing of them in his others. The blind controls of his page (87.6 % and 93.4 % on made-up codes) were not rerun here. The earlier verdict that no. 20 was blocked for lack of key material was therefore wrong in one respect: a key could be built, by a reader who could look at the images and the clear stretches together. This project’s annealer, validated on a control, had stopped at function words.

An initial-letter code is usually weak for one reason: if each letter’s list is in alphabetical order, the number tells you roughly where in the dictionary the word sits. That was the first thing tested. The distribution of the numbers within each initial was compared with where frequent Italian words fall in an alphabetical list, against shuffled orders. No. 20 scores z = −0.5. The same test run on Castiglione’s letters encoded with a genuinely alphabetical code scores about +6.5. Ranzo’s numbering is not alphabetical , so a number says nothing about its word beyond the initial. What is left is a word substitution under one constraint, the initial letter, with about 550 group types in no. 20 and 730 in Ranzo’s own letters. All 1,315 groups of no. 20 were transcribed from full-resolution scans, and about 2,600 more from the six Ranzo pages. The two share 316 group types, which confirms the key is one table. An annealer then assigned each group a word with the right initial, treating the z groups as nulls, and scored the result with a word-bigram model built from Castiglione’s Lettere (diplomatic Italian written from Spain in these same years) and Guicciardini. It was first run on a control: 3,900 words of Castiglione held out of the model and encoded the same way. Test Tokens right Group types right Control, 3,900 encoded words of Castiglione about 46 % about 9 % No. 20 and Ranzo, 3,900 groups Same function words on every restart; content words vary from run to run That is the limit of the method, and the control shows it. Frequent words come out, because their contexts fix them: c170 che , i100 il , p149 per , n38 non , r41 re , s233 sua , m170 mi , p246 più . The words that carry the news occur once or twice each and do not. Nor was there a crib to be had. No Ranzo page repeats a passage of no. 20 (the longest shared run is a stock three-group phrase), the copy marked “dup.ª” duplicates another Ranzo letter rather than this one, and the Clairambault copy carries no decipherment. The other “pièces en chiffre” of fr. 2988 are a different, French, symbol cipher.

The code is open at the margin. Ranzo’s letters in fr. 2988 are deciphered; what remains is no. 20, 0.6 point short of the bar, where both keys’ readings should be compared with the images page by page, and fr. 4050 and fr. 6638, which this project has not seen and where Lasry’s tentative values have no second key to confirm them. Ranzo’s own base table would settle the rest: any of his letters that was deciphered at the time or survives in clear. The places to look are Gattinara’s papers in the Archivio di Stato di Vercelli, the imperial correspondence in Simancas and Vienna, and the other side of the Garbino network. The transcriptions and the solver are ready for a key or a crib; with even a few hundred words of known plaintext the substitution would close quickly.

Però de qui avanti li advertirai meglio, et farai le line e de la scripta con inchiostro più larghe l'una da l'altra, perchè meglio si possano poi legere quelle scripte con la cte. Et quanto a la detta materia de [?Milano], io non la posso quasi credere, et mi [?maraviglio] che per le più recente tre non ne ha detto altro; cercarai bonamente de sape[s]rne più oltre et darne aviso, perchè è cosa [?incerta] di fatto. Io spero che non mi mancarano li officii deputati in Napoli, pur che le cose de quello regno si [?spie]ghino per soa Maestà, sì como spero, attento quanto tu e Iacomo me ne haveti scripto. Il che, con havere etiam detti officii, saria cosa che più ne potesse [?rende]re de quante al presente haver potesse, maxime per exaltacion de [?Agostino] nostro. Et de tutto spero havere resolution avanti [?Pasqua], la qual ti notificaro subito. E perchè penso de valermi forse de uno [?despecto] per passare in ogni evento più certamenti, che è de mostrar partirmi di qua disconten[t]o per repatriare, haria grandemente a car che havesi in pronto el salvo conducto [?rechiest]o, di che aspetto con desiderio aviso. Dio [?elegga] de tutto il meglio et me [?guardi] et con[?duc]a [?salvament]o. Et le lettere che ti scribero per terra et adrizaro ad Adano [?Centurione] saranno breve, como lui ha recordato. Altro non mi accade che dire al presente, remettendomi a quanto ho scripto per le altre. De Madrid, a venti sei de marzo mille cinquecento venti otto. Sono a dì trenta uno. "His Majesty" (*soa Maestà*) is Charles V; "cte" is the liquid used for the secret lines, left as written. ## Translation To the other letters [?today] I have replied, to the three mentioned in them. I have also received another by way of [?Lyon], [?dated] [L78] [?twelve] February, with some lines written with the cte on the matter of [?Milan]; but most of them could not be read, because you did not take care to write them with the pen so full of the cte, and that it should leave the rest, though incorporated in the [?paper]. So from now on you will take better care, and you will make the lines of the writing in ink wider apart from one another, so that those written with the cte can then be read better. And as for the said matter of [?Milan], I can hardly believe it, and I [?wonder] that in the three most recent he has said nothing more of it; you will try in good faith to learn more of it and send word, because it is a thing [?uncertain] in fact. Of the office I affirm what I have written in the others, and not so that the work done or to be done by Stefano de [g171] may [p196] and His Caesarean Majesty and [L39] in [?vain]. I hope that the offices assigned in Naples will not fail me, provided that the affairs of that kingdom are [?settled] for His Majesty, as I hope, considering what you and Iacomo have written to me about it. And I do not yet despair that, if the death of [?Sor] Pere[?a] in Rome, assigned by [n83], [?shall] have been [?true], His Majesty may perhaps make use of me in that place, and will at once send me there to stay in his [?affairs] with good [?treatment] and also [?enjoying] the profit of the said offices in their absence from them; for these lords have spoken of it, and the Grand Chancellor wishes it and is working for it. Which, with having the said offices as well, would be a thing that could [?yield] more than I could have at present, especially for the advancement of our [?Agostino]. And on all of it I hope to have a decision before [?Easter], which I shall notify you at once. And because I think perhaps of making use of a [?grudge] so as to get across more surely in any event — that is, to make a show of leaving here discontented to go home — I would be very glad if you had ready the [?requested] safe-conduct, of which I await news with longing. But take care above all, as you hold my life dear, not to communicate this to anyone in the world other than your mother, for you see already how much the secret [p141] more [r194]. May God [?choose] the best of all and [?guard] me and [?bring] me to [?safety]. I affirm that I have given our Cataneo another large packet of letters, which you will receive [?safely]; and keep on writing continually all the news under the assigned names, until you know of my actual [?departure] from this side, because it will serve several purposes. And the letters that I shall write to you by land and address to Adano [?Centurione] will be short, as he has advised. I have nothing else to say at present, referring myself to what I have written in the others. From Madrid, the twenty-sixth of March, one thousand five hundred and twenty-eight. It is the thirty-first. Since then I have received another of yours in cipher, dated the fourth of this month, in answer to which it is enough to tell you that I have seen what you have gone through with messer [?Simon] about the matter of the coming, which I was pleased to hear; and on it I shall make every effort to have obtained here what is needed for that purpose, as I shall write more fully later, not having time now to go on further. Again, farewell. Your father greets you. Dove resi darti loco de intendere giorno per giorno il tutto, et nel medemo instante farne recordo, acciò quando poi tu me scribe potesi de ogni coso dar particular et [?distinct]o aviso, sapendo tu quanto simile [?discors]i e possiano giovare a me et a te; sì che farailo nel advenire con grande studio. Con tutto che mi haverai a scribere di novo che sia da mostrare a soa Maestà, scriberailo per lettere a parte in [?canceller]esco et ben ordinatamente con zifra grande nostro presente, sotto el modo io facio, sottoscribendole in nome de [h51] o de messer Carlo Gazino, et adrizatole qua a Hieronimo Ranzo con lettera contrafatta, che non se per tua; non facio de tale lettere alcuna mencion in le altre tre lettere, perchè in ogni evento potessi negare di saperne cos[a] alcuna. Mandato de qui avanti tutte le lettere che mi scriberai adrizate in [?mia] absentia a messer Bartolomeo Manno [?mercante]; li lassaro ordine in mia che dia al secretario quelle che saranno adrizate al detto Hieronimo Ranzo de [?zoe], che io niuno haverò da lassare copia di zifra. Et considera che le tale lettere haverano da esser viste da imperatore et da tutti questi signori di consiglio, con li quali ti ho posto in bona opinion; et però sforzati tanto più a farle ben ornate e con [?prudentia], acciò più presto si [?augmenti] che si ha a sminuire la bona opinion di te impressa. Et non mi [?pare] che sia inconveniente a scribere tu in zifra sotto el predetto modo, perchè sempre haverai form de dare o far dare le lettere che manderai per [?mare] ad alcun amico [?securo] che le porti certamente, de modo che non te hanon da esser tolte in [?preda]; et per assicurarli più farai ne alcuna altre [?fogli]a che mand pari [?public]a sotto lettere de [?alcuno], et le [?secrete] adrizerai in [?Barcellona] a [b25] [t66]o, o in Valentia a Bernabè Grimaldo, o in Cartagenia a Nicolò de Fornari et compagnia, con ordine che le mandino subito a me, e et mia absentia al detto Bartolomeo Manno. Maggior inconveniente incontro io in quello che a te scribese in zifra, perchè le lettere a te scripte possano più facilmente [?cader]e in [?preda] a mano de governanti che quelle che tu scriberai sotto il modo antedetto; et però io non ti scribero in zifra senza grande necessità et modo certo. Ho inteso quanto hai scripto havere passato teco [n84] sopra el fatto de la venuta. Et perchè per me non fa al presente esser intromiso in questo, nè altro da la corte, dovendo occuparmi in servitio di imperatore, et satisfacendomi più exercitarme in officii perpetui e utili, con li quali possia [?sustenta]re la vita mia honesta et exaltare casa nostra, che in cose momentanee et per [?consequent]e ingrato, di che, oltre el [?tlgar] proverbio, ne sono già, como sai, ben scarmentato; però se intendesi che me ne volesseno dare alcuna cura, dirai che sai de certo che non mi trovarano più qua, et che [?debb]o senza dubio esser partito per repatriare, acciò con [?honesta] ne posia esser excusato; et avisarai me di seguito. Di officio de [?general] di stato de [?Milano] non è da farse più [?cas]o, perchè non è dubio che, poi la morte de Borbon, ha conosciuto soa Maestà convenire che in ogni evento restituia in quello stato el [?duca], et a niuno modo poterlo [?reten]e per se, volendo quietare Italia como desidera et si sforza a fare; de modo che è resoluto in questo, nè altro po fare. Per il che, e perchè durante le guerre non si po exercitare esso officio, qual non si po [?calcul]are stabile, io son consigliato et persuaso da [c146] et da altri intimi amici che non faci per me perdermi [?dietro] a speranze vane, et che più presto procura alcun altro officio honesto et utile per tutta vita mia; perchè, havendo già cosa stabile per il mantenimento mio et de casa mia, mi procurara soa signoria sempre a la giornata altri [?exercitii] e cure extraordinarie, tale che con esse posia exalt[?armi]. Però, essendomi [?resolut]o in questo, procura soa signoria de farmi provedere de una presidentia in la camera de la sumaria de Napoli, che ha vacato, e di officio che haveva il [?quondam] [?Sor], et risegno in detto loco, essendo ambi officii molto principali, honesti et utili ad vitam; et se non lo preiudica una [?dificulta] di esser stato [?dotor] e quello per chi è vacata detta presidentia, spero haverla, perchè il favor che mi fa il detto gran cancelliero confido che superara li molti [?compet]itori che al detto officio de presidentia sono, abenchè li sia chi per esso solo [?offre] quatro milia ducati, attenta la bona volunta che soa Maestà mi dimostra et la [?deliberatione] de volersi serve di me in cose [?importante]; di che si vedera presto la resolution. [m66] Translation letter2_en.md # Letter 2 (BnF fr. 2988 ff. 9r-10v; parallel copy fr. 20506 ff. 136-138): Hieronimo Ranzo, Madrid, March 1528 — English Translation of `letter2_reading.md` (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026), with the same holes: `[?word]` = a tentative value (Lasry's seen once or twice, or Rosson's alone), `[h51]` = a code with no value. "His Majesty" (*soa Maestà*) and "the Emperor" are Charles V; "His Lordship" (*soa signoria*) is the Grand Chancellor Gattinara. `cte` (the liquid for secret lines) and `tlgar` are left as written. ## Translation As I have written to you many times already, you are very sparing in your reports of events, so that if I had not been more fully informed by Iacomo through a letter of his of [?ten] February, received with the three of mine of the eighth, I could have given His Majesty little [?information] about them, and above all about the things that happened in [?Savoy], of which no other report was [?enclosed], nor did other letters arrive with them. Wherever you have the chance to learn everything day by day, make a note of it at that very moment, so that when you then write to me you can give particular and [?distinct] news of everything, knowing how much such [?accounts] can help me and you; so do it in future with great care. Whenever you have anything new to write to me that is to be shown to His Majesty, write it in separate letters in a [?chancery] hand and in good order with our large cipher sent herewith, in the way I do, signing them in the name of [h51] or of messer Carlo Gazino, and addressing them here to Hieronimo Ranzo with a counterfeited letter, so that it is not taken for yours; make no mention of such letters in the other three letters, so that in any event you can deny knowing anything about it. From now on send all the letters you write to me addressed, in my absence, to messer Bartolomeo Manno, [?merchant]; I shall leave him orders in mine that he give to the secretary those that are addressed to the said Hieronimo Ranzo of [?zoe], since I shall have to leave nobody a copy of the cipher. And consider that such letters will have to be seen by the Emperor and by all these lords of the council, with whom I have put you in good opinion; and therefore strive all the more to make them well composed and with [?prudence], so that the good opinion impressed of you may rather [?increase] than diminish. And it does not [?seem] to me inconvenient for you to write in cipher in the aforesaid way, because you will always have the means of giving, or having given, the letters you send by [?sea] to some [?safe] friend who will carry them surely, so that they need not be taken from you as [?booty]; and to secure them further you will make some other [?leaf] that looks [?public] under letters of [?someone], and you will address the [?secret] ones in [?Barcelona] to [b25] [t66]o, or in Valencia to Bernabè Grimaldo, or in Cartagena to Nicolò de Fornari and company, with orders that they send them at once to me, and in my absence to the said Bartolomeo Manno. And sometimes, if you [?fear] that the letters in cipher [?may] be looked at and not let through, especially those you send by land, you can make use of another new cipher that I am sending you with the said Cataneo, with which you can write briefly in [?small]; and to arrange everything better you can share with Iacomo both the practice of the cipher and the news you will have to give day by day, because in this way you will train yourself sooner and better in everything. I meet a greater difficulty in what I write to you in cipher, because the letters written to you can more easily [?fall] as [?booty] into the hands of the governors than those you will write in the aforesaid way; and therefore I will not write to you in cipher without great necessity and a sure means. And sometimes I shall use the cte, and when I do, you will notice it at the beginning of the letters, which will [?begin] "Fili dilectissime" (Dearest son), whereas I am used to writing "Amantissime fili" (Most loving son); and I shall use the Lyon route, through Polo [?Sper]ato, partner. Take care also always to keep the ciphers and my letters written in cipher, and the copies of those that you too write in cipher, so surely hidden that if the three written ones were searched for they would never be found; and with the said means you can deny everything with good boldness and [?firmness]. I have understood what you write that [n84] has gone through with you about the matter of the coming. And because it does not suit me at present to be involved in this, nor in anything else away from the court, since I must occupy myself in the Emperor's service, and since it satisfies me more to exercise myself in perpetual and profitable offices, with which I can [?sustain] my life honourably and raise up our house, than in momentary things and [?consequently] thankless ones, of which, besides the [?tlgar] proverb, I have already, as you know, been well taught by experience; therefore, if you heard that they wanted to give me some charge in it, you will say that you know for certain that they will not find me here any longer, and that I [?must] without doubt have left to go home, so that I may [?honestly] be excused from it; and you will inform me at once. Of the office of [?general] of the State of [?Milan] there is no more [?account] to be made, because there is no doubt that since the death of Bourbon His Majesty has recognised that it is fitting in any event to restore the [?duke] to that state, and in no way to [?keep] it for himself, since he wishes to pacify Italy, as he desires and strives to do; so that he is resolved on this and can do nothing else. For which reason, and because during the wars that office cannot be exercised, and it cannot be [?reckoned] stable, I am advised and persuaded by [c146] and by other intimate friends that it does not suit me to lose myself [?chasing] vain hopes, and that I should rather seek some other honourable and profitable office for my whole life; because, having already something stable for the maintenance of myself and my house, His Lordship will always procure for me, day by day, other [?employments] and extraordinary charges, such that with them I may [?advance myself]. Therefore, having [?resolved] on this, His Lordship is working to have me provided with a presidency in the Camera della Sommaria of Naples, which has fallen vacant, and with the office held by the [?late] [?Sor], and I resign in the said place, both offices being very important, honourable and profitable for life; and if it is not prejudiced by a [?difficulty] — that he for whom the said presidency fell vacant was a [?doctor] — I hope to have it, because I trust that the favour the said Grand Chancellor shows me will overcome the many [?competitors] there are for the said office of the presidency, although there is one who offers four thousand ducats for it alone, considering the good will that His Majesty shows me and the [?decision] to make use of me in [?important] matters; of which the decision will soon be seen. [v27] [g73] [?informed]: Tomaso de Fornari, who has left for Italy [?together with] [?Giuliano] to [?carry] a sum of money for the payment of the bills of exchange which he and [s327] have made payable to the [?army], has worked hard, through the said [?Giuliano], to be provided with the office of receiver in the said [?army], and would not otherwise make the exchange; and [?cort], because [s213] in that necessity, as he has done at great loss and risk to himself, he has [?referred] him to the [?ministers] with [?tlgare] letters of recommendation from His Majesty, which is a [?little] of [a89]; and he has fed himself on this [?smoke], and I judge his affairs badly. But let everything stay buried in you and your mother, and of me always say that I am to go home. Do not cease to seek the safe-conduct [r61] for every good [?reason], and send me word. I send you another addition to the cipher herewith, with which you will [?go over] it and [?add] to it in order what it lacks, and then you will send it to [h51] and let me know.
