Di che soa excellentia ne haverà posuto conoscere bon [?segno] quando soa Maestà [d135]e a li ambasciadori de la lega a la [?totale] poi [?summa] restaur[?atio]ne de soa excellentia; facio ancora conoscerli non esser questo novo in soa mente, secondo che etiam ho [?advisat]o soa excellentia per de Hiero, de ordine di cavalier Bilia, suo amico, el qual [L87] para [d161]o in compagnia de li altri ambasciadori[…]nti e [g7] malicio[…]. Il signor gran cancelliero li è in vero bon amico, et [?sforzo]ne io di esserlo tanto [?studios]o in quello che so et posso como se tutta mia vita havese mangiato el pane de soa excellentia, sì como ne potra e bon [?testimonio] el proprio orator suo. Tutto questo reste in voi, se non havete modo de farlo intendere certissimamente a soa excellentia solo. ⟨Per il Sor Prior de Barleta ho procurato & procuro quanto posso, como ne potra esser certificato da li soi agenti qua, essendo li seruitor di Cor:; hauete credo(?) receputo le lettere de soa Maesta per soi ministri che vi ho mandato sopra il bisogno del dicto Sor Prior, et se in altra cosa me vorra adoperare me trouera semper promptissimo ad ogni suo seruicio, et cosi li potrete far intendere, che dubitando del recapito de le lettere non li scriuo in resposta de una soa, et in soa bona gratia mi racomandarete.⟩ Soa Maestà ha proveduto in Italia de [?quasi] [?seicento] milia ducati, et pagara altri [?sette] [?cento] che [?Ansaldo] ha pigliato [?nova]mente in [?Milano] da [?mess]; aspetta [?saper] quello sia seguito de li exerciti nel regno, et [?pensa] che hano fatto giornata, et ne [?sper]a bene, attento li avisi[…]i da [?Genova]. ⟨In la fabrica et armamento de le 50 Galer si procede con dilligencia, et soa Maesta ha gia racolto in questo regno de Castillia un millione de ducati, et altri 500 millia ne cauara de la Corto de li tre Regni de Aragon che va a tenere, et da le Indie ne aspeta etiam bona summa.⟩ Li è stato proposto et recordato de valersi di oro et argenti superflui de le giesie per [?alcuni] [?anni] in presto, dicendo esser cosa a niuno preiudiciale, et che ne [?cave]ria di subito una infinita de denari, essendo richisime; ma non lo ha [?ancor] voluto fare, [?reserv]ato questo tal [?suplement]o a maggior necessità. Pur, se la guerra perseverara, credo metera mano ad ogni cosa, perchè è [?deliberat]o [?giu]carli di resto. Ma in [?vano] è [?pensa]re de metteli in [?capo] el recordo di consiglio [c164] in Italia, non obstante quante ragion se li possano [?allegar]e et quante se posia [?imagina]re, che non ne [o208]no sentir parlare; et però bisogna lassir quella consideracion da canto. La più [?pericolos]a cos[a] che [?regna] in [?cort]e è la inresolution, che mai o tanto [?tardi] si resolveno in tutte, che ogni effecto loro è le più volte [?fora] di tempo, che se Dio non li havese aiutati, [?questi] [?ministr]i stariano freschi. Ne [f291] qui se sono [?ancor] resoluti de li [?provision] che ha da mandare in Italia, si pigli la [?restitution] de Roma, como per il governo di regno de Napoli: alcuna volta si è parlato di gran cancelliero, et alcuna de [d306], et alcuna di [?arcivescovo] de Toledo, poi de altri secundi, et mo de niuno se parla più, aspettato intendere prima alcun [?success]o de detti exerciti. Sì che vedete como se governano qua le cose, et se così facilmente se resolu[e68] in simil materia como quella di sopra detto consiglio. Et non vedendo che [?alcun] basti a remediare tali inconvenienti, resto talmenti [?atonit]o che ogni [?calculo] [?perdo]. Ho vi voluto far questa [b215], perchè, conoscendo quanto [?differe]no questi [?giudici] da le consideracion vostre, non vi [?havere]te più a [?funda]re in li soliti dissigni, salvo [?guida]rli de qui avanti secundum subiectam materiam. Ben vi prego che, poi mi allargo con voi confidentementi de simile cose, [?tenet]i il tutto in voi, che già vedete quanto importa ponere os in celum. ⟨& per giornata vi raguaglerò etiam de quanto piu oltra sucederà.⟩ Qua si conosce optimamente quanto convien a soa Maestà la amicitia con Venetiani, et ne ha qua molto tentato in secreto lo orator suo; ma lui non ha voluto prest[?ar]e orechie, dicendo non poterlo fare senza ordine de la Signoria; et però ha dato [?commission] [?chiar]a a suoi ministri in [?Italia] che la procurano per quante vie potrano, [?etiam] con mand[?ar]e persona [?accord]ata a recordandoli il [c92]. Ma mi dubito che li disfidi poi seguiti [?non] preiudichino quella [?inclina]cion. Voglia Dio che ne riesca alcun [?frutto]; et [g138] detti Venetiani si volesseno [?accord]are a la pratica, ho per certo che haveriano da soa Maestà tutte le honeste conditioni che sapesino [?demand]are, et senza alcun dubio de inobservantia, perchè, oltre che soa Maestà è observatore di fede, conosce perfettamente già convenirli più la dis[?avantaggi]osa pace con loro che qui si voglia utile [?discor]dia. A lo amico [?Sanchez], che s deve già esser [?venut]o da Venetia, acciò el Naqua[?gie]ro possia etiam [?lev]arse di qua. ⟨Qua restaua la Imperatrice con il Consiglio de Castilla, perche la e gia nel setimo mese de la soa grauidanza; el Principe primo genito sara jurato qua la prima septimana da tutti questi regni, & heredo et legitimo successor di essa. Altro non mi acade che dire al presente; a voi de core mi offero. (?) De Madrid xj de aprili 1528. Vro.⟩ ⟨Post datum non e poi innouato altro; hogi hano jurato el prencipe, & lo Imperatore partira per Valencia a li xxij. Datum ut supra, die 19.⟩ Translation letter3_en.md # Letter 3 (BnF fr. 3022 no. 20, ff. 44r-47r): [Hieronimo Ranzo] to "Garbino", Madrid, 11 April 1528 — English Translation of `letter3_reading.md` (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026), with the same holes: `[?word]` = a tentative value (Lasry's seen once or twice, or Rosson's alone), `[q24]` = a code with no value; ⟨ ⟩ = in clear in the letter. "His Majesty" (*soa Maestà*) is Charles V; "His Excellency" (*soa excellentia*) the Duke of Milan, Francesco II Sforza; the Grand Chancellor is Gattinara. ## Translation ⟨Reverend sir, as a brother. Since having written to you in several letters addressed⟩ to [?Genoa] by the hand of Hieronimo, ⟨I have received yours of 23 November, 3 and 28 December and 4 February, most welcome, to which I have not made a particular answer⟩, and I have [?made up for it] with what I have written continually to Hieronimo, whom I have ordered always to send you a sure copy of [?testimonio], since, finding myself without any help, and notwithstanding the [?occupations] that are continually given me here, I have [?served] both with one writing. And now I have not wanted to fail to make you the present, more particular answer to all your said letters, without however repeating the [a64] [d27] of the events here, since through the said Hiero you will have understood everything; who also tells me he has sent you a copy of our cipher, which you will be able to use. ⟨I have continually urged on the lord Grand Chancellor your coming here, letting him understand your wish and the account that he should hold of it and of all your other qualities; but although he knows it all and responds to it no less, his means are still so tight so far that not only can he not extend himself to what he would wish and what would be needed, but he has even had to cut down his expenses, inasmuch as His Majesty does not provide for him according to what his authority, quality and the merits of such great service, and His Majesty's promises, require; which he still hopes will not be much longer put off. And so he has concluded to me, after many conversations, that it much displeases him not to be able at present to take you in and keep you, and still less to place you in some other way as would be right; but that, having any opportunity of doing so, you will at once be called by him, as he holds you in special memory and esteem. And therefore I would not know how to advise you to come here, fearing that, things standing thus, you would not find what would persuade you and what you need; nor has there been any way to bring about your going to the camp in the manner and with the help suggested, which I promise you I have worked for not a little; but things here proceed so differently from what is being contrived there, though in fact, as I shall let you understand more fully some day, that no foundation can be laid on one's own ideas. With all this I shall never fail to work for you as I would for myself;⟩ and if I am to come to Italy with [q24] good [c98], as I hope [?must] soon follow, you will [?share], to your heart's content, in all my fortune, as I have always told you. On which, God willing, I hope to be resolved in any case, having [?gone] to Valencia, where His Majesty [?leaves] for on the twentieth of this month; ⟨and you will be informed of what follows.⟩ ⟨I have always given your letters to the aforesaid lord Grand Chancellor, and continually communicated to him what you have also written to me, and all of it has been welcome to him,⟩ and he [?asks] you to continue, [?since] you have a [?copy] of the said ⟨z15; he is at present struck by his usual gout; God grant that he be cured before His Majesty's departure.⟩ [q118]a [L57] the [?particulars] that you have assigned concerning the lord Duke, he has also been very glad to learn your news after [d227]; and His Lordship greatly desires that His Excellency [?securely] [?keep] himself in the good graces of His Majesty, as he is at present, so that His Majesty may be assured of [?carlo] his [?mind] being [?bent] on his usual [?devotion] and service to His Majesty, and that his contrary [?deeds] [?done] were not voluntary but [?forced]; because he does not doubt that this is the [?true] and [?only] way to [?bring] him to [?port]. Of which His Excellency will have been able to see a good [?sign] when His Majesty [d135] to the ambassadors of the League at the [?total] then [?sum] restoration of His Excellency; I also make him understand that this is not new in his mind, as I have also [?informed] His Excellency through Hiero, by order of Cavalier Bilia, his friend, who [L87] seems [d161] in the company of the other ambassadors […] and [g7] malicio[…]. The lord Grand Chancellor is truly a good friend to him, and I [?strive] to be one, as [?zealous] in what I know and can do as if I had eaten His Excellency's bread all my life, as his own ambassador can be good [?witness] of it. Let all this stay with you, if you have no way of making it understood most surely to His Excellency alone. ⟨For the lord Prior of Barletta I have worked and am working as much as I can, as he can be assured by his agents here, being servants of Cor:; you have, I think, received the letters of His Majesty to his ministers that I sent you about the said lord Prior's need; and if he wishes to employ me in anything else, he will find me always most ready for any service of his; and so you can let him understand that, being in doubt about the delivery of the letters, I do not write to him in answer to one of his; and you will commend me to his good graces.⟩ His Majesty has provided in Italy [?nearly] [?six hundred] thousand ducats, and will pay another [?seven] [?hundred] that [?Ansaldo] has [?newly] taken up in [?Milan] from [?mess]; he waits to [?know] what has happened to the armies in the Kingdom [of Naples], and [?thinks] that they have given battle, and [?hopes] well of it, considering the news […] from [?Genoa]. ⟨In the building and arming of the 50 galleys they proceed with diligence, and His Majesty has already collected a million ducats in this kingdom of Castile, and he will draw another 500 thousand from the Cortes of the three kingdoms of Aragon which he is going to hold, and from the Indies he also expects a good sum.⟩ It has been proposed and suggested to him to make use of the superfluous gold and silver of the churches as a loan for [?some] [?years], saying it is a thing prejudicial to no one, and that it would at once yield an infinity of money, as they are very rich; but he has not [?yet] wanted to do it, having [?reserved] this [?supplement] for greater need. Still, if the war goes on, I believe he will lay hands on everything, because he is [?determined] to [?play] his last card. But it is [?vain] to [?think] of putting into their [?heads] the suggestion of a council [c164] in Italy, notwithstanding however many reasons may be [?alleged] to them and however many can be [?imagined], for they [o208] not hear it spoken of; and so that consideration must be left aside. The most [?dangerous] thing that [?reigns] at [?court] is irresolution, for they never, or so [?late], resolve in everything, that their every effect is most times [?out] of season; so that if God had not helped them, [?these] [?ministers] would be in a fine state. Nor [f291] have they here [?yet] resolved on the [?provisions] to be sent to Italy, both for the [?restitution] of Rome and for the government of the Kingdom of Naples: at times there has been talk of the Grand Chancellor, at times of [d306], and at times of the [?Archbishop] of Toledo, then of other, secondary men, and now no one is spoken of any longer, as they wait first to hear of some [?outcome] of the said armies. So you see how things are governed here, and whether they so easily resolve [e68] in a matter like that of the said council above. And not seeing that [?anything] is enough to remedy such troubles, I remain so [?astonished] that I [?lose] all [?reckoning]. I wanted to make you this [b215] because, knowing how much these [?judgements] [?differ] from your considerations, you will no longer have to [?ground] yourself on the usual designs, except to [?guide] them from now on according to the matter in hand. I do beg you, since I open myself to you confidentially on such things, to [?keep] it all to yourself, for you see already how much it matters to set one's mouth against heaven. ⟨And day by day I shall also inform you of whatever further happens.⟩ Here it is very well known how much friendship with the Venetians suits His Majesty, and his ambassador here has sounded it out a good deal in secret; but he would not lend an ear, saying he could not do it without orders from the Signoria; and so he has given [?clear] [?commission] to his ministers in [?Italy] to seek it by every way they can, [?even] by [?sending] a person [?agreed] upon, reminding them of the [c92]. But I fear that the defiances that have since followed [?will] prejudice that [?inclination]. May God grant that some [?fruit] come of it; and [g138] the said Venetians were willing to [?agree] to the negotiation, I hold it certain that they would have from His Majesty all the honourable conditions they could [?ask], and without any doubt of non-observance, because, besides His Majesty being a keeper of faith, he already knows perfectly that a [?disadvantageous] peace with them suits him better than any profitable [?discord]. To the friend [?Sanchez], who must already have [?come] from Venice, so that [?Navagero] may also [?leave] here. ⟨The Empress was staying here with the Council of Castile, because she is already in the seventh month of her pregnancy; the Prince, the first-born, will be sworn here in the first week by all these kingdoms as heir and legitimate successor to them. I have nothing else to say at present; to you I offer myself with all my heart. (?) From Madrid, 11 April 1528. Yours.⟩ ⟨After the date nothing else new has happened; today they have sworn the Prince, and the Emperor will leave for Valencia on the 22nd. Dated as above, the 19th.⟩ Letter 4: BnF fr. 4050 ff. 79-81 decoded, not read Hieronimo Ranzo, Madrid, 10 March 1528, to his agent: Cavalier Bilia's commission to inform the Duke (of Milan) through Ranzo; the declarations of war; Charles V's offer to the League envoys at Poza to restore the Duke, which they refused; advice to keep to the safer side; ships armed in Biscay seize 46 French vessels off Bordeaux; the Doña Guiomar money business and messer Iacomo; news to Garbino; a cipher addition sent. A mechanical decode with holes in most sentences: shown so that the transcription and the key can be checked and improved, not as a reading. Three Latin letters of the Palatine envoy Johann Joachim von Rusdorff to Axel Oxenstierna, London, February 1625 (Riksarkivet E 701, DECODE R4336–R4337, catalogued The Hague 1628). George Lasry recovered the key from the cipher alone: a homophonic table with numbers 24 apart and an alphabetical three-digit nomenclator. The Swedish and Danish offers for the Palatinate, the French marriage and a French subsidy; two codes open. 38 32 24 34 56 19 25 62 86 49 37 73 38 · 678 bus · 517 to s e c r e t i s s i m i s · propositionibus · legato 16 40 64 = a · 32 56 80 = e · 744 = Rex · 760 = Rusdorff London → Axel Oxenstierna · homophonic table and alphabetical nomenclator · February 1625 · key recovered by George Lasry Rusdorff to Oxenstierna: London, February 1625 to Axel Oxenstierna Go to the full text ↓ Three Latin letters from the Palatine envoy in London to the Swedish chancellor, on the plans to restore the Palatinate and Prince Charles’s French marriage. George Lasry recovered their key from the cipher alone. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete Contributed by George Lasry (solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letters Johann Joachim von Rusdorff, envoy of the exiled Elector Palatine Frederick V in London, to Axel Oxenstierna: 15/25 February 1625, 26 February 1625 (old style), and the opening of a third, undated letter. All in Latin. Where Riksarkivet, Stockholm, Oxenstierna af Södermöre, Ser. B, E 701; DECODE R4336 and R4337, catalogued as The Hague, 1628, not deciphered. The cipher Key words only. Each letter has three two-digit numbers 24 apart (A = 16, 40, 64), and three-digit codes stand for names and words in alphabetical order (187 Britannicus … 760 Rusdorff). How it was solved George Lasry transcribed the five photographs in CTTS, took the letter table from its built-in cryptanalysis and the 24-step rule, and recovered the codes with Claude Opus 5.5 from context and the Latin endings written beside them. Re-checked here mechanically and statistically. What it says London welcomes the secret Swedish proposals but leans to Christian IV of Denmark, whose terms are modest; Buckingham prepares to fetch the French bride, but the papal dispensation and Parliament stand in the way; France offers 500,000 livres to the confederation. Credit Key, transcription, edited Latin and translation by George Lasry (pull request 72, 21 October 2026). Still open Codes 628 and 701, and 24 code readings marked tentative. The pages missing from the photographs. These two DECODE records were filed on this site with three other Rusdorff letters from the same volume, R4333–R4335 . Those are a different cipher, with their own page: R4333 is in German and uses numbers from 8 to 107, which this table does not have.

The opening of the first letter. Multa possem de 38·32·24·34·56·19·25·62·86·49·37·73·38 ( secretissimis ) illis 678 bus ( propositionibus ) et 490 ne … The British envoy’s name follows as a run of letter signs: Roberto Enstrutero . Image: Riksarkivet, Stockholm, Oxenstierna af Södermöre Ser. B, E 701, Rusdorff to Oxenstierna 15/25 Feb. 1625, image 1, via DECODE R4336. Rusdorff enciphered only the words that mattered: kings, envoys, places, numbers and a few sensitive nouns. The rest of the Latin is in clear. There are two kinds of cipher group. Two-digit numbers for letters. The alphabet has 24 letters (I/J and U/V shared), and each has three numbers exactly 24 apart: A is 16, 40 or 64; B is 20, 44 or 68. Inside the first range the letters step by 4 in runs of six: A–F are 16 to 36, G–M 17 to 37, N–S 18 to 38, T–Z 19 to 39. U and V share 23. W, Y and Z do not occur in these letters. Three-digit codes for words. They run from 187 to 760 in alphabetical order of their meanings: 418 Gallia, 428 Germania, 517 Legatus, 526 Londini, 620 Palatinatus, 631 Parlamentum, 678 Propositio, 738 Rex Galliae, 740 Rex Magnae Britanniae, 744 Rex, 745 Rex Daniae, 746 Rex Sueciae, 760 Rusdorff. Rusdorff wrote the Latin ending in clear above a code: 678 bus is propositionibus , 517 to is legato . George Lasry’s key. Bold numbers occur in the letters; grey ones follow from the 24-step rule. Codes in italics with a question mark are tentative; a question mark alone is unknown. Image: George Lasry, key chart drawn from DECODE R4336–R4337 (Riksarkivet E 701).

Illustrissime Domine, Multa possem de secretissimis illis propositionibus et [490: intentione?] Regis Legato Britannico Roberto Enstrutero exposita et declarata de rebus in Germania collapsis, Palatinatu et [636: Principe?] restituendis, scribere: nam Legatus ipse, sub fide quidem religiosi silentii, cuncta mihi communicavit, et suas [701?] es le(g)endas exhiberi curavit. Sed cum sciam Invictissimum Regem Sueciae de omnibus istis tam ab [363: Electore?] , cum quo Rex Daniae ea de causa [444: Hamburgi?] convenire et colloqui statuit, quam aliunde, certiorem fieri, merito supersedeo prolixus et fastidio esse longa recitatione. Hoc saltem quasi per transennam dicam, propositiones istas summa cum animi alacritate hic acceptas, et eo magis aestimatas fuisse, quo inopinatius et contra spem in melius mutatus videbatur Regis in rem publicam animus. Jam in eo sunt ut viam ac media anquirant, quibus utrique regi , et Sueciae et Daniae , satisfieri queat: nam [598: oblationes?] utriusque tales sunt, ut nullo modo, absque detrimento boni publici, negligi possint. Pro Rege Daniae plurimae causae apud Regem Magnae Britanniae considerationem movebunt, ut sunt affinitas vetus, necessitudo, vicina [734: regnorum?] coniunctio; praesertim quod valde moderata sint ea, quae Rex exigat. Nam sex tantum millia peditum et equitum mille cum tormentis, pulvere et reliquis appertinentibus ab Rege Magnae Britanniae petit, ex sua parte quatuor peditum millia et equitum unum offerens, et reliquum onus belli a [670: Proceribus?] [429: Germaniae?] sustineri et procurari posse sperans. Sed causa ista, et quomodo cuncta accommodari possint, relicta Regis Sueciae [302: declaratione?] , belli in proximo conventu [240: Confoederatorum?] examinabitur: proinde necesse erit, ut Legati eo mittendi in eum finem sufficientibus mandatis instruantur, ne tempus inutiliter teratur, et consilia absque fructu sint, in fumum abeant magnanimi isti conatus. Si interea Ser.mus [747: Rex Sueciae?] aliquid ea de re praemonere et praecipere velit, quae sint Regis Magnae Britanniae animo melius praeparando et in priori sententia confirmando, parati promtique erimus exequendi: et hic praecipuus finis est harum literarum, quas benigna fronte Ill.ma Dom.o V.ra accipiet, et inde perspiciet me nullam occasionem praetermittere velle, qua devotum meum obsequium indicio aliquo declarem et prodam. Ill.m V.m Dom.m Deus diu incolumem florentemque in solatium attritae rei Christianae et in bonum florentissimo Regi Regnoque Sueciae conservet sospitetque. Dabam Londini 15/25 februarii 1625. V.a Ill.ma Dom.is [the subscription continues beyond the photographed page] English translation (George Lasry) Most illustrious Lord, I could write much about those most secret propositions and the [intention?] of the King , set out and declared to the British envoy Robert Anstruther , concerning the affairs that have collapsed in Germany and the restoration of the Palatinate and its [Prince?] : for the envoy himself, under the pledge of religious silence, communicated everything to me and had his [701?] shown to me to read . But since I know that the most invincible King of Sweden will be informed of all this both by the [Elector?] , with whom the King of Denmark has resolved to meet and confer on this matter at [Hamburg?] , and from elsewhere, I rightly refrain from being prolix and from wearying you with a long account. This much I will say, as if through a lattice: those propositions were received here with the greatest eagerness, and were valued all the more because the King’s disposition towards the common cause seemed, unexpectedly and against hope, to have changed for the better. They are now seeking a way and means to satisfy both kings , of Sweden and of Denmark , for the [offers?] of each are such that they cannot be neglected without harm to the public good. In favour of the King of Denmark many reasons will weigh with the King of Great Britain : the old kinship , close relationship, the neighbouring union of the [kingdoms?] ; above all, that what the King asks is very moderate . For he asks of the King of Great Britain only six thousand foot and a thousand horse , with artillery, powder and the other appurtenances, offering on his own part four thousand foot and one thousand horse, and hoping that the rest of the burden of the war can be borne and provided for by the [princes?] of [Germany?] . But this business, and how everything can be accommodated, setting aside the King of Sweden’s [declaration?] , will be examined at the next meeting of the [Confederates?] on the war : so the envoys to be sent there must be furnished with sufficient powers for that purpose, lest time be wasted, the deliberations come to nothing, and these magnanimous efforts end in smoke. If in the meantime his Serene Majesty the [King of Sweden?] wishes to advise or direct anything on this, which might serve to prepare the mind of the King of Great Britain better and to confirm him in his earlier view, we shall be ready and prompt to carry it out. And this is the chief purpose of this letter, which Your Most Illustrious Lordship will receive with a kindly countenance, and from it perceive that I wish to let pass no opportunity of declaring and showing my devoted service by some token. May God long preserve Your Most Illustrious Lordship safe and flourishing, for the comfort of the worn-down Christian cause and for the good of the most flourishing King and Kingdom of Sweden. Given at London , 15/25 February 1625.

Rusdorff (1589–1640) was Frederick V’s envoy in London from 1622 to 1627. These letters fall in the last weeks of James I’s reign; he died on 27 March (6 April) 1625. They belong to the negotiations of 1624–25 for a Protestant coalition to win back the Palatinate. Gustavus Adolphus and Christian IV both offered to lead an army in Germany, and the first letter explains why the Danish offer weighed more in London. The coalition that followed, the Hague alliance of December 1625, joined England, Denmark and the United Provinces without Sweden. Sir Robert Anstruther was the British envoy to Denmark and the German princes; Sir James Spens served both James I and Gustavus Adolphus. The second letter is about the French marriage of Prince Charles and Henrietta Maria. Buckingham went to Paris to fetch the bride in May 1625. Parliament feared that the marriage articles would suspend the laws against Catholics, as the articles of the Spanish match had promised in 1623.

George Lasry transcribed the five photographs in CTTS (CrypTool Transcriber and Solver), boxing each two-digit group, each three-digit code and each stretch of clear text. CTTS’s built-in cryptanalysis gave a first letter table; the 24-step rule completed it, and every letter sign in the five images fits it. Claude Opus 5.5 then recovered the codes from their context and the Latin endings beside them. The alphabetical order of the codes was the check: each reading must fall between its neighbours. Checked here on 21 October 2026: Mechanically. decode.py applies George’s key file to his transcription and gives the same counts: 438 cipher groups, 376 letter signs (every one with a value) and 62 codes (36 confident, 24 tentative, 2 unknown). R4336 has 183 groups, R4337 255. Statistically ( docs/_validate.py , Latin letter model, letter signs only). The reading scores −2.00 per letter; random keys of the same shape score −5.20 (7.4 standard deviations lower), and a key fitted to the same signs shuffled scores −2.72 (28.5 lower). Verdict: pass. Earlier readings. None found. DECODE still lists both records as not deciphered, with no documents attached, and nothing turned up on Cryptoole, Cryptiana or in print. An unchecked source. Kröger’s life of Rusdorf (1876, pp. 9–10) describes Rusdorf’s own papers at the Landesbibliothek in Kassel, now the Universitätsbibliothek Kassel: four folio volumes, the third of which holds “exclusively” his correspondence with Oxenstierna from 1624 to 1628. It was unprinted in Kröger’s day and has not been found online. It very probably contains Rusdorff’s clear drafts or copies of these letters, and would confirm or correct the 24 tentative codes and fill in 628 and 701. It has not been consulted.

Illustrissime Domine, Multa possem de secretissimis illis propositionibus et intentione? Regis Legato Britannico Roberto Enstrutero exposita et declarata de rebus in Germania collapsis, Palatinatu et Principe? restituendis, scribere: nam Legatus ipse, sub fide quidem religiosi silentii, cuncta mihi communicavit, et suas <701>es le(g)endas exhiberi curavit. Sed cum sciam Invictissimum Regem Sueciae de omnibus istis tam ab Electore?, cum quo Rex Daniae ea de causa Hamburgi? convenire et colloqui statuit, quam aliunde, certiorem fieri, merito supersedeo prolixus et fastidio esse longa recitatione. Hoc saltem quasi per transennam dicam, propositiones istas summa cum animi alacritate hic acceptas, et eo magis aestimatas fuisse, quo inopinatius et contra spem in melius mutatus videbatur Regis in rem publicam animus. Jam in eo sunt ut viam ac media anquirant, quibus utrique regi, et Sueciae et Daniae, satisfieri queat: nam oblationes? utriusque tales sunt, ut nullo modo, absque detrimento boni publici, negligi possint. Pro Rege Daniae plurimae causae apud Regem Magnae Britanniae considerationem movebunt, ut sunt affinitas vetus, necessitudo, vicina regnorum? coniunctio; praesertim quod valde moderata sint ea, quae Rex exigat. Nam sex tantum millia peditum et equitum mille cum tormentis, pulvere et reliquis appertinentibus ab Rege Magnae Britanniae petit, ex sua parte quatuor peditum millia et equitum unum offerens, et reliquum onus belli a Proceribus? Germaniae? sustineri et procurari posse sperans. Sed causa ista, [IMG R4336 P2] et quomodo cuncta accommodari possint, relicta Regis Sueciae declaratione?, belli in proximo conventu Confoederatorum? examinabitur: proinde necesse erit, ut Legati eo mittendi in eum finem sufficientibus mandatis instruantur, ne tempus inutiliter teratur, et consilia absque fructu sint, in fumum abeant magnanimi isti conatus. Si interea Ser.mus Rex Sueciae? aliquid ea de re praemonere et praecipere velit, quae sint Regis Magnae Britanniae animo melius praeparando et in priori sententia confirmando, parati promtique erimus exequendi: et hic praecipuus finis est harum literarum, quas benigna fronte Ill.ma Dom.o V.ra accipiet, et inde perspiciet me nullam occasionem praetermittere velle, qua devotum meum obsequium indicio aliquo declarem et prodam. Ill.m V.m Dom.m Deus diu incolumem florentemque in solatium attritae rei Christianae et in bonum florentissimo Regi Regnoque Sueciae conservet sospitetque. Dabam Londini 15/25 februarii 1625. V.a Ill.ma Dom.is [...] [IMG R4337 P1] [...] illi scopum sibi certum, nec dicunt apertius quid velint; nos etiam a vero tramite, quem calcare instituimus, non deflectemus. Quid responsum sit proprie Legato Britannico? D.no Anstrutero ad propositiones Regias, nondum adhuc plane scio: quae tamen scimus, illa Illustris Dominus Spens perscribit; ego nihil addere possum ultimis meis 25/15 febr. scriptis. Quanquam Dux Bukinga[m] magnifico et sumtuoso apparatu iter suum in Galliam adornet, et ubique ad nuptias fiant regiae praeparationes, tamen matrimonium videtur iterum aliquam tragulum et sufflaminationem pati: Dispensatio quidem a Papa concessa est, sed cum principalibus? insertis, quae videantur aliquo modo duriuscula et vix posse accipi sine aliqua concussione aut agitatione huius status; ne dicam iam Regem Galliae praetendere et petere, sicut rumor crebrescit non sine fundamento, ut a Parlamento arti(i)culi prius ratihabeantur et approbentur, quam matrimonium consumatur. Sciunt enim populum Parlamentumque, ut oppido quam vehementem zelotypiamque executionis? legum in Papistas?, non amare matrimonia cum Pontificiis?, utpote quae non possint contrahi sine larga indulgentia in <628>is Pontificiae? professores. Deinde articuli, quorum iam vulgata est notitia, videntur illis, si non duriores, attamen aeque duri ac illi, qui in favorem Hispaniae? ante biennium pacti fuerunt. Dicendum iam est, quomodo haec superanda sint: a tempore, mora et occasione, et a prudenti persuasione et Domin[...] consilia et remedia petuntur. Sed de his suo tempore plura, cum sine nube solem inspicere poterimus. Valeat Ampl.ma [IMG R4337 P2] V.ra Dig.tas, et hanc importunitatem, quam amor in publicum expressit, aequi bonique consulat. Dabam Londini 26 Febr. veteri stylo 1625. Illus.ma V.a Dig.ti omni obsequio addictus Rusdorff [IMG R4337 P3] Illustrissime Domine, Quanquam haud dubitem Nobil.m Dom. Belinium perscripsisse, quousque res circa Confoederationem? ineundam perducta sint in Gallia, tamen si fortasse, ut fieri solet, literae ipsius non fuissent redditae, aliquid etiam significare volui, qui superfluam cautelam non nocere ex Jurisconsultorum regulis didici. Rex Galliae non tantum valde approbat intentionem et dispositionem Procerum?, sed in Confoederationem? intrare etiam, et sua consilia? promittit. Mentio jam facta fuit m/500 librarum turnensium, quas in anticipationem numerare paratum fore spem facit. Sed conditio annectitur, ut, quoniam omnia bella tandem sopiantur et finiantur pactis et transactionibus, Rex Galliae Rex Magnae Britanniaeque coniunctim arbitri sint pactorum et conditionum?, componantque omnes alias controversias, quae essent oritura[e] in Germania inter Proceres?. Nihil aliud intenditur hoc pacto, quam ut aeque Romanorum et ecclesiasticorum quam protes(t)antium et secularium curam habere causamque ex pari tueri velint. Sed utrum omnino Galli hoc pacto circumscripta et definita esse velint ipsorum auxilia, sicuti ex coniectura timeo, hoc Dominus Belinius brevi dicet, cum quo ea de re consultare constituerunt. Si aliter non possumus, et ne demus occasionem suspicionis, acceptanda est nobis illa conditio; JC.torum praescripto utendum erit, ut terminis scilicet habilibus illas salvo iure accipiamus et intelligamus, quod fortuna et prosper successus nobis progressu temporis concedent. Two despatches of Georges de Selve, bishop of Lavaur, ambassador at Venice, to Francis I (BnF fr. 3091 f. 25 and fr. 3045 ff. 42–49; DECODE R3697, R4232), both listed as not decrypted. Satoshi Tomokiyo had published the key as a table, with no plaintext; it was applied and extended with further homophones, nulls and a name code. Georges de Selve (1508–1541), son of the first president of the Parlement of Paris and one of the two men in Holbein’s Ambassadors , was Francis I’s ambassador at Venice in 1535–36. Two of his despatches to the King carry cipher: DECODE R3697 : BnF fr. 3091 f. 25r–v, no. 14, dated at Venice “IIIIe” (DECODE: 14) September 1535. A letter in cleartext with eight cipher runs; four of them are ruled through by the decipherer with the plaintext written above or in the margin. The catalogue card put it in fr. 3045; it is in fr. 3091, in the same volume as letters of Raince and Gramont deciphered earlier in this project. DECODE R4232 : BnF fr. 3045 ff. 42–49, no. 31, “A Venise, ce cinquiesme de juillet mil cinq cent XXXVI”, signed “G. de Selve e. de Lavaur”. Fourteen pages, cipher on ff. 43v, 44r, 44v, 45r and 48r. Satoshi Tomokiyo’s cryptiana gives the key as “Selve’s Cipher”, reconstructed from the 1536 letter, and names fr. 3091 f. 25 as the same cipher: a simple substitution with an invented sign for each letter, two signs for a, three for e and three for l, and a null. No text of either letter had been published. Ernest Charrière’s Négociations de la France dans le Levant (vol. I, 1848) prints four other Selve letters of 1535–36, in cleartext; it does not print these two. f. 43v, the first five cipher lines, after the clear words ville fut : “en tres grand danger, combien que le nombre des assiegeans fust sans comparaison moindre que celuy qu’il entend d’y mener. Et comme ainsi soit que ladicte ville soit prenable …”. The diagonal strokes are a later cancellation. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3045 f. 43v, via Gallica (btv1b9060156p, view 84). The letters themselves add to the table. There are further homophones: a curled d-shaped sign for a, a tall looped sign for f, and a Latin R for o in the 1535 letter. The slash stands for c as well as l, and the two hooks for c and d are used interchangeably, so the French decides. X serves m as well as u. The cipherer also puts a null between doubled letters: Suis·ses , ambas·sadeur , ar·rivé , af·faires , oc·casion . The null is a small p joined to an e-sign, a vf shape, an upright S or a dot. He also writes one in mar·chant and Empe·reur . One six-sign group on f. 44r does not spell anything under the table. The decipherer’s gloss renders it “mons r de Rang…”, so it is a name code, very likely for Guido Rangone.

Charles V was then gathering the army with which he would cross the Var into Provence on 25 July. Selve reports what is thought at Venice of his plan. The cipher is shown in roman type, and the clear words that frame it are in brackets. [… la ville fut] en tres grand danger, combien que le nombre des assiegeans fust sans comparaison moindre que celuy qu’il entend d’y mener. Et comme ainsi soit que ladicte ville soit prenable, comme il en faict son compte, estant une clef de vostre royaulme si importante comme elle est, ce luy semble que, la voyant en dangier, vous vous vouldrez tirer aupres avec vostre puissance pour la secourir. [… son] allee a Marseille sera cause de luy donner l’occasion du combat [qu’il desire … ou bien le tiendra vostre puissance] loing, sans secourir ladicte ville, qu’il en viendra au dessus et la conquestera, [qui est bien la chose que plus il desire, car elle le feroit] patron de la Prouvence, et ne luy resteroit pas beaucop a gaigner pour avoir le passaige franc par terre d’Italie en Espaigne, comodité pour luy si grande qu’il ne la sçauroit cher achapter; et vous leveroit la navigation de la mer Mediterrenée, lequel luy asseureroit Gennes, Naples et Sicille. [Et quand les predictes raisons que] l’invitent a ladicte entreprise de Marseille, luy semble qu’estant vostre armee de mer dans le port de ladicte ville, qu’elle ne luy peult eschapper, aiant armee de mer plus puissante qui sera suffisante pour la garder de sortir. [Et estant ledict] port tellement exposé a la baterie de ceulx qui seront assis du costé de la montaigne de la Garde, qu’il n’y aura vaisseau qui s’y peusse saulver dedans. [f. 44v:] [Sire, ledict S r ] de Vaulx est tousiours d’oppinion que pour la sauveté de voz galeres […] de mettre hors vostre armee de mer et l’envoyer vers Naples. [Ce qui … seullement la vous] pourroit conserver, mectant dessus nombre de gens de guerre suffisant. [f. 45r:] … le retardation n’a esté cause en voz affaires; le bruict qui s’est faict par dela, lequel a mon advis se pourra estre amorty. [… audict] s r (?) de la Forest du [N] e de may […] a l’expresse rupture de la guerre d’entre vous et l’Empereur. [f. 48r:] … le Pape l’avoit asseuré que l’Empereur n’auroit aucunes decimes de luy pour ceste annee, quelque descente et armee que Barbarousse face. In English. Marseille would be in great danger even with far fewer besiegers than the army the Emperor means to bring. It can be taken, as he reckons, and it is a key to the kingdom, so he expects the King to march to its relief. That would give him the battle he wants. If the King stays away, he takes the town. Marseille would make him master of Provence and give him a free land road from Italy to Spain, which he could not buy too dearly. It would also take the Mediterranean from France and make Genoa, Naples and Sicily safe for him. His stronger fleet would keep the French galleys shut in the port, and guns on the hill of Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde would leave no ship safe there. De Vaulx advises sending the fleet out towards Naples with enough soldiers aboard. Jean de La Forest, the King’s envoy at the Porte, has written of an open breach with the Emperor. The Pope has promised to grant Charles no clerical tenths that year, whatever landing or fleet Barbarossa brings. f. 48r: the cipher ruled through by the King’s decipherer, with his decipherment in the left margin: “Le pape lavoit asseure que lempereur n’auroit aucunes decymes de luy pour [cest annee] quelque descente & armee que Barberousse far[a]”. The key gives the same words; the doubtful margin word is ceste annee in the cipher, with a null S between ceste and annee . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3045 f. 48r, via Gallica (btv1b9060156p, view 94).

fr. 3091 is known only from a black-and-white film scan, and the hand is looser. It needed three passes. The first applied the table as published. The second added the new signs, and the third used the decipherer’s glosses as cribs for the struck runs. DECODE’s own images of the record are screenshots of the same film at lower resolution. [f. 25r] […] au marchant [gloss: “au marchant”] […] ung sansacque cy prochain [gloss: the same; “a sanjak-bey near here”] … [Il est force, Sire, qu’il] passe par le chemin des Suisses, car l’aultre ne luy seroit pas seur, a cause que l’ambassadeur qui est [..] ça(?) pour l’Empereur, tost apres que le susdict marchant fust arrivé, comme des l’heure [.]e fus adverty, meu de coniecture qu’il fust venu pour aller en France, a pr[…] Anthon[e](?) de Le[…](?) de luy tenir le guet, pour le retenir s’il passe par … [… ledict Gueny(?)] marchant, [a]insi [comme …] [….] ambassa[deur] luy avoit dict qu’il seroit bon qu’il trouvast façon, soubz umbre de marchandise ou d’aultre occasion, de faire son voyage en France et aller en vostre court, pour entendre en quelz termes estoient vos affaires avec l’Empereur, et s’il se faisoit point quelque accord entre vous … [struck; gloss: “Il a consumé ses facultez et la plus part de ses amys … et grand du T[urc](?)”] … ses amis et gran[d] … avoit … [f. 25v, struck; margin: “en Hongrie — Hiero[nimo] … — amiablement pour la charge qu’il a de Vesprym de la guerre …”] …tretienent(?) amiablement pour la charge qu’il a de Vesprim de la guerre(?) en luy … on fait … contre ses … [… entreprinse cy dessus,] ne failloient pas d’adviser et faire adviser par d’aultres des occurrances de ça, sans especifier aultrement; entendre, et les advis qu’ilz donnent au Turc, et qu’ilz luy font donner par le marchant susdict, [.] quand en ont quelquefois tenu propos comme d’eux deux(?), [vous] sçaurés(?) … In English. A merchant must travel to France by the Swiss road, because the other route is not safe for him. As soon as he arrived, the Emperor’s ambassador at Venice guessed that he was going on to France. He asked someone, probably Antonio de Leyva, governor of Milan (the name is not secured), to watch for him and hold him if he came that way. The same Imperial ambassador had earlier told the merchant to find a way, under colour of trade, to go to the King’s court and learn how the King stood with the Emperor, and whether any agreement was being made. The merchant, in other words, was being used as an informant. The verso turns to a Hungarian matter (a Hieronymus and the see of Veszprém) and to persons at Venice who report the news of the place and pass advice to the Turk through the same merchant. f. 25r, the first block: “passe par le chemin des Suis·ses, car l’aultre ne luy seroit pas seur, a cause que l’ambas·sadeur qui est … pour l’Empe·reur …”, with a null between the doubled letters. Film scan, contrast raised. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3091 f. 25r, via Gallica (btv1b9060253s, view 27).

The cipher runs were located on the Gallica images and cut into strips of three to five lines. Each page went to a separate transcription pass, which transcribed every sign, applied the table and wrote out the French. Doubtful spots were then checked again on the native files at full resolution: an eleven-sign “verb” on f. 48r is ceste annee with a null in the middle, and a four-sign word on f. 45r is guerre . Wherever the King’s decipherer left a gloss, it was compared letter by letter. On the 1535 letter the glosses also served as cribs, lining the known plaintext up against the struck signs; that is how au marchant , ung sansacque cy prochain and amiablement pour la charge qu’il a de Vesprim were confirmed. Counts are measured on per-sign files, with one character per sign and undecrypted signs marked: 2,248 of 2,481 non-null signs decrypted (90.6%). R4232 is 1,417 of 1,430 plus the glossed name code; R3697 is 831 of 1,051, and 709 of 747 outside the struck runs. A stricter count ( sense.py , 5 October 2026) credits only signs inside French words of the period vocabulary: R4232 1,408 of 1,430 (98.5%), R3697 822 of 1,051 (78.2%), both 2,230 of 2,481 (89.9%) .

Reading audit, 22 October 2026. The 1536 letter and the unstruck cipher of the 1535 letter read as French sentences; the decipherer’s struck runs of 1535 (304 signs) give only fragments and are decoded, not read. Signs in text that reads: 2,177 of 2,481 (87.7%). A re-reading the same day took the King’s decipherer’s glosses as the decipherment of the struck runs they cover ( READING_R3697_struck.md ): four runs, 169 signs, now carry French clauses word for word from the glosses, checked against the signs where they separate from the strike (“au marchant”, “ung sansacque cy prochain”, “Il a consumé ses facultez et la plus part de ses amys”, “amiablement pour la charge qu’il a de Vesprim de la guerre”). As text they are still fragments (one clause in four clean), so they stay decoded, not read with the other 135 struck signs, which have no legible gloss and need a colour image or the original. Counted word by word on 24 October 2026, the written-out reading of the 1535 letter (R3697) builds coherent sentences but reads at 91.1% of its words, under the 95% a complete reading needs. Re-measured 5 October 2026. Both letters 2,230 of 2,481 signs inside French words (89.9%). The struck runs of the 1535 letter were tried again on 5 October: Gallica has only the film scan of fr. 3091; the native views were re-fetched and f. 25v and f. 25r re-transcribed at 1.6–2×; removing the strike by a fitted line erases the sign bodies with it; gloss-led candidates ( de ses maistres , grand credit , du Turc ) do not fit the signs. Nothing moved. 95% would need about 127 more signs and the unstruck gaps hold about 50, so it cannot be reached on these images. 1536 letter : 13 single signs, all blots, corrections under the ruling or one slip; none affects the sense. The day in “du [N] e de may” is a figure that the decipherer copied without resolving. The crossed sign before “de la Forest” is taken as an abbreviation for sieur (M). The name code is known only through its gloss (C). 1535 letter, struck runs (182 signs): the decipherer’s ruling runs through the middle of every sign, and the film scan cannot separate the two. The glosses give most of the plaintext. The strike ink is lighter than the cipher ink, so a colour image of the leaf would very likely make them legible. 1535 letter, f. 25r : the stretch “a pr[…] Anthon[e] de Le[…]” (17 signs). A blot and two cancellation strokes cross four of the signs; Antoine de Leyve fits the sense and the legible shapes, but is not secured (I). Four signs before ambassa[deur] , two after est and the first sign of r7 fit no word. Five signs were erased by the writer, and one is a solid blot. 1535 letter, f. 25v : the last cipher group before the text breaks into struck clear writing (seven signs), a lone a before quand , and d’eux deux against d’eux vous (M). Readings marked (?) in the text above are M or I; everything else is H or C. The sibling fr. 3019 f. 97r (Rodez and Selve, 16 November 1536) carries three short glossed runs in the same cipher, and none of them helps with the open name.

Three Spanish despatches of 1593 in the Spanish office cipher of 1592–93 (BnF fr. 3983 nos. 45, 79; fr. 3984 no. 47), with no published decipherment. Tomokiyo’s reconstructed key lacked the code list; the Spanish office’s own key, found through DECODE in BnF fr. 3995 f. 97, supplied it. 92.5% of the groups read as sense, checked against the 1593 gloss on no. 47. A fourth letter filed with them, in another cipher, has its own page. ṗ ∂i 16. Ṃ 81 ʒ 1̊9 73 73 92 ṗ. 21 16. 27 23. 81 el · [alla] · con · es te · a cha que · que si en do · con fi den te Naples, Rome, Paris · syllabic numerical ciphers with code lists · February to July 1593 Spanish despatches of 1593: Miranda, Sessa, Ibarra to Philip II Go to the full text ↓ BnF Français 3983 nos. 45, 79 and Français 3984 no. 47 · Spain’s management of the Estates of 1593 and the Infanta’s candidature · no decipherment published Three despatches in the Spanish office cipher of 1592–93, whose key Satoshi Tomokiyo had reconstructed and published as an image; the office’s own key, with the code list his table lacks, was found through DECODE in another volume, and 92.5% of the three letters’ groups now read as sense. Arya Sanketbhai Patel · posted 19 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (75% of the cipher) · On the map With Arya Sanketbhai Patel (solution) and Satoshi Tomokiyo (key or decipherment used) · Also credited · Satoru (pointer to a source) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (75% of the cipher) The letters Four Spanish despatches of 1593: Conde de Miranda to Feria (no. 45), Sessa to Diego de Ibarra (79), Sessa to Philip II (47) and Ibarra from Paris (68). The catalogue lists them with no decipherment. Where BnF fr. 3983 ff. 98 and 162 and fr. 3984 ff. 108 and 145, via Gallica. The office key for the first cipher is fr. 3995 f. 97. The cipher Two ciphers: a syllabic one (two-digit consonant+vowel numbers) with a code list, and the Feria–Mansfeld syllabic cipher used on f. 145. How it was read Tomokiyo’s published key tables (syllables only) were applied; f. 97 of the Nevers key book gave the missing nomenclature. The decipherer’s gloss on no. 47 agrees with the result. What it says Nos. 45 and 79 discuss a legate, an election and a request for a safe way to send word; no. 47 reports delay waiting for news by sea. Still open Measured sense: nos. 45, 47 and 79 together 1,212 of 1,310 groups (92.5%); no. 68 only 224 of 598 (37.5%), since the Feria–Mansfeld code list is unpublished (374 groups).

The catalogue cites piece numbers, which are not folios. BnF fr. 3983 and fr. 3984 are two volumes of the Collection Mémoires de la Ligue , and their catalogue notice carries a piece-by-piece dépouillement that gives both. Taken from it: piece folio the entry fr. 3983 no. 45 f. 98 “Lettre, avec chiffre, d’«el conde DE MIRANDA,… al duque de Feria,… De Napoles, a 25 de hebrero 1593». En espagnol.” fr. 3983 no. 79 f. 162 “Lettre, avec chiffre, d’«el duque DE SESSO,… a don Diego de Ibarra,… De Roma, 11 de março 1593».” fr. 3984 no. 47 f. 108 “Lettre, avec chiffre et commencement de déchiffrement, d’«el duque DE SESSA» à Philippe II. «De Roma, 30 de junio 1593». Copie.” Neither volume’s canvases are labelled, and neither is foliated at a constant rate: some pieces are shot page by page, others as openings, and the leaves carry piece numbers and folio numbers in different corners. The map was built by reading folio numbers off a full-width top strip at intervals: for fr. 3983, c178 = f.98, c200 = f.111, c220 = f.122, c276 = f.156; for fr. 3984, c188 = f.103, c228 = f.123, c266 = f.144. That places the three letters at canvases 178, 286 and 198 , and each was confirmed on the image. fr. 3983 f. 98 (canvas 178), the Conde de Miranda to the duque de Feria. Seventeen lines of cipher, the date in clear at the foot ( “Dios Gu[arde]… al S. de Nap[oles] a 25 de hebre[ro] 1593” ), Miranda’s signature, and the docket “S. duq de feria” . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3983 f. 98 (canvas 178), via Gallica.
sessa1593.html#keys

Tomokiyo’s page for Philip II’s reign carries 32 images, two of which are the keys that matter here: phelippes2.png , “Spanish Cipher (1592–1593)” : the cipher used among Philip II, Parma, Feria, Sessa, Acuña, Olivares, Fuentes, Tassis, Ibarra, Doria and Miranda , which he cites at fr. 3983 ff. 98, 158 and 162. That is nos. 45 and 79. spanish3mansfeld.png , the syllabic cipher for the duke of Feria and the count of Mansfeld of July 1593, cited at fr. 3984 ff. 130 and 145. That is fr. 3984 no. 68, Ibarra’s letter from Paris, once filed with these three and now on its own page : a different cipher. As with the Maisse ciphers, the local copy of that page in this repository is a text dump, so the tables are absent from it and the leaves look keyless. Tomokiyo reconstructed the keys from other letters. He lists these letters as “undeciphered” , which on cryptiana means that no contemporary decipherment is known; no decipherment of them had been published. Applied, the tables give Spanish. The syllables are two-digit numbers for consonant + vowel, so 38 94 68. 31 73 40 89 23 91: decrypts to yo · su · pon · go · que · ha · va · de · ser . Every line also carries code groups the table does not have.

The catalogue entry ends “Verify first. Tomokiyo’s Spanish keys of 1589–93; DECODE for Sessa .” DECODE’s record search returns two records for these correspondents, and both are keys: DECODE name sender type 4076 BNF_Français_3995_094 Don Diego de Ibarra Key — homophonic substitution, nomenclatures 4077 BNF_Français_3995_096 Don Diego de Ibarra, Duc de Sessa Key — homophonic substitution, nomenclatures Both point into BnF fr. 3995 , the Nevers cipher key book, a volume this repository already fetches for the Lorraine cipher . Folio numbers there run about canvas − 91 in this stretch (c188 = f.97, c190 = f.98, c194 = f.101). Folio 97 is the key itself, and it is complete. BnF fr. 3995 f. 97 (canvas 188): the letter alphabet across the top, and beneath it the syllable table: ba 10 … bu 14, ca 19 … cu 15, da 24 … du 20, on through za/ze/zi/zo/zu. It is identical to Tomokiyo’s reconstruction from other letters, and so confirms it. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3995 f. 97 (canvas 188), via Gallica. The sheet gives the letter alphabet with its symbol equivalents (a = 4 / ʒ, e = n / f / ʃ, g = 3, i = y / 6, n = x / ·, o = 7₂, r = y / :, s = ∆, u = o, y = q, z = ∂), the syllable table, a row of Nulles and, beneath them, the code list that Tomokiyo’s table does not have. The code list (nomenclature) of the same sheet: aunque ʒo, aviso ʃes, exercito xel, estados vul, Francia gam, lettera ra, mucho hur, manera cer, magestad ʒum, mas dox, negocios norî, quando nes, que ʒot, Rey tas, Reyno tis, remedio sas, reputacion pem, Roma vos, seignor ʒus. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3995 f. 97 (canvas 188), via Gallica. These are the groups that were open on the leaves. With them the diacritics can be fixed, and two of the marks are confirmed on plaintext: the ring is −h−, giving 1̊9 = cha in achaque , and the dot above is final −l, giving 13 with a dot = bol in bolsa . A trailing dot is final −n, a colon final −r, a circumflex final −s, a bar means the number itself, an umlaut doubles the consonant, and ⊤ marks a code group. Added 2 October 2026: the back of the sheet (f. 97v) carries the endorsement “1592 Chifre d’entre le Duc de Parme et le Roy Cat.co en l’an 1592, lequel sert aussi pour le Duc de Sessa et Don Diego de Ybarre”, so the key is the office’s own for Sessa and Ibarra; f. 98 is a different, French key (an earlier version of this page put the endorsement there). The nomenclature has over a hundred word entries, not the forty first transcribed; the rest were transcribed again from the image, and thirteen groups of the three leaves that had stayed open now resolve ( tim = intención, hus = príncipe, nur = ninguna, pol = duque, 50T = Su Magestad, 61T = tiempo, and others), with Vor corrected to opinión. The gloss “en particular” on f. 108 stands over ʒir , which the sheet gives as particular . The note that prompted the re-reading came from satorunet (satoru.net/crypt).

The key was applied to the three leaves. Each was fetched at native resolution, deskewed (the angle within ±3° that maximises the variance of the row profile) and cut into centred line strips. no. 45, f. 98: the Conde de Miranda to the duque de Feria, Naples, 25 February 1593 Every cipher line on the leaf is deciphered. The one band without a decipherment is a blank gap with show-through from the verso and holds no cipher: … el [alla] con este achaque , que siendo confidente … se po[drá] procurar … a costa de la bolsa … yo supongo que hava de ser … residencia … sobre esto … a que hava dado ya alguna [Roma] … no [se] verá lo que en esto convernà hazer, que yo me remito a su prudencia. Solo le suplico que … tuviere [lettera] me mande [causa] r … la persona que se eligirá … donde le po [drá] escribir a dar algun recado, si fue [re] … dar de manera que no se entienda, por que la hora que … le tengan por … perderá mucho [s] … no. 79, f. 162: the duque de Sessa to Diego de Ibarra, Rome, 11 March 1593 Every cipher line on the leaf is deciphered. There is no cleartext; the only bands without cipher are the folio number 162 and the docket 11 de Março 93 : … de ver los testemonios que a todos levantan … a [legato] … de feria … constantes, si bien los que bivimos en [ Roma ] no desemos de … por [ aviso ] que no dura 4 dias, ni pasa a los sucesores. Se hazen tan estas ordinarias … difi [cul] tades en la [ election ] … con todo eso es [ negocio ] tan importante … que espero que le a de favorecer … de [ manera ] que … conviene … que entre los … que siguen la … [di] versas pretensiones … en cada uno … si no me espanto … no puedo dexar de hazerlo, a lo menos, de que no estén [ ministro ] s conformes … ganados, de que no se pue [den] denfiar … no. 47, f. 108: Sessa to Philip II, Rome, 30 June 1593 This leaf carries a partial contemporary decipherment above the cipher. Where both survive, the decryption agrees with the gloss, which checks the office key on a third letter of the group: cipher decoded here the 1593 decipherer’s gloss ʒ 3̄0 23 65 g̈o 21 16. 30 · de pa ssa do · con a 30. del Passado con 68: 87 4 23 55: … 22 26 77 21 23 22 4 n. 22 7 por via de mar … di fe ri do de di a en di a por una [via] de mar … ha ydo defiriendo de dia en dia Further on: a ve esperando a ver si venia … de los … de que no tiene … de [ legato ] [ mucho ] … , against the gloss “si ver[n]ia alguna nueva cierta” and “fres[ca] carta” . fr. 3983 f. 162 (canvas 286), Sessa to Ibarra; there is no cleartext on the leaf. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3983 f. 162 (canvas 286), via Gallica.

The key gives plaintext on all three letters, on none of them completely. Written out as Spanish and measured word by word on 24 October 2026, no. 79 builds coherent sentences but reads at 87.5% of its words and no. 47 at 91.7%, under the 95% a complete reading needs. What is still open: Re-measured 5 October 2026. Every cipher line of the three letters was re-transcribed and scored for sense ( sense.tsv ): no. 45 230 of 254 groups (90.6%), no. 79 504 of 546 (92.3%), no. 47 478 of 510 (93.7%), 1,212 of 1,310 (92.5%) . Open: 22 code groups that are not on the f. 97 sheet, each once or twice; about 75 syllable groups of doubtful reading. nos. 45 and 79 are deciphered across every cipher line on their leaves. Open in them are scattered single groups, marked · in the decipherment files: mostly rarer code words and a few diacritics that are ambiguous at this resolution. The other leaves of fr. 3995 near the key (ff. 94, 96, 98) hold further Spanish keys of the same office, including the one already identified here as “1592 / Chifre d’entre le Duc de Parme et le Roy Cath[olique]” at f. 98. They have not been worked.

Five letters of Michel de Seure, Henri II’s ambassador in Lisbon (BnF fr. 3151 nos. 39–41, 43–44), in a homophonic cipher of 118 signs with syllable and word signs, 21 nulls and a cancellation sign. Angus Robinson (pull request #40) recovered the key from three deciphered paragraphs bound beside no. 44, annealing and sign-by-sign correction against the scans, and deciphered all 9,405 positions; 8,819 of 8,857 signifying signs carry a key value. Peruvian silver, the Spanish fleets, the Medina fairs and Seure’s debts. The 12 December letter to the king survives in three copies. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, français 3151 nos. 39–41 and 43–44 (Gallica btv1b9059865k, views 72–87); catalogue item 10. No. 42 is a letter of Marshal Brissac. The cipher 118 sign types: 55 letter signs, most letters with two or three of them, 18 syllable signs, 22 word signs ( portugal , perou , roy d’espaigne …), 21 nulls and a sign that cancels the one before it. The text runs on without word breaks. How it was deciphered A leaf bound with the letters holds three short deciphered paragraphs, A, B and C, matching no. 44. Robinson used them as cribs, transcribed every letter, annealed the key and corrected it sign by sign against the scans. What it says The Peru fleet’s arrival at Seville with silver, treasure unloaded in the Azores and handed to Philip’s officers, Spanish ships gathering at Málaga, Alicante and Cádiz, debts at the Medina fairs, and Seure’s own unpaid allowances. Still open One word sign with no value (once, probably vostre ), one conjectural value ( escuz ), and 27 damaged or unidentified signs. Measured word by word on 24 October 2026, the reading of no. 39 builds coherent sentences but reads at 90.9% of its words, under the 95% a complete reading needs. Michel de Seure, a Knight of Malta (commandeur), was Henri II’s ambassador at the Portuguese court. Five of his letters in fr. 3151 mix clear French with long cipher passages. The counts are measured here from Robinson’s transcription. A “position” is one written sign, nulls included. A “signifying” position is one that is neither a null nor cancelled. seure1558.html#cipher

Robinson’s key has 118 sign types. Many are letters of the secretary hand, Roman or Greek, used as cipher signs, which hid the system at first. His transcription labels name the shapes ( H# , 3bar , Tarrow , beta …); KEY.svg draws each one. Letters: 55 signs. Most letters have two or three homophones: a is H# , o or ss , and e is 3bar , ff or q . Syllables: 18 signs for 16 values: au, ce, co, con/com, de, est, et (three signs), il, le, luy, moy, on, par/per, que, qui, si. Words: 22 signs: argent, arme, castille, dict, dire, escuz, espaigne, faict, faire, la royne Marye, l’empereur, mais, navires, nous, Perou, Portugal, pour, roy de Portugal, roy d’Espaigne, sire, vostre, vous. A 23rd sign, N10_4 , has no value. Nulls: 21 signs, among them the numerals 7, 12, 13, 14, 23, 30, 40 and 100. The survey of 21 September had taken these numerals for code groups. Nulls make up 499 of the 9,405 positions. Cancellation: the sign tri voids the sign before it (49 positions).
seure1558.html#no39

No. 39, Gallica view 72: the end of the clear text, « a estimer selon la facon », then the first nine rows of the cipher. The numerals are nulls. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3151 no. 39, Gallica btv1b9059865k view 72. The cipher passage of the letter to de Fresne is twenty rows. It opens on rumours of a withdrawal and asks for news of the outcome, « car nous commenceons a aprocher du temps »: Seure’s two-year posting was nearly over. The rest asks de Fresne to help recover his unpaid allowances and to speak for him to the Cardinal. Seure says he is in debt and wants to leave. Only one of the 366 signifying positions is unread: the word sign N10_4 in row 10, which Robinson proposes is vostre .
seure1558.html#king

12 December (nos. 41, 43, 44). The Peru fleet has reached Seville with silver; Robinson’s reading values it at about two million in gold and silver. More treasure was unloaded in the Azores, and the queen of Portugal has ordered it handed over to Philip’s officers. She has also lent Philip money from the young king’s treasury. Seure reports two French ships taken at Havana, the death of Don Diego de Azevedo and the naming of a new viceroy, and a spice fleet due to sail for Flanders. The money owed at the Medina fairs comes up as well: « ilz devoient huict cens mille escuz aux foires de Medina ». Of the three copies, no. 43 is the longest and the worst preserved. Its opening passage names a Portuguese, Anthoine Galean, and the death of Queen Mary (« le decez de la royne Marye »). 27 December (no. 40). So far Philip’s men have recovered only two hundred thousand escuz confiscated from a churchman, and the queen of Portugal has let Philip send armed ships to Terceira. Ships are gathering at Málaga, Alicante and Cádiz, and Genoa has made a loan. Seure has had no letters from the king for five months. Robinson’s walkthrough gives the continuous French reading of every section, with an English translation: angusrobinson.github.io/historical-decipherment/seure .
seure1558.html#method

The method is Robinson’s, from his summary and walkthrough. Cribs. A leaf with three short deciphered paragraphs, labelled A, B and C, is bound in the middle of a sentence. They overlap no. 44’s cipher sections A, B and C. He later found two more parallels. No. 43’s postscript enciphers the same text as no. 44 C, and no. 40’s enciphered passages have clear copies. Transcription and annealing. He transcribed all five letters as well as he could (397 rows, 9,405 positions). He then ran simulated annealing from the cribs, four runs in parallel. Splitting look-alikes. Annealing worked only in part, because several sets of similar signs had been taken as one. He split them by comparing the scans again and again across the whole corpus. About 230 proposed characters came down to 118 sign types. Held-out test. A section held back from the fitting deciphered cleanly with the final key. Robinson reports that his AI collaborator, asked to transcribe one section, filled in signs from a parallel plaintext instead of reading the scan. About 19% of that section’s signs (68 of 360) were wrong, and he corrected them against the images.
seure1558.html#checks

Counts. The sign and output rows of KEY_AND_DECRYPTION.txt give 9,405 positions in 397 rows, as Robinson states. Of the 8,857 signifying positions, 8,819 carry a key value (99.6%). The other 38 are 28 unread signs and 10 read only from context. Language. The project’s language models put the decipherment of every letter first as sixteenth-century French (−1.99 to −2.13 per letter, ahead of modern French). Statistical test. The test uses 9,367 read tokens and 121 types, scored with the 1530s French despatches model. The key’s reading scores −2.269 per letter. Random keys of the same shape score −5.41 (z 13.0), and the best key annealed onto shuffled ciphertext scores −3.65 (z 56). Verdict: pass. Images. Rows 1–9 of no. 39 were compared with view 72. The nulls 14, 13, 30, 12 and 100 and the syllable sign 55 fall where his rows put them. Three copies. The three copies of the 12 December letter were enciphered separately, and they decipher to the same text under one key.
seure1558.html#open

N10_4 , once, no. 39 row 10: no value. Robinson proposes vostre , with Seure referring to himself (grade C). longs_x = escuz : conjectural, one occurrence (grade C). 27 damaged or unidentified signs, most of them in no. 43 on views 82–83, are left unread. Ten more are given values from context only, for example [france] and [par] (grade M). Robinson estimates that the clerk made at least 18 errors in the 9,405 positions; for example, a p sign is written for g five times. Printed sources for Seure’s embassy have not been searched for these letters.

The letter-level decryption is `no39_decryption.txt`. ## Reading Lettre du Commandeur de Seure à monsieur du Fresne, Secretaire d’estat sous le regne du Roy Henry second, estant pour lors son ambassadeur en Portugal. Monseigneur, Je ne vous feray longue lettre, d’aultant que pourrez veoir par celle que J’escriptz au Roy ce qui se passe pardeça. Je vous escripviz dernierement par ung nommé Anthoine Galuan, courrier Portugais, et peu paravant J’avois faict le mesme, me resiouissant grandement de l’honneur que avez receu de sa Majesté d’avoir succeddé à feu Monsieur de Marchaumont, mon bon seigneur et amy. Lors Galuan fist assez de difficulté de retourner [en France]. Toutesfoys J’estime [qu’il] seroit allé jusques à vous. Je sçay que au temps [qu’il] partit noz voisins tenoient la [paix] pour faicte. Je n’ay eu nulles nouvelles de vous depuis le retour de [Jeannoy], comme Je n’ay encores du Roy. Vray est que J’ay bien entendu que l’on m’a escript par ung qui n’est encores [venu], lequel J’actends avec grande devotion et le sçavoir de voz bonnes no[uve]lles et de celles de mon seigneur. J’actends avec grande devotion quelque advis de ce que vous faictz. Toutesfoys Je demeure à estimer [veu] la façon > dont noz voysins parlent de la retraicte des mansulmans s’ilz disent verité la chose sera autrement que ne l’ay > esperé quoy qu’il en soit ce me sera plaisir d’entendre la resolucion car nous commenceons à approcher du temps que > [vostre] amy aye achevé ses deux ans > nous avons tenu icy la paix pour faicte je ne sçay ce qu’il en sera qui my faisoit encores avoir plus de doubte je > ne veulx plus demeurer icy guieres longuement et au pis aller n’y veux que achever mes deux ans je suis en > necessité et ay eu tout plein dettes cest esté J’escriptz à la [Royne] [qu’elle] poursuive davantaige l’assigna[tion] de mes estatz de ceste Cour, qui demeura le [xx]e d’avril dernier, a ces[…] c[on]signé à Condé, affin que Je ne tombe trop [necessiteux], Je vous supplye bien humblement luy ayder à la recouvrer, et luy faire faveur à l’endroict de Monseigneur le Cardinal, a qui J’en escriptz, et par tout où avez [credit]. Comme [savez], dont Dieu vous lou[…] de vous m’obligerez de plus en plus à vous faire humble servi[ce]. J’envoyeray cest hyver ung de[s] myens pardela affin de faire recouvrer quelque parties extraordinaires que J’ay faictes en ceste charge, sans [celles] [de] s[…]me aprés [guerre], et par mesme moyen Je envoyray quelque chose de beau et bien nouveau à Monseigneur le Cardinal, suivant ce que m’avez [conseillé]. et deux marbres de […]. Je n’ay sceu congnoistre [s’il est] allé pardela auecque [le] Sieur […] ou envoyé, qui fu[st] [si] beau ou si desdaigneux de [ne] me vouloir faire sçavoir son allee. Pourquoy vous supplye me faire tant de bien par la premiere depesche que l’on fera de moy escrire ung mot affin que vous […] [l’asseurance] à cognoistre […] bonnes h[…]eurs. C’est l’endroict où Je feray fin à la [presente], aprés avoir rendu mes treshumbles et affectionnees [recommendations] à vostre bonne grace, en priant nostre seigneur Monseigneur, vous donner en santé tresbonne vye longue. De Lisbonne le [xij] jour de decembre 1558. Vostre humble serviteur et certain amy, Le chevalier de Seure. Monseigneur, Monseigneur le duc de Guise, Pair et Grand Chambellan de France. […] le Mareschal de Brissac, du [xxvj]me novembre 1558. Translation no39_en.md # Seure no. 39, Lisbon 1558: English translation Angus Robinson's English, copied 23 Oct 2026 from his edition (letter 39); `>` = enciphered in the manuscript. ## Translation Letter from the Commander de Seure to Monsieur du Fresne, Secretary of State under King Henry II, while Seure was his ambassador in Portugal. My lord, I shall not write you a long letter, since you will be able to see from the one I am writing to the king what is happening here. I wrote to you recently through a man named Antoine Galuan, a Portuguese courier, and shortly before that I had done the same, rejoicing greatly at the honour you have received from His Majesty of succeeding the late Monsieur de Marchaumont, my good lord and friend. Galuan then made a good deal of difficulty about returning [to France]. Nevertheless I believe [that he] would have gone on as far as you. I know that, at the time [when he] left, our neighbours regarded the [peace] as concluded. I have had no news at all from you since the return of [Jeannoy], just as I have none yet from the king. It is true that I have indeed heard that a letter has been sent to me through someone who has not yet [arrived]; I await him with great devotion, and to hear your good news and that of my lord. I await with great devotion some word about what you are doing. Nevertheless I still have to assess it, [given] the manner > in which our neighbours speak of the withdrawal of the Muslims. If they are telling the truth, things will turn out > otherwise than I had hoped. Be that as it may, I shall be glad to hear the outcome, for we are beginning to > approach the time when [your] friend will have completed his two years. > We have regarded the peace here as settled; I do not know how it will turn out, which made me still more doubtful. > I do not wish to remain here very much longer, and at worst I want only to complete my two years. I am in need and > ran up a great many debts this summer. I am writing to the [queen] to press further for the [assignment] of my allowances from this court, which remained [unpaid] last [20th] April, […] [assigned] at Condé, so that I do not fall into too great [need]. I very humbly beg you to help recover them, and to put in a good word with my lord the Cardinal, to whom I am writing about it, and wherever you have [influence]. As [you know]—may God [reward] you for it—you will bind me ever more closely to your humble [service]. I shall send one of my people over there this winter to recover some extraordinary expenses I have incurred in this office, not counting [those incurred] […] after [the war]. By the same means I shall send something beautiful and quite new to my lord the Cardinal, following what you have [advised] me. and two pieces of marble from […]. I have not been able to find out [whether he has] gone over there with [the] sieur […], or [was] sent, who [was] [so] grand or so disdainful as [not] to want to let me know of his departure. Therefore I beg you to do me the kindness, by the first dispatch that is sent, of writing me a word, so that you […] [may be assured of] […] [goodwill]. This is where I shall end the [present letter], after paying my most humble and affectionate [respects] to your good grace, while praying Our Lord to grant you, my lord, health and a very good, long life. Lisbon, [12] December 1558. Your humble servant and faithful friend, the Chevalier de Seure. My lord, the Duke of Guise, Peer and Grand Chamberlain of France. […] the Maréchal de Brissac, [26] November 1558.
