Translation no40_en.md # Seure no. 40, Lisbon 1558: English translation Angus Robinson's English, copied 23 Oct 2026 from his edition (letter 40); `>` = enciphered in the manuscript. ## Translation Letter from the same Commander de Seure to King Henry II, while he was his ambassador in Portugal. Sire, I wrote to you on the twelfth of this month by way of Lyon and Bordeaux of the great joy among our neighbours in Seville at the arrival of the fleet from Peru, which arrived there at the end of October, and of the registered money it had brought. But because these routes for writing to you are so uncertain, and I do not really know whether what I have written in my various earlier dispatches has reached you, I did not wish to fail to repeat a word about it to Your Majesty in this dispatch, which goes by way of Lyon, so that you may be informed of everything that occurs here. The fleet consisted of twenty-two ships: four were armed for war and the rest were merchant ships of every kind. Those four ships brought eight hundred thousand écus for King Philip, from the revenue of his rights; of the others, a million in registered silver for private persons or merchants; another eighty thousand for the deceased; and three hundred thousand écus' worth of cochineal and fabrics. Besides this they unloaded safely in the Azores, where by their good luck they no longer found the ships that had gone out to escort them (for these had withdrawn to Cádiz, despairing of meeting it this year), nearly a million in gold, most of which is said to belong to the Viceroy of Peru. That is all that has come to my knowledge. I am told that, beyond these registered sums, which King Philip's officers have seized, there was still a good sum which was not [registered], which the merchants had hidden in secret, without the knowledge of the officers of the Indies, among the sugar and other kinds of merchandise; it may be worth very nearly as much as the registered money. The officers of Seville have been remarkably diligent about it. > Nevertheless, up to the present they have been able to get hold of only two hundred thousand écus belonging to a > churchman, which they have confiscated. The Queen of Portugal has permitted and agreed that King Philip may send > armed ships and officers to the island of Terceira to recover the money left there in passing, with power to punish > and make arrangements concerning it as he pleases. The honourable people of this country find this very strange, as > indeed it is, for the late kings of Portugal would never have allowed it on any account. They have sent there with > all diligence. God grant that they do not recover it, as I think they will not do so very easily. > Since my last dispatches I have had news that they are assembling ships at Málaga, Alicante and Cádiz, and say that > this is to send to Sicily and Naples soldiers whom the Marquis of Tarifa, who has been appointed viceroy there, is > having raised to send out. He himself is to leave very soon, if he has not already done so. Oran has not been > besieged, as they expected it would be during this winter. They also speak of sending some soldiers to La Goleta to > reinforce the garrison. > They have already paid the eight hundred thousand écus they owed at the fairs of Medina, and have also made an > agreement for six hundred thousand écus with a Genoese who is to deliver it to them in Flanders in two instalments, > the last falling due next March. The Genoese makes a profit of eighteen per cent on it. They propose to send it > from Laredo to Flanders on the ships which were to carry Queen Mary. > Don Juan de Vega has died, who was president in Spain and a man of service. It is said that the Constable of > Castile has also died. Of this I have as yet no certain information. I have had no letters from you for five months. That is all I can write to you. Sire, I pray that Our Lord may grant you, in perfect health, a very happy and very long life. Lisbon, 27 December 1558. > I forgot to tell you that Queen Mary left more than four hundred thousand écus in gold to King Philip by her will, > and also that, it is said, she made heir to her patrimonial property a bastard son whom the emperor acknowledged at > his death as a son he had had in the city of Augsburg, who is thirteen years old. King Philip’s officers have > nevertheless laid hands on that property and are seeking to raise money upon it. They are also preparing a large > fleet loaded with merchandise to go to Peru, which will leave at the end of February. Your most humble and most obedient servant and subject, the Chevalier de Seure. Nevertheless, up to the present they have been able to lay hands on only two hundred thousand écus which belonged to a churchman and which have been confiscated. The Queen of Portugal has allowed and agreed that King Philip may send armed ships and officers to the islands of Terceira to recover the money left there in passing, with authority to punish and arrange matters there as he pleases. Honourable people in this country find this very strange, as indeed it is: the deceased kings of Portugal would never have allowed it for anything. They have sent there with all haste. May God grant that they do not recover it, for I judge that they will not do so very easily. Since my last dispatches I have had news that they are assembling a gathering of ships at Málaga, Alicante and Cádiz. They say it is to send soldiers to Sicily (Cicelle) and Naples, whom the Marquis of Tariffe, appointed viceroy there, is raising for that purpose. He is to leave very soon himself, if he has not already done so. Oran has not been besieged as they had thought it would be during this winter. They also speak of sending some soldiers to La Goleta to reinforce the garrison. They have already satisfied the eight hundred thousand écus they owed at the fair of Medina. They have also made a financial agreement for six hundred thousand écus with a Genoese who is to deliver it in Flanders in two instalments. The last is due this coming March. The Genoese makes a profit of eighteen per cent. They intend to send it to Flanders through Laredo on the ships which were to carry Queen Mary. Don Juan de Vega has died. He was president [of the council] of Spain and a man of service. It is said that the Constable of Castile has died too. I have as yet no certain news of this. I forgot to tell you that Queen Mary left more than four hundred thousand écus in gold to King Philip by will, and also that she is said to have made heir to her patrimony a bastard son whom the emperor acknowledged at his death having had in the city of Augsburg, who is thirteen years old. Nevertheless King Philip’s officers have laid hands on that patrimony and are trying to raise money on it. They are also preparing a large fleet loaded with merchandise to go to Peru, which will leave at the end of February. Sir, Monsieur du Fresne, Councillor to the king and secretary of his finances. Chevalier de Seure, 27 December 1558. No. 41, Lisbon, 12 Dec 1558, to Henri II Seure to Henri II, one of three copies (nos. 41, 43, 44) of the same letter of 12 Dec 1558: its three passages carry the same text as no. 44's A, B and C (Spanish treasure, the Medina fairs, 'huict cens mille escuz', Queen Mary's death and Philip II). Reading no41_reading.md # Seure no. 41, Lisbon 1558 (BnF fr. 3151): the reading Written 23 Oct 2026 (verification 3): Angus Robinson's French reading of the whole letter, copied from his edition <https://angusrobinson.github.io/historical-decipherment/seure/readings.html> (letter 41); he contributed the key and decipherment to this repository in PR #40. Passages quoted with `>` are in cipher in the manuscript; the rest is clear. His conventions: scribal abbreviations expanded, consonantal u written v, a few diacritics added, and in the cipher passages word spaces and doubled letters added back (the cipher writes no doubled letters). `[word]` = his contextual reading, `[…]` = unread. The letter-level decryption is `no41_decryption.txt`. ## Reading Autre lettre du mesme Commandeur de Seure au dit Roy. 1558. Sire, Je vous escripviz par mes dernieres lettres du xxvme d’octobre, que Je donnay à ung Courrier Portugais nommé Anthoine Galuan, le decez de la Royne Marie et la peyne en quoy estoient noz voisins pour le peu d’esperance qui leur restoit que la flotte qu’ilz attendoient du Perou deust venir ceste annee, à cause que don Alvaro de Bassan, qui l’avoit attendue es Isles des Assores l’espace de deux mois, s’en estoit retourné sans y avoir eu nulles nouvelles. Depuis ladicte flotte est arrivee à Seville dès le xije du mois passé, ce que Je n’ay peu escrire plustost à vostre majesté pour n’avoir eu la commoditté d’envoyer les lettres, et aussi que J’attendoys de sçavoir particulierement la verité de toute la somme qu’elle a apportee, laquelle se monte à deux millions d’or en argent, sçavoir huict cens mille escuz pour le Roy Philippes, et ung million pour les particuliers, et cent quatre vingtz mille pour les deffunctz qui ont leurs heritiers pardeça. Et oultre ce la valeur de troys cens mille escuz en cochenille et aliofre qui sont perles de semence. De quoy l’Espaigne a faict une merveilleuse feste, comme de chose dont ilz commençoient desja à desesperer pour ceste annee, et aussi pourautant que toute l’esperance et Recours du Roy Philippe, comme autresfoys Je vous ay escript, est desormais fondé là dessus. Ilz estoient en tout vingt deux navires, dont il y en avoit quatre de guerre qui ont amené avecques eulx deux navires de voz subiectz qu’ilz prindrent au port de la Havana, qui est en l’Isle de Cuba à l’opposite de la Florida, où ilz estoient attendant ladicte flotte, que si la bon heure eust voulu qu’elle ne feust point venue acompaignee de navires de guerre comme ilz pensoient, ou bien que lesdictz subiectz (qui estoient de Dieppe et de la Rochelle) eussent eu encores troys navires avecques eulx, Il n’y a point de faulte, ainsi comme J’ay entendu de quelque vingt mesmes qui y estoient, qu’ilz eussent tout emmené en France, et vous eussent faict pour ung coup ung tresgrand et notable service. > et par là sire vostre magestu peult assez evidemment congnoistre combien suivant ce que je vous en ay autresfoys > escrit je seroyz aisé d’oster à vostre ennemy ce grant soullaigement qu’il a de ce monde de dela ou pour mieulx > dires tout le nerf et tout le moyen qu’il a desormais de maintenir la guerre cotre vous > la dicte flotte oultre la susdicte somme qu’elle a apportee à seville avoit aussi desbarqué es isles des assores > une grande quantité d’argent qui est à plusieurs particuliers et se monte bien à huict ou neuf cens mille escuz > dont la pluspart apparient à celluy qui est maintenan viro [...] au perou qui l’avoit faict desbarquer esdictes > [...] les de paeur que s’il feust venu jus [...] à seville les officiers du ro [...] philippes ne s’en feussent > saiz comme ilz avoient accoustumé de les ans passez > mais à ce que je veoy cela ne luy servira pas beaucoub car la royne de portugal a accordé et consenty aulx ssdictz > officiers et ministres du ry philippes que ledict argent seroit enlev porté en espaigne et sur ce a envoyé mandeens > fort ripoureux esdictes les pour le leur faire delivrer ne vou [...] nt poinct permectre que quelque soe d’argent > qui vienne du perou tant petit soit elle se puisse desbarquer en royaume > qui est chos que beaucoup de ge de bien de ce pays icy ont trouvé bn estrange et laquelle le feu roy de portugal > quelque alance qu’il y eust entre eulx neu [...] jamais permise mais il me semble sire que vous luy puez bien > pardonner celle cy puis [...] nest pas la premiere chos où el sest monstree fort passionnee pour roy d’espaigne r > j’ay entendu que par la derniere ote des hurques qui partit d’icy à la my tobre pour aller en flandres elle luy > avoit advance une bonne som d’argent qu’elle avoit tiree des cores du petit roy son neveu La Royne Marie laissa plus de quatre cens mille escuz contant qui estoient la plus part en [portugaises], qu’elle donna à ce que l’on dict au Roy Philippes par son testament. Mais elle donna son bien patrimonial à ung filz bastard que le feu Empereur advoua à sa fin, avoir en la ville D’auguste, auquel ledit seigneur a aussi laissé tout plein d’autres biens. Je vous avois escript que le Roy Philippe envoyoit pour Visroy du Perou Don Diego d’Aze[vedo], gentilhomme Castellan de fort bon entendement. Mais il est advenu qu’il est decedé durant le mois passé, et y a Ja esté nommé par la princesse ung autre en son lieu que l’on dict estre homme bien entendu. La flotte qui le portera pardela partira de Caliz à ceste fin de Janvier. > et peu avant cela en partira d’icy une autre de vingt hurque chargees d’espiceries pour flandres qui vauldroit bien > la peyne que ceulx de dieppe ou de sainct malo y entendissent car elle vaudra infiniement et si n’y aura que deux > meschans navires de guerre à l’accompaigner et elles sont mal armés de toutes choses > celle qui partit d’icy en octobre est encores de present en palice actendant meilleur temps qu’elle n’a eu il s’en > est perdu quelques navires qui estoient de grande valleur les turqs ont poinct assiegé oran où noz voisins avoient > envoyé deux mille hommes comme ilz pensoient qu’ilz deussent faire Qui est tout ce que puis escrire pour ce present à vostre majesté, à laquelle, Sire, Je prie nostre seigneur donner en parfaicte santé tresheureuse et treslongue vye. De Lisbonne le xijme jour de decembre 1558. > ilz devoient huict cens mille escuz aux foires de medina qu’ilz avoient faict retarder pour n’avoier moyen de les > fournir que aprés l’arrivee de la flotte lesquelz ilz ont ja payez et depuis trouvé nouveau credit > ces jours passez ung navire normant print ung petit navire de guerre de la royne qui l’alla à ce que l’on dict > assaillir le prendre dont elle a esté en grant collere et faict retenir les navires de voz subjectz qui estoient > par son royaume mais à la fin je luy ay si bien remonstré le tort que avoit sondict navire qu’elle les a delaisez Vostre treshumble et tresobeissant subiect et serviteur, Le chevalier de Seure. Au Roy, Mon souverain Seigneur. Chevalier de Seure, du [xxvij]me decembre 1558. [R…] […]. Translation no41_en.md # Seure no. 41, Lisbon 1558: English translation Angus Robinson's English, copied 23 Oct 2026 from his edition (letter 41); `>` = enciphered in the manuscript. ## Translation Another letter from the same Commander de Seure to the said king. 1558. Sire, by my last letters of 25 October, which I gave to a Portuguese courier named Antoine Galuan, I wrote to you of the death of Queen Mary and of the distress of our neighbours at the little hope left to them that the fleet they were expecting from Peru would come this year, because Don Álvaro de Bazán, who had waited for it in the Azores for two months, had come back without any news of it. Since then the fleet has arrived at Seville, on the 12th of last month. I could not write this to Your Majesty sooner, because I had no means of sending letters, and also because I was waiting to learn exactly the whole sum it has brought. It amounts to two million in gold, in silver: namely eight hundred thousand écus for King Philip, a million for private persons, and another one hundred and eighty thousand for the deceased whose heirs are here. Besides this there is three hundred thousand écus' worth of cochineal and aliofre, which are seed pearls. Spain has made a marvellous celebration of it, as of a thing they were already beginning to despair of for this year, and also because all King Philip's hope and resource, as I have written to you before, now rests on it. There were twenty-two ships in all, four of them warships, which brought with them two ships of your subjects that they had taken in the port of Havana, which is on the island of Cuba opposite Florida, where they were lying in wait for the fleet. If luck had willed that the fleet had not come escorted by warships, as they expected, or if the said subjects (who were from Dieppe and La Rochelle) had had three more ships with them, there is no doubt at all, as I have heard from some twenty of the very men who were there, that they would have carried it all off to France and done you, at one stroke, a very great and notable service. > From this, Sire, Your Majesty can clearly see how—following what I have previously written to you—I would be glad > to deprive your enemy of this great advantage he draws from the New World: or, more precisely, all the sinews and > resources he now has to sustain the war against you. > Besides the sum already mentioned which it brought to Seville, that fleet had also unloaded in the Azores a large > quantity of silver belonging to several private individuals. It amounts to a good eight or nine hundred thousand > écus. Most of it belongs to the man who is now [viceroy] of Peru. He had it unloaded in those islands for fear > that, if it reached Seville, King Philip’s officers would seize it, as they had been accustomed to do in previous > years. > But, as far as I can see, this will not help him much. The Queen of Portugal has agreed and consented with King > Philip’s officers and ministers that the silver should be removed and carried to Spain. She has therefore sent very > stringent orders to the islands to have it handed over to them, refusing to allow any sum of silver coming from > Peru, however small, to be unloaded in this kingdom. > Many respectable people here have found this very strange. The late King of Portugal would never have allowed it, > whatever alliance existed between them. But it seems to me, Sire, that you can well forgive her this one, since it > is not the first matter in which she has shown such strong attachment to the King of Spain. I have heard that, > through the last fleet of [hulks] which left here in mid-October for Flanders, she advanced him a substantial sum > of money which she had drawn from the treasury of the young king, her nephew. Queen Mary left more than four hundred thousand écus in ready money, mostly in [Portuguese gold coins], which she is said to have given to King Philip by her will. But she gave her patrimonial property to a bastard son whom the late emperor acknowledged at the end of his life as a son he had in the city of Augsburg; the said lord also left him many other possessions. I had written to you that King Philip was sending Don Diego d’[Azevedo] as Viceroy of Peru, a Castilian gentleman of very good understanding. But he died during the past month, and the princess has already named another in his place, said to be a man of good understanding. The fleet which will carry him over there will leave Cádiz at the end of January. > Shortly before that, another fleet of twenty hulks loaded with spices will leave here for Flanders. It would be > well worth the while of the men of Dieppe or Saint-Malo to concern themselves with it, for it will be worth an > immense amount. There will be only two wretched warships to accompany it, and those are poorly armed and equipped > in every respect. > The fleet which left here in October is still at present in Galicia, waiting for better weather than it has had. > Some ships of great value have been lost. The Turks have not besieged Oran, where our neighbours had sent two > thousand men, as they thought the Turks would do. Which is all I can write for the present to Your Majesty, to whom, Sire, I pray that Our Lord may grant, in perfect health, a very happy and very long life. Lisbon, 12 December 1558. > They owed eight hundred thousand écus at the fairs of Medina. They had delayed payment because they had no means of > providing the money until after the fleet’s arrival. They have already paid those sums and have since obtained > fresh credit. > A few days ago a Norman ship captured a small warship of the queen which, it is said, had attacked it in order to > take it. She was very angry at this and had the ships of your subjects then in her kingdom detained. But in the end > I explained so clearly to her the wrong committed by her own ship that she let them go. Your most humble and most obedient subject and servant, the Chevalier de Seure. To the king, my sovereign lord. Chevalier de Seure, [27] December 1558. […]. Translation no43_en.md # Seure no. 43, Lisbon 1558: English translation Angus Robinson's English, copied 23 Oct 2026 from his edition (letter 43); `>` = enciphered in the manuscript. ## Translation Letter from the Commander de Seure to King Henry II, while he was his ambassador in Lisbon. Sire, I wrote to you in my latest letters of 25 October + […] > which I gave to a Portuguese named Antoine Galean, of the death of Queen Mary and of the distress of our neighbours > at the little hope left to them that the fleet they were expecting from Peru would come this year, because Don > Álvaro de Bazán, who had waited for it in the Azores for two months, had come back without any news of it. Since > then the said fleet has arrived at Seville, on the twelfth of last month. I could not write this to Your Majesty > sooner because I had no means of sending letters, and also because I was waiting to learn exactly the whole sum it > has brought. It amounts to two million écus in silver, namely eight hundred thousand écus for King Philip, a > million for private persons, and one hundred and eighty thousand for the deceased whose heirs are here. Besides > this there is three hundred thousand écus’ worth of cochineal and aliofre, which are seed pearls. > Spain has made a marvellous celebration of it, as of a thing they were already beginning to despair of for this > year, and also because all King Philip’s hope and resource, as I have written to you before, now rests on it. There > were twenty-two ships in all, four of them warships, which brought with them two ships of your subjects that they > had taken in the port of Havana, which is on the island of Cuba opposite Florida, where they were lying in wait for > the fleet. If luck had willed that the fleet had not come escorted by warships, as they expected, or if the said > subjects, who were from Dieppe and La Rochelle, had had three more ships with them, there is no doubt at all, as I > have heard from some of the very men who were there, that they would have carried it all off to France and done > you, at one stroke, a very great and notable service. > From this, Sire, Your Majesty can clearly see how—following what I have previously written to you—I would be glad > to deprive your enemy of this great advantage he draws from the New World: or, more precisely, all the sinews and > resources he now has to sustain the war against you. > Besides the sum already mentioned which it brought to Seville, that fleet had also unloaded in the Azores a large > quantity of silver belonging to several private individuals. It amounts to a good eight or nine hundred thousand > écus. Most of it belongs to the man who is now [viceroy] of Peru. He had it unloaded in those islands for fear > that, if it reached Seville, King Philip’s officers would seize it, as they had been accustomed to do in previous > years. > But, as far as I can see, this will not help him much. The Queen of Portugal has agreed and consented with King > Philip’s officers and ministers that the silver should be removed and carried to Spain. She has therefore sent very > stringent orders to the islands to have it handed over to them, refusing to allow any sum of silver coming from > Peru, however small, to be unloaded in this kingdom. > Many respectable people here have found this very strange. The late King of Portugal would never have allowed it, > whatever alliance existed between them. But it seems to me, Sire, that you can well forgive her this one, since it > is not the first matter in which she has shown such strong attachment to the King of Spain. I have heard that, > through the last fleet of [hulks] which left here in mid-October for Flanders, she advanced him a substantial sum > of money which she had drawn from the treasury of the young king, her nephew. > Queen Mary left more than four hundred thousand écus in ready money, mostly in Portuguese gold coins, which she is > said to have given to King Philip by her will. But she gave her patrimonial property to a bastard son whom the late > emperor acknowledged at the end of his life as a son he had in the city of Augsburg; the said lord also left him > many other possessions. I had written to you that King Philip was sending Don Diego de Azevedo as Viceroy of Peru, > a Castilian gentleman of considerable understanding. But he died during this past month, and the princess has > already named another in his place, said to be a man of good understanding. The fleet which will carry him over > there will leave Cádiz at the end of January. > Shortly before that, another fleet of twenty hulks loaded with spices will leave here for Flanders. It would be > well worth the while of the men of Dieppe or Saint-Malo to concern themselves with it, for it will be worth an > immense amount. There will be only two wretched warships to accompany it, and those are poorly armed and equipped > in every respect. > The fleet which left here in October is still at present in Galicia, waiting for better weather than it has had. > Some ships of great value have been lost. The Turks have not besieged Oran, where our neighbours had sent two > thousand men, as they thought the Turks would do. Which is all I can write for the present to Your Majesty, to whom, Sire, I pray that Our Lord may grant, in perfect health, a very happy and very long life. Lisbon, 12 December 1558. Your most humble and most obedient servant and subject, the Chevalier de Seure. > They owed eight hundred thousand écus at the fairs of Medina. They had delayed payment because they had no means of > providing the money until after the fleet’s arrival. They have already paid those sums and have since obtained > fresh credit. > A few days ago a Norman ship captured a small warship of the queen which, it is said, had attacked it in order to > take it. She was very angry at this and had the ships of your subjects then in her kingdom detained. But in the end > I explained so clearly to her the wrong committed by her own ship that she let them go. End. To the king. Seure no. 44, Lisbon 1558 (BnF fr. 3151): the reading Written 23 Oct 2026 (verification 3): Angus Robinson's French reading of the whole letter, copied from his edition <https://angusrobinson.github.io/historical-decipherment/seure/readings.html> (letter 44); he contributed the key and decipherment to this repository in PR #40. Passages quoted with `>` are in cipher in the manuscript; the rest is clear. His conventions: scribal abbreviations expanded, consonantal u written v, a few diacritics added, and in the cipher passages word spaces and doubled letters added back (the cipher writes no doubled letters). `[word]` = his contextual reading, `[…]` = unread. The letter-level decryption is `no44_decryption.txt`. ## Reading Autre lettre dudit Commandeur de Seure au mesme Roy. Sire, Je vous escripviz par mes dernieres lettres du xxvme d’octobre, que Je donnay à ung Courrier Portugais nommé Anthoine Galuan, le decez de la Royne Marie et la peyne en quoy estoient noz voisins pour le peu d’esperance qui leur restoit que la flotte qu’ilz attendoient du Perou deust venir ceste annee, à cause que don Alvaro de Bassan, qui l’avoit attendue es Isles des Assores l’espace de deux mois, s’en estoit retourné sans y avoir eu nulles nouvelles. Depuis ladicte flotte est arrivee à Seville dès le xije du mois passé, ce que Je n’ay peu escrire plustost à vostre majesté pour n’avoir eu la commoditté d’envoyer les lettres, et aussi que J’attendoys de sçavoir particulierement la verité de toute la somme qu’elle a apportee, laquelle se monte à deux millions d’or en argent, sçavoir huict cens mille escuz pour le Roy Philippes, et ung million pour les particuliers, et autres quatre vingtz mille pour les deffunctz qui ont leurs heritiers pardeça. Et oultre ce la valeur de troys cens mille escuz en cochenille et aliofre qui sont perles de semence. De quoy l’Espaigne a faict une merveilleuse feste, comme de chose dont ilz commençoient desja à desesperer pour ceste annee, et aussi pourautant que toute l’esperance et Recours du Roy Philippe, comme autresfoys Je vous ay escript, est desormais fondé là dessus. Ilz estoient en tout vingt deux navires, dont il y en avoit quatre de guerre qui ont amené avecques eulx deux navires de voz subiectz qu’ilz prindrent au port de la Havana, qui est en l’Isle de Cuba à l’opposite de la Florida, où ilz estoient attendant ladicte flotte, que si la bon heure eust voulu qu’elle ne feust point venue acompaignee de navires de guerre comme ilz pensoient, ou bien que lesdictz subiectz (qui estoient de Dieppe et de la Rochelle) eussent eu encores troys navires avecques eulx, Il n’y a point de faulte, ainsi comme J’ay entendu de quelque vingt mesmes qui y estoient, qu’ilz eussent tout emmené en France, et vous eussent faict pour ung coup ung tresgrand et notable service. > la sire vostre magesté peult assez evidemment cognoistre combien suivant ce que je vous en ay autresfoys escrit je > seroys aisé d’oster à vostre ennemy ce grant soullaigement qu’il a de ce monde de dela ou pour mieul dires tout le > nerf et tout le moyen qu’il a desormais de maintenir la guerre cotre vous > la dicte flotte oultre la susdicte somme qu’elle a apportee à seville avoit aussi desbarqué es isles des assores > une grande quantité d’argent qui est à plusieurs particuliers et se monte bien à huict ou neuf cens mille escuz > dont la pluspart appartient à celluy qui est maintenant viroy au perou qui l’avoit faict desbarquer esdictes isles > de paeur que s’il feust venu jusques à seville les officiers du roy philippes ne s’en feussent saisiz comme ilz > avoient accoustumé de faire les ans passez > mais à ce que je veoy cela ne luy servira pas beaucoup car la royne de portugal a accordé et consenty aux susdictz > officiers et ministres du roy philippes que ledict argent seroit enlevé et porté en espaigne et sur ce a envoyé > mandemens fort rigoureux esdictes isles pour le leur faire delivrer ne voulant poinct permectre que quelque somme > d’argent qui vienne du perou tant petite soit elle se puisse desbarquer en ce royaume > qui est chose que beaucoup de gens de bien de ce pays icy ont trouvé bien estrange et laquelle le feu roy de > portugal quelque alliance qu’il y eust entre eulxe n’eust jamais permise mais il me semble sire que vous luy pouvez > bien pardonner celle cy puisque ce nest pas la premiere chose où elle sest monstree bien fort passionnee pour le > roy d’espaigne car j’ay entendu que par la derniere flotte des hurques qui partit d’icy à la my octobre pour aller > en flandres elle luy avoit advance une bonne somme d’argent qu’elle avoit tiree des coffres du petit roy son > neppveu La Royne Marie laissa plus de quatre cens mille escuz contant qui estoient la plus part en portugaises, qu’elle donna à ce que l’on dict au Roy Philippe par son testament. Mais elle donna son bien patrimonial à ung filz bastard que le feu Empereur advoua à sa fin, avoir en la ville d’Auguste, auquel ledit seigneur a aussi laissé tout plain d’autres biens. Je vous avoys escript que le Roy Philippes envoyoit pour Visroy du Perou Don Diego d’Azevedo, gentilhomme Castellan de fort bon entendement. Mais il est advenu qu’il est decedé durant ce mois passé, et y a Ja esté nommé par la princesse ung autre en son lieu, que l’on dict estre homme bien entendu. La flotte qui le portera pardela partira de Caliz à ceste fin de Janvier. > et peu avant celle en partira d’icy une autre de vingt hourques chargees d’espiceries pour flandres qui vauldroient > bien la peyne que ceulx de dieppe ou de sainct malo y entendissent car elle vauldra infiniement et si n’y aura que > deux meschans navires de puere à l’accompaigner et elles sont mal armés de toutes choses > celle qui partit d’icy en octobre est encores de present en galice actendant meilleur temps qu’elle n’a eu il s’en > est perdu quelques navires qui estoient de grande valleur les turqs ont point assiegé oren où noz voysins avoient > envoyé deux mille hommes comme ilz pensoient qu’ilz deussent faire Qui est tout ce que puis escrire pour ce present à vostre majesté, à laquelle, Sire, Je prie nostre seigneur donner en parfaicte santé tresheureuse et treslongue vye. De Lisbonne le xijme jour de decembre 1558. > ilz devoient huict cens mille escuz aulx foires de medina qu’ilz avoient faict retarder pour n’avoir moyen de les > fournir que aprés l’arrivee de la flotte lesquelz ilz ont ja payez et depuis trouvé nouveau credict > ces jours passez ung navire normant prist ung petit navire de guerre de la royne qui l’alla à ce que l’on dict > assaillir pour le prendre dont elle a esté en grant collere faict retenir les navires de voz subjez qui estoient > par son royaume mais à la fin je luy ay si bien remonstré le tort que avoit sondict navire qu’elle les a delaisez Vostre treshumble et tresobeissant serviteur et subiect, Le chevalier de Seure. Et par là, Sire, vostre majesté peult assez evidemment cognoistre combien suyuant ce que je vous en ay aultresfoys escript, Il seroyt aisé d’oster à vostre ennemy ce grant soullaigement quil a de ce monde de dela, ou pour myeulx dire tout le nerf et tout le moyen quil a desormais de maintenir la guerre contre vous. Ladicte flotte, oultre la susdicte somme quelle a apportee à Seville, avoit aussi desbarqué es Isles des Assores une grande quantité dargent qui est à plusieurs particuliers, et se monte bien à huit ou neuf cens mil escus, dont la pluspart appartient à celluy qui est maintenant Visroy au Perou, qui lavoit faict desbarquer es Isles de peur que sil fust venu jusques à Seville les officiers du Roy Philippes ne sen feussent saisiz, comme ilz avoient accoustumé de faire les ans passez. Mais à ce que je voy cela ne luy servira pas beaucoup. Car la Royne de Portugal a accordé et consenty aux susdictz officiers et ministres du Roy Philippes que ces argens soient enlevez et portez en Espaigne. Et sur ce a envoyé mandemens fort rigoreux esdictes Isles pour les leur faire delivrer, ne voullant poinct permettre que quelque somme dargent qui vienne du Perou, tant petite soit elle, se puisse desbarquer en ce Royaulme. Qui est chose que beaucoup de gens de bien de ce pays dicy ont trouvé bien estrange, et laquelle le feu Roy de Portugal, quelque alliance quil y eust entre eulx, neust jamais permise. Mais il me semble, Sire, que vous luy pouvez bien pardonner celle cy, puisque ce nest pas la premiere chose où elle sest monstree bien fort passionnee pour le Roy despaigne. Car jay entendu que par la derniere flotte des hourques qui partit dicy à la my octobre pour aller en Flandres, elle luy avoit advance une bonne somme dargent quelle avoit tiree des coffres du petit Roy son nepveu. Et peu avant cela en partira dicy une aultre de vingt hourques chargees despiceries pour Flandres, qui vauldroient bien la peine que ceulx de Dieppe ou de Sainct Malo y entendissent. Car elles vauldra infiniment. Et si ny aura que deux meschans navires de guerre a laccompaigner, et ceulx sont mal armez de toutes choses. Celle qui partit dicy en octobre est encores de present en Galice attendant meilleur temps quelle na eu. Il sen est perdu quelques navires qui estoient de grande valleur. Les Turcqs nont point assiegé Oran, où noz voisins avoient envoyé deux mil hommes, que ilz pensoient quilz deussent faire. Ilz debvoient huict cens mil escus aux foires de Medina, quilz avoient faict retarder pour navoir moyen de les fournir que aprés larrivee de la flotte. Lesquelz ilz ont ja payez, et depuis trouvé nouveau credict. Ces jours passez ung navire normand print ung petit navire de guerre de la Royne qui lalla, à ce que lon dict, assaillir pour le prendre. Dont elle a esté en grand collere, et faict retenir les navires de voz subjectz qui estoient par son Royaume. Mais à la fin je luy ay si bien remonstré le tort que avoit son navire quelle les a relaschez. Au Roy, Mon souverain Seigneur. Chevalier de Seure, du xijme de decembre 1558. Dupplicata. Translation no44_en.md # Seure no. 44, Lisbon 1558: English translation Angus Robinson's English, copied 23 Oct 2026 from his edition (letter 44); `>` = enciphered in the manuscript. ## Translation Another letter from the said Commander de Seure to the same king. Sire, by my last letters of 25 October, which I gave to a Portuguese courier named Antoine Galuan, I wrote to you of the death of Queen Mary and of the distress of our neighbours at the little hope left to them that the fleet they were expecting from Peru would come this year, because Don Álvaro de Bazán, who had waited for it in the Azores for two months, had come back without any news of it. Since then the fleet has arrived at Seville, on the 12th of last month. I could not write this to Your Majesty sooner, because I had no means of sending letters, and also because I was waiting to learn exactly the whole sum it has brought. It amounts to two million in gold, in silver: namely eight hundred thousand écus for King Philip, a million for private persons, and another eighty thousand for the deceased whose heirs are here. Besides this there is three hundred thousand écus' worth of cochineal and aliofre, which are seed pearls. Spain has made a marvellous celebration of it, as of a thing they were already beginning to despair of for this year, and also because all King Philip's hope and resource, as I have written to you before, now rests on it. There were twenty-two ships in all, four of them warships, which brought with them two ships of your subjects that they had taken in the port of Havana, which is on the island of Cuba opposite Florida, where they were lying in wait for the fleet. If luck had willed that the fleet had not come escorted by warships, as they expected, or if the said subjects (who were from Dieppe and La Rochelle) had had three more ships with them, there is no doubt at all, as I have heard from some twenty of the very men who were there, that they would have carried it all off to France and done you, at one stroke, a very great and notable service. > From this, Sire, Your Majesty can clearly see how—following what I have previously written to you—I would be glad > to deprive your enemy of this great advantage he draws from the New World: or, more precisely, all the sinews and > resources he now has to sustain the war against you. > Besides the sum already mentioned which it brought to Seville, that fleet had also unloaded in the Azores a large > quantity of silver belonging to several private individuals. It amounts to a good eight or nine hundred thousand > écus. Most of it belongs to the man who is now [viceroy] of Peru. He had it unloaded in those islands for fear > that, if it reached Seville, King Philip’s officers would seize it, as they had been accustomed to do in previous > years. > But, as far as I can see, this will not help him much. The Queen of Portugal has agreed and consented with King > Philip’s officers and ministers that the silver should be removed and carried to Spain. She has therefore sent very > stringent orders to the islands to have it handed over to them, refusing to allow any sum of silver coming from > Peru, however small, to be unloaded in this kingdom. > Many respectable people here have found this very strange. The late King of Portugal would never have allowed it, > whatever alliance existed between them. But it seems to me, Sire, that you can well forgive her this one, since it > is not the first matter in which she has shown such strong attachment to the King of Spain. I have heard that, > through the last fleet of [hulks] which left here in mid-October for Flanders, she advanced him a substantial sum > of money which she had drawn from the treasury of the young king, her nephew. Queen Mary left more than four hundred thousand écus in ready money, mostly in Portuguese gold coins, which she is said to have given to King Philip by her will. But she gave her patrimonial property to a bastard son whom the late emperor acknowledged at the end of his life as a son he had in the city of Augsburg; the said lord also left him many other possessions. I had written to you that King Philip was sending Don Diego de Azevedo as Viceroy of Peru, a Castilian gentleman of very good understanding. But he died during this past month, and the princess has already named another in his place, said to be a man of good understanding. The fleet which will carry him over there will leave Cádiz at the end of January. > Shortly before that, another fleet of twenty hulks loaded with spices will leave here for Flanders. It would be > well worth the while of the men of Dieppe or Saint-Malo to concern themselves with it, for it will be worth an > immense amount. There will be only two wretched warships to accompany it, and those are poorly armed and equipped > in every respect. > The fleet which left here in October is still at present in Galicia, waiting for better weather than it has had. > Some ships of great value have been lost. The Turks have not besieged Oran, where our neighbours had sent two > thousand men, as they thought the Turks would do. Which is all I can write for the present to Your Majesty, to whom, Sire, I pray that Our Lord may grant, in perfect health, a very happy and very long life. Lisbon, 12 December 1558. > They owed eight hundred thousand écus at the fairs of Medina. They had delayed payment because they had no means of > providing the money until after the fleet’s arrival. They have already paid those sums and have since obtained > fresh credit. > A few days ago a Norman ship captured a small warship of the queen which, it is said, had attacked it in order to > take it. She was very angry at this and had the ships of your subjects then in her kingdom detained. But in the end > I explained so clearly to her the wrong committed by her own ship that she let them go. Your most humble and most obedient servant and subject, the Chevalier de Seure. From this, Sire, Your Majesty can see quite plainly how easy it would be, as I have written to you before, to take from your enemy the great relief he draws from that world over there, or rather the whole sinew and means he now has of keeping up the war against you. The said fleet, besides the sum mentioned above which it brought to Seville, had also unloaded in the Azores a large quantity of money belonging to several private persons. It amounts to fully eight or nine hundred thousand écus. Most of it belongs to the present viceroy of Peru, who had it unloaded in the islands for fear that, if it went as far as Seville, King Philip’s officers would seize it, as they had been accustomed to do in previous years. But from what I can see, this will not help him much. For the Queen of Portugal has agreed with the aforesaid officers and ministers of King Philip that this money should be taken away and carried to Spain. She has therefore sent very strict orders to the islands to make it be delivered to them. She does not wish to allow any sum coming from Peru, however small, to be unloaded in this kingdom. Many honourable people here have found this very strange. The late King of Portugal would never have allowed it, whatever alliance there may have been between them. But it seems to me, Sire, that you can readily forgive her this instance, since it is not the first matter in which she has shown herself strongly partial to the King of Spain. For I have heard that, by the last fleet of hulks which left here in mid-October for Flanders, she had advanced him a considerable sum of money taken from the coffers of the young king, her grandson. Shortly before that, another fleet of twenty hulks loaded with spices will leave here for Flanders. It would be well worth the while of the men of Dieppe or Saint-Malo to concern themselves with it, for it will be worth an immense amount. There will be only two wretched warships to accompany it, and those are poorly armed and equipped in every respect. The fleet which left here in October is still at present in Galicia, waiting for better weather than it has had. Some ships of great value have been lost. The Turks have not besieged Oran, where our neighbours had sent two thousand men, as they thought [the Turks] would do. They owed eight hundred thousand écus at the fairs of Medina. They had delayed payment because they had no means of providing the money until after the fleet’s arrival. They have already paid those sums and have since obtained fresh credit. A few days ago a Norman ship captured a small warship of the queen which, it is said, had attacked it in order to take it. She was very angry at this and had the ships of your subjects then in her kingdom detained. But in the end I explained so clearly to her the wrong committed by her own ship that she released them. To the king, my sovereign lord. Chevalier de Seure, 12 December 1558. Duplicate. Key: KEY_AND_DECRYPTION.txt , KEY.svg

siena12.html#date

The letter gives only the day and the indiction: “a dì dieci de marzo, sesta indictione”. George Lasry dates it to 10 March 1413. The sixth indiction fell in 1413, a king was then on the throne of Naples, and Ludovico Migliorati, lord of Fermo from 1405 to 1428, was alive. That puts the letter three weeks before the captain’s letter from Perugia of 30 March 1413, when Ladislaus was gathering Sforza, Tartaglia and his other captains against Paolo Orsini in the Marche ( nos. 20 and 23 ). Sforza had been a widower since 1411 and married Caterina Alopo in 1415, so the King’s offer came to nothing. The Malatesta and Brancaleoni girls are not yet identified.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 14 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (78% of the cipher) Contributed by George Lasry (solution) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (78% of the cipher) The letters Two reports to the Signori of Siena from a Cristofano writing on the Milanese side of the war over Lucca. No. 6 is dated 19 February with no year. No. 24 has no date, and its signature is on the back. Where Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2, nos. 6 and 24, photographed on DECODE as R4795 and R4812 (catalogued “1500–1599”, no transcription). The key is in fasc. 1 of the same busta, DECODE R4755. The cipher Homophonic substitution. There are 36 signs for 21 letters, four each for a, e, i, o and u. The key also has 7 nulls and 18 signs for whole words, five of which occur here (Lucca, Piccinino, Duca di Milano, Viniziani, Fiorentini). There is no word division. How it was deciphered George Lasry recovered the key from the ciphertext alone with the built-in cryptanalysis of CTTS, and refined it with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. The filed key sheet R4755 was found to match afterwards. Here, our own transcription of 24 September was decoded with that key. With the key read off the sheet by eye, it gives the same letters as his reading at 69% of positions. After fitting our sign labels, the figure is 88–91%. What it says Piccinino “cominciò a mandare quatrocento per fare aprire la via per andare a Lucca”. No. 24 reports that the marquis of Mantua and Taliano have come to terms with the Duke of Milan, and that the Emperor will not come. Still open About a quarter of no. 24 decrypts to letters that make no sense, probably from misread signs on a small photograph. The back of no. 24 is decoded here only in stretches. No. 24 is therefore decoded, not read: only no. 6 reads, about 29% of the cipher. On 23 October 2026 no. 24 and its neighbouring records (R4811, R4813) were fetched again: they carry no attachment, transcription or decipherment, and the images are the same small photographs (20–25 px a sign), so a sign-level re-check needs the original in the Archivio di Stato di Siena. The writer’s surname is unread. Credit Solution by George Lasry, with CTTS built-in cryptanalysis, refined by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, sent to Daniel Bourdeau on 14 October 2026 and restated in his report of 17 October 2026 on the Concistoro 2308 ciphers. The verification, the decoding of no. 24’s back, its signature and the dating check were done here.

The two letters belong to fascicle 2, “Lettere in cifra”, of Concistoro 2308 in the Siena state archive. Our survey of the busta ( siena1421 ) transcribed both on 24 September 2026. It found that they share one system, but no filed key fitted and every ciphertext-only solver failed on them. Each opens with a clear salutation, “Magnifici et potentes domini domini mei singularissimi”, and continues in cipher to the end. No. 6 (DECODE R4795): 15 lines, 1,051 signs in our transcription (1,007 in the solver’s count). It is dated 19 February and signed “Cristofano de Mont[…] si racomanda”. No. 24 (DECODE R4812): 38 lines on the text side, 2,638 signs in our transcription (2,559 in his). Eight more cipher lines run over onto the back, above the address “Magnifici et potenti signiori e … Capitano di popolo della citta di Siena”. The key, R4755, is a single sheet in fascicle 1 headed “Cifra cum Christofano” followed by a surname that is hard to read. DECODE reads it “Ghinucci[?]”. The signature of no. 6, “Mont‹vccia›” in the solver’s reading, suggests something like Montucci instead. That is left as a question. Our own survey had listed this sheet on 24 September but never tried it on these two letters. The key R4755. The cipher signs stand under the alphabet, with the extra homophones in columns under a, e, i, o and u. Below are the nulls, “Nichil importantes”. The 18 word signs follow further down the sheet. Image: Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308 fasc. 1, via DECODE R4755. On the DECODE photograph the sheet gives 36 letter signs (k, h and x included, nothing for y), 7 nulls and 18 word signs. The word signs are Papa, Fiorentini, Viniziani, Duca di Milano, Nicholo Piccinino, Conte Francesco, Luccha, Pisa, Pistoia, Siena, Pontremoli, Parma, Pietrasanta, Genova, Bologna, Messer Thomaso, Cavagli and Fanti. This matches the solver’s description. His count of word signs that occur also holds: five of the 18. Our transcription had already marked the same point-framed signs as “probable name codes”.

Square brackets mark letters he supplied; ‹…› marks letters that decrypt but make no sense. … e crede di certo lui s[t]a aconcio co’ Viniziani … [se] avete bis[o]gnio di gente d’arme, qua se n’ trovarebbe degli uomeni valenti, e ven[i]r{d}e a dì quatordici di questo Piccinino cominc[i]ò a mandare {eo} quatrocento per fare [e] [a]prire la via per andare a Lucca; e à mandato i tronbetti per le brigate, {v} che sieno q[u]i per questa semana; e se ’l tenpo sarà mai più buono, se partiranno per tucto questo mese. … E data a dì dicenove di Febrai[o]. Cristofano de Mont‹vccia› ‹·› si rac[o]manda. E il ea non s’achordarà col Duca di Milano, perché vuole troppe cose. A man has settled his accounts with the Venetians and is thought to have taken service with them. Men-at-arms could be had for Siena. On the 14th Piccinino began sending four hundred men to open the road to Lucca, and trumpeters have gone to call up the companies. The chancellor of messer Antonio Petrucci has come back from Milan. A postscript says someone will not come to terms with the Duke of Milan “because he wants too many things”. In this reading 62 of the 941 decrypted letters (6.6%) stand in ‹…›, scattered single words. Three of them come from one sign. The key writes z as a compound, an S with a small o attached (“So”), while a plain S is o ; read as two signs, the z disappears. Restored, it gives “d’avere buona aduertenza ” (good care), “per facti di Vincenzo da Camerino”, and “tornò da Milano senza avere fact[o] nula ”: Petrucci’s chancellor came back from Milan without having done anything , where the reading above has him going “to Siena” (the last word needs the key’s 4 = u ). All three places were checked on the photograph. With them no. 6 reads 896 of 939 decrypted letters as sense (95.4%). The revised reading is kept beside the submitted one in the repository.

… e Lucca tiene de certo il {e}r[e] s’achordarà con lui … e q[u]i à man{n}dato uno ‹svvfai›‹iglioatire› a Lucca che no[n] t[i] besogniarà ‹lvinaoa› a sochorare Lucca … il marchese di Manto{·}[v]a è acordato col Duca di Milano … e certo si tiene lo ’npe[r]adore non ver{e}rà; e Lucca dice che Taliano [s]’è aconcio col Duca di Milano … Ambassadors of Lucca, Camerino and the Florentines are present. The castles of the countryside have been ordered to bring in provisions. Lucca is confident that “the king” will come to terms with it and that no relief will be needed. Duke Albert, the King of Hungary and the Council of Basel are named. A company has stopped ninety miles away. No. 24 is much harder to read than no. 6: 623 of its 2,286 decrypted letters (27.3%) stand in ‹…›, in runs of up to 24 letters. The photograph gives only 20–25 pixels per sign, half the resolution of no. 6. Our own transcription of this page flagged c/ĉ/e, a/□ and 0/θ as unsafe there, and the key separates exactly those signs. The same correction, then a pass run by run against our transcription and the photograph, turns 23 of these gaps into words. Seven are settled on the image, among them “e grandi ghiacciate ” (great frosts), “lo a Chamerino ”, and three word signs the reading above had dropped (two Viniziani and a Duca di Milano , each framed by points). Three follow from the z and u of the key: “perché e’ or ’l tenpo si cominca a dirizare ” (the weather begins to mend) and “ senza fallo il marchese di Mantova è acordato col Duca di Milano”. Thirteen more are fixed by the sense around them, such as “uno suo famiglio a dire a Lucca” and “il ducha Alberto, duca d’Isterlic, che è a facto re d’Ongnaria”. No. 24 now reads 1,815 of 2,279 decrypted letters as sense (79.6%; 75.2% counting only the changes checked on the image). The longest runs still do not read: on the photograph their signs are as transcribed, or too small to tell apart. The back, decoded here. The solver’s reading stops at the foot of the text side, but the letter runs on for eight lines on the back. Our first-pass transcription of those lines (637 signs), mapped onto the key, gives these stretches among unread runs: “… cose sono … segrete …” “… umilemente mi racoma[ndo] …” “… a la uostra … Signoria …” and at the end “… Signioria. Crist[ofa]no … si racoman[d]a”. So no. 24 is not unsigned. It is by the same Cristofano as no. 6 (graded C, probable).

As the solver tells it, the key was first recovered by cryptanalysis from the ciphertext only. His PDF of 14 October put this to Claude with the help of Astra, and the find of the matching key sheet, among the 43 filed keys of fascicle 1, to Astra. His consolidated report of 17 October puts it as CTTS’s built-in cryptanalysis, refined by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, with the filed key R4755 found to match afterwards. His PDF gives the reading and the key, but not his sign-by-sign transcription. The test here therefore uses ours: made on 24 September by three transcribers working from the DECODE photographs, before any key was known, with its own names for the signs. Test No. 6 No. 24 Our transcription, key read off the sheet by eye (31 sign labels, no fitting): same letter as his reading 650/941 = 69.1% 1,586/2,286 = 69.4% Same, sign labels fitted by alignment, one value per label 751/941 = 79.8% 1,743/2,286 = 76.2% Same, labels that our transcribers used for two key signs counted for both 852/941 = 90.5% 2,017/2,286 = 88.2% Italian n-gram score of our decode, per letter (key by eye / fitted) −3.53 / −3.06 −3.62 / −3.34 Shuffled-key control, mean of 20 (best) −4.77 (−4.22) / −4.03 (−3.63) −4.77 (−4.19) / −4.04 (−3.56) His reading, same model −2.42 −2.69 The language model is the project’s Renaissance Italian model (it-cinquecento, order 5, without spaces). Where our decode and his reading differ, the cause is our transcription, not his key. Our label t covers three key signs: + (o), t (q) and an o+t ligature (f). Our c covers h and an e-like n. Our 0 sometimes stands for the i-sign “+o” with its cross unseen. Our d and u are one a-sign. The circle we called CIRC is both Lucca and Piccinino. No key value had to change. The doubled p p that our notes had flagged as a unit is the key’s fourth sign for e.
siena1431.html#date

The PDF dates both letters to about 1431–1432, during the war of Florence against Lucca (1429–1433). It reasons from Piccinino, from Sigismund in Italy (1431–1433), from the Council of Basel (1431) and from the marquis of Mantua. That fits no. 6. No. 24 fits a second campaign at least as well. Sigismund made Gianfrancesco Gonzaga marquis of Mantua in September 1433, after the peace of Ferrara had ended that war in April. Gonzaga left Venetian service for Filippo Maria Visconti in 1438, when Florence was again at war with Lucca. Albert of Austria became King of Hungary in December 1437; the revised reading of no. 24 has “il ducha Alberto, duca d’Isterlic, che è a facto re d’Ongnaria”, made king. No. 24 also has “a Fer[r]ara pe[r] lo presente”: the Council moved from Basel to Ferrara in January 1438. No. 24 therefore belongs to early 1438. Sigismund died the same month, and “the Emperor will not come” fits either period. So the range here is c. 1431–1438. No. 6 falls in February 1431 or February 1437/38 (1430 or 1436/37 in Sienese style). This is graded M: it comes from the decrypted content, and the archive dates neither letter.

A papal dispatch intercepted and printed as 955 digits by Mazzini’s paper in 1848, with a prize for its decipherment. The key was recovered from the ciphertext alone: two-digit letters and syllables, 5 as word divider, and a four-digit alphabetical code. The text is a counter-order written the day after the nuncio had left; eleven code groups stay open. 37 34 46 8247 5 01 8734 8760 8904 8739 8413 5 64 8 5 41 21 16 46 11 96 44 69 70 09 26 5 12 5 43 94 70 67 76 42 5 92 70 36 74 46 70 70 5 42 · di Lutzovv di Rome → Innsbruck · numerical nomenclator: two-digit letters and syllables, four-digit alphabetical code · 15 June 1848 Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà, Rome, 15 June 1848 from Cardinal Soglia → to Viale Prelà Go to the full text ↓ Intercepted in the post at Turin and printed by Mazzini’s L’Italia del Popolo , Milan, 30 June 1848, as 955 digits with “a prize of some size for the best interpreter of these figures” · posted on Cipherbrain in 2014 as an open challenge; no decipherment was posted there, and none was found elsewhere The key was recovered from the ciphertext alone: 5 is the word break, pairs of the other digits are letters and syllables, 8XXX is a code in alphabetical order. Everything decrypts except eleven code groups. The dispatch is a counter-order telling the nuncio to stay with the Emperor, written the day after he had left. Where A Roman broadsheet (Tip. Puccinelli, 1848), posted by Klaus Schmeh on Cipherbrain in December 2014; the image came from Tony Gaffney. The cipher A small nomenclator: the digit 5 separates words, two-digit groups are letters with homophones and syllables, and four-digit groups beginning with 8 are a one-part code in alphabetical order. How it was read The key was recovered from the ciphertext alone, from a 955-digit block using Joe’s transcription (corrected on line 12). Ten code words were supplied from context and checked against the alphabetical order. What it says A counter-order: because of new circumstances the nuncio is to stay at Innsbruck with the Emperor, and the earlier instruction about asking for his passports is suspended. Still open Eleven code groups, among them the date of the earlier letter, cannot be recovered from this one message.
soglia1848.html#document

The image Schmeh posted, which Tony Gaffney had sent him, is not the Milan paper itself but a Roman broadsheet: Dispaccio del Card. Soglia. Tratto dal giornale l’Italia del Popolo 30 Giugno , printed by Clemente Puccinelli in Via Lata. Commenters identified the paper within a day (Helmut Winkler, Hans Jahr: L’Italia del Popolo , the organ of Mazzini’s Associazione nazionale italiana, year I, no. 40). Its preface says what the editors knew: The broadsheet’s head and preface: “a faithful and most exact copy of a letter and a dispatch of Cardinal Soglia to Mgr Viale Prelà, apostolic nuncio to the Emperor of Austria at Innsbruck. The cipher is, for now, unknown to us, and we entrust it as it is to the curiosity of our readers … Letter and dispatch, though dated at Rome, were posted on 20 June at Turin, addressed to … Mgr Michele Viale Prelà, archbishop of Carthage, Innsbruck.” Image: Broadsheet Dispaccio del Card. Soglia (Rome, Tip. Puccinelli, 1848), image from Tony Gaffney via K. Schmeh, Cipherbrain (13 December 2014). Two documents follow. The first is a letter wholly in clear, no. 6235: the Pope has read the nuncio’s two letters of 27 May and approves his decision to follow the Emperor at the Austrian foreign minister’s invitation; “what the instructions are, you will learn from my contemporary dispatch in cipher”; the language of the Ministry is not to be confused with the Pope’s own will. The second is the cipher dispatch, which opens in clear (“having news of your departure from Vienna and of your removal to that city, where His Imperial Majesty now resides, I take the occasion to send you this dispatch there”), then runs fourteen lines of digits, breaks into clear for one sentence (“To save time you must at once make the present dispatch known”), ends with two more lines of digits, and is signed G. Card. Soglia , Rome, 15 June 1848. At the foot: Un premio non tenue è destinato al migliore interprete di queste cifre . The dispatch begins. The first line reads 37 34 46 8247 5 01 8734 8760 8904 8739 8413 5 , Con mio (foglio) del [date] … The vertical rules are fold lines of the sheet; the scattered dots above and below the digits are ignored, and the decryption does not need them. Image: Broadsheet Dispaccio del Card. Soglia (Rome, Tip. Puccinelli, 1848), image from Tony Gaffney via K. Schmeh, Cipherbrain (13 December 2014). The transcription used is Joe’s, posted as the fourth comment under Schmeh’s article on 15 December 2014. It was checked line by line against the scan cut into strips, and it is right except in one place: on line 12 the printed …2251242496774740906… lost a 4 . Corrected, the block is 955 digits. The printer made one error of his own, taken up below. Where the print has a dot in the line ( 3099.7.39 , 67367.067 ), it is ignored likewise: the text decrypts without it.
soglia1848.html#system

Three things are visible in the digits before any key is guessed. 5 divides words. Split at every 5, the block falls into 102 non-empty runs, and 92 of them have an even number of digits. The ten odd ones are seven lone digits 1 to 4, one run that ends in such a digit, one print error and one stray 8. A lone 1 , 2 , 3 or 4 is punctuation: comma, semicolon, colon, full stop. The full stop 4 stands immediately before the printed clear sentence. The 5 is not written at every word boundary; short words are often run together ( conmio , oper , perdilui ). 8 marks a code group. The digit 8 never occurs as the second digit of a pair. Where it occurs it begins a four-digit group: 8247 , 8319 , 8620 . Pairs are drawn from the eight digits 0 1 2 3 4 6 7 9, which gives a table of 64 cells. The pairs are letters and syllables. 355 pairs in all, 56 distinct: more symbols than an alphabet needs, far fewer than a code. The table as recovered. Rows are the first digit, columns the second; a dash is a cell that does not occur in this message. 0 1 2 3 4 6 7 9 0 – del no k s ta al a 1 chi m in – ma c – p 2 gli e ne la n che – – 3 qu da – b mi t con d 4 de l di se e o al r 6 il f – per si st i te 7 v (u) ti g – z to b p 9 c f l d g m n s Homophones: e 21, 44; b 33, 77; c 16, 90; d 39, 93; f 61, 91; g 72, 94; l 41, 92; m 11, 96; n 24, 97; p 19, 79; s 04, 99; al 07, 47. The eight empty cells (00 13 17 27 29 32 62 73) do not occur in this message. a has one cell, 09, and it is the commonest group in the text (38 times). 70 is u and v ; doubled, it is the w of 92 70 36 74 46 70 70 Lutzovv . Code words and stems. The 8XXX groups stand for whole words or for stems that letters complete: 40 20 8424 67 degli (ordin)i , 19 09 04 99 09 8446 67 passa(port)i , 41 21 8433 16 67 19 46 le (parte)cipo . Nine are fixed by their context beyond reasonable doubt, and their values rise with the alphabet: 8319 8340 8374 8422 8424 8429 8433 8446 8620 Imperatore istruzione Monsignor opportuno ordin- Padre parte port- Roma This is the design Kent Ramliden described in his comment of 7 January 2015 from the cipher of the Vienna nunciature at the Congress of 1814: dinomes for letters and syllables, a four-digit series for words and names, and 5 as a word divider. There, the word series began with 7 and the dinomes avoided 5 and 7; here it begins with 8 and they avoid 5 and 8. His parse, with 7 as the marker, could not work on this text; with 8 it does. The print error: the first passaporti is printed 19 09 0 5 99 09 8446 67 . A 5 inside it would cut the word in two. The second passaporti , later in the text, is 19 09 04 99 09 8446 67 , so the printer set a 5 for a 4. A lone 8 after si on line 1 is unexplained.
soglia1848.html#method

Simple substitution fails, and the failure is informative. With 5 taken as the word break, a simple-substitution solver (simulated annealing, one letter per pair) with 5-gram models in Italian, French and Latin got nowhere, about −3.4 nats a character in each language. The same solver was run on a synthetic control: an Italian text of the same length, enciphered homophonically in 68 two-digit symbols with the same word breaks ( synth.py ). It decrypted the control exactly. So the solver was sound, and the pairs could not all be single letters. A nomenclator solver. The next solver let each pair stand for a letter or a common syllable, one value per pair, with the 8XXX groups held out as unknown words. Among its outputs, runs such as circostanze , intendendosi and indirizzata were whole Italian words of chancery prose that no chance key would give. Fixed words, then decryption by hand. Those three words were fixed and the solver rerun; after that the text was decrypted by hand, word by word, one pair at a time, each value checked against every other occurrence of the pair. Lutzovv and Inspruck fell out of the letters. Morichini is spelled out in the last line. The code. Once the letters were known, the 8XXX groups could be parsed out and set in order: Imperatore 8319 before istruzione 8340 before Monsignor 8374, and so on to Roma 8620. A one-part code in alphabetical order lets the value of an unknown group be estimated from where it falls between known ones (§05).

Ten code groups are supplied from context: foglio , Signor , Colonia , è , lontan- , guerra , com- , Tuttavia , cotest- , col fine di . An alphabetical code allows a check that is independent of context. A straight line was fitted to the nine firm anchors, code value against rank in a sorted list of the 1,500 commonest words of a 19th-century Italian corpus (slope about 0.47 code values per word; rankfit2.py ). The anchors themselves scatter about the line by 10 to 60 values, so that is the tolerance. Each context reading then gets a predicted value from its own rank: Code Reading Predicted Off by 8110 col (fine di) 8114 −4 8116 Colonia 8117 −1 8120 com(e) 8122 −2 8122 cotest(a) 8145 −23 8211 è 8199 +12 8247 foglio 8245 +2 8310 guerra 8289 +21 8346 lontan(a) 8339 +7 8632 Signor 8596 +36 8737 Tuttavia 8665 +72 Firm anchors against the same line: Imperatore +24, istruzione +21, Monsignor −14, opportuno −10, ordin- −11, Padre −10, parte −18, port- −41, Roma +60. Four readings land within five values of prediction, five more within the anchors’ own scatter, and one, Tuttavia , beyond it. The two largest residuals, Signor and Tuttavia , both lie beyond Roma , the last firm anchor, and both are positive, as is Roma ’s own: the late alphabet is denser in this code than in the word list, and the line extrapolates past it. The readings also come out in the right order among themselves ( col < Colonia < come < cotesta < è < foglio < guerra < lontano ) and in the right places among the anchors, which context alone would not guarantee. The order also rules things out. The obvious reading of con mio [8247] del is dispaccio , but a d -word cannot sit above è at 8211; foglio , predicted at 8245, can. Conte for [8227], before di Lützow , would have to fall between come (8120) and cotesta (8122), and the firm anchors alone put it near 8133; 8227 is in the e – f range. Both exclusions lean on the context readings nearest them, so they are as good as those readings.
soglia1848.html#history

The Emperor Ferdinand had left Vienna for Innsbruck on 17 May 1848. The nuncio followed him there, at the invitation of the Austrian foreign minister, and wrote to Rome on 27 May; the clear letter printed with the cipher is the Pope’s approval of that. Rome and Vienna were near rupture: papal volunteers were fighting the Austrians in the Veneto, and Count Lützow, the Austrian ambassador, had received his passports in the first days of May (the Rome Gazzetta of 9 May announced them) and left Rome on the evening of 16 May, according to the diary of Prince Agostino Chigi. The earlier instruction the cipher refers to, whose date is in the open groups, was the papal answer: the nuncio should likewise ask for his passports and go home, or to Cologne, away from the war. The cipher countermands it. What the nuove sopraggiunte circostanze were, it does not say. Carlo Luigi Morichini, archbishop of Nisibis and until April the Papal States’ finance minister, had left Rome on 27 May as extraordinary apostolic delegate to the Emperor and to Charles Albert and reached Innsbruck on the night of 10 June (Chigi); the Pope wanted his nuncio to stay beside the Emperor while Morichini negotiated, and wanted Morichini to see the order. It came too late on both counts. The Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani says that on 14 June the nuncio left Innsbruck and went as papal delegate to Frankfurt and to Cologne, returning to his post at Vienna in September. The dispatch is dated the 15th. A copy was posted at Turin on the 20th and never reached him; Chigi heard that it had been intercepted at Turin or Milan. It was printed in Milan on the 30th and posted up in the streets of Rome on 5 or 6 July. On 8 July Chigi noted that the feared ministerial crisis would not come of it, and that the Pope was said to have had no difficulty in showing the Ministry the part in cipher. The published guesses fare unevenly against the decipherment. Spada’s informant said the cipher contained the Pope’s approval of the nuncio’s conduct in keeping on good terms with the court and avoiding the scandal of his dismissal. The approval is in the clear letter; the cipher is an order, and the rupture it heads off was one that Rome itself had ordered. Il Labaro of 7 July, as summarised on Cipherbrain in 2016, guessed at a departure from the court and a role for the bishop of Nisibis, which is nearer to the truth, though in the reverse direction.

Eleven code groups occur once each and are not fixed by their context. The alphabetical order gives each a window: its place between the known values, converted to a stretch of the sorted word list ( windows2.py , piecewise between all anchors; roughly ±15 words). Code Window Context 8734 8760 8904 8739 8413 tr–tu / venti–vo(lgente) / beyond v / tu–u / n–o the date of the earlier letter: con mio foglio del … , probably an early-June date such as tre volgente with a reference 8227 ess–età–ex–fa il Signor, […] di Lützow ; Chigi calls him ex-ambasciatore 8704 te–ti come […]e lo avesse creduto opportuno 8093 8102 ch–ci / ci–co Le partecipo […] […] del Padre 8131 8136 cr–da / da–dar interessa […] al Padre ; delibera […] relativa Scoring every candidate in these windows with the character model picks only function words ( ciò , da , esse ), which gives no sense. 8904 lies above every word in the list, which in a code of this kind may be z -words or an appendix of numbers or names. Filling these needs the 1848 papal codebook or other messages in the same code: the Secretariat of State and the Vienna nunciature archive in the Vatican, or Austrian intercepts in the Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv, which Ramliden pointed to in 2015. Tried again on 30 September 2026, when Lasry asked for fewer gaps in the quoted passage. The code evidently starts at 8000: a line through Colonia (8116) and Imperatore (8319) in the sorted word list puts the first a -word at 7996–8005. Interpolating from 8000 through Colonia and the firm anchors predicts col at 8113–8114 and come at 8120–8122, both where the context readings sit, and narrows the first pair: 8093 falls at ce - ( cenno is predicted at 8093–8097) and 8102 at ch – ci . The words the sense asks for after Le partecipo and before del Padre are all excluded by position: volontà , mente , desiderio , ordine (8424 is ordin- ), comando and commissione fall after Colonia , beneplacito well before. Cenno (‘per cenno del Santo Padre’, at the Holy Father’s behest) fits 8093, but no ch – ci word then makes a phrase with it, so the pair stays open. For [8136], presa (‘delibera presa’) is a p -word and cannot sit at 8136; the window is early d ( da – dar ), and the clause reads complete without it. [8131] is also early d ; an adverb such as d’assai (‘interessa d’assai al Padre cotesta nuova istruzione’, this new instruction matters greatly to the Holy Father) would make the sentence grammatical, but that is a conjecture of sense (I), not a reading. A 1,000-word Italian list with the same interpolation also predicts cotesta near 8145–8159, 23 to 37 above its place at 8122: that context reading is the least supported of the c -group.

The eleven groups above, and so the date of the earlier letter and the exact wording of three clauses. The ten context readings are checked by order, not proved. The weakest are guerra (8310, only nine values below Imperatore at 8319, so nearly all h - and i -words would have to fit between them) and lontan- (8346, six above istruzione , leaving five values for everything from istr - to lon -). Both fit the sentence and the order, but a code this sparse there would be unusual. Tuttavia is furthest from its prediction, for the reason given in §05. della guerra where dalla guerra is expected, and the stray 8 after si on line 1, are as printed; whether they are the cipher clerk’s or the Milan compositor’s cannot be told from a reprint. The broadsheet is a Roman reprint of the Milan paper. The Milan issue itself (on repubblicaromana-1849.it) was not collated digit by digit.

Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà, Rome, 15 June 1848 (L'Italia del Popolo no. 40) The papal Secretary of State's counter-order to the nuncio at Innsbruck, where the Emperor had fled: instead of asking for his passports after Lützow's departure from Rome, he is to remain with the Emperor wherever he goes, and show the dispatch at once to Mgr Morichini. Printed in cipher by Mazzini's L'Italia del Popolo (30 June 1848) and posted by Klaus Schmeh as unsolved; the key was recovered here, some code words remain unread ([8xxx]). Three letters to the dukes of Bavaria in one homophonic key (system L), two of them filed under Cornelio Sperantio, who received them under cover. The key was recovered from contemporary glosses (adjacent plaintext): first from one word on a Latin letter from King John Zápolya’s side of 18 April 1533 (R9415, 95.8%), then from the full interlinear decipherment of King John’s letter of 6 February 1534; it also deciphers a German newsletter from Buda of 8 February on Werbőczy’s peace with the Turk. 1,274 of 1,334 cipher words (95.5%) measured, words supplied from sense counted unread. R9411: King John Zápolya of Hungary to the dukes of Bavaria, Buda, 6 February 1534, in Latin. R9412: a German newsletter from an agent at Buda to a duke of Bavaria, 8 February 1534. The cover is addressed to Cornelio Sperantio, the dukes’ man at Buda; DECODE lists him as the sender. Where Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591, ff. 248, 250–251 and 260–261; DECODE R9411 and R9412 (catalogue 163), “partially decrypted”, and R9415 (catalogue 162). The cipher A homophonic substitution on graphic signs, without word division, with a few signs for pairs and words and clear Latin passages left standing: system L of the volume. How it was deciphered R9411 carries a contemporary interlinear decipherment over every line; the key was fixed from it by a solver held to the gloss values, then refitted for German and applied to R9412, which has none. The same key had already been recovered from a one-word gloss on R9415 with a solver; the two agree sign for sign. What it says R9415: Ferdinand opened a treaty with King John while secretly suing the Sultan for peace. King John on the Hungarian gold and silver mines and his servant Nicolaus Freiberger; the newsletter on Werbőczy’s everlasting peace with the Turk, Peterwardein, Titel and Salankamen, plans against Transylvania, and the mines. Measured Cipher words only, every supplied word counted unread ( measure.py , 5 October 2026; R9415 r9415/count.py ): R9415 388 of 405 (95.8%), R9411 340 of 356 (95.5%), R9412 546 of 573 (95.3%), together 1,274 of 1,334 (95.5%). Counted word by word on the written-out readings, with doubtful and supplied words as holes (24 October 2026): R9411 92.2%, R9412 89.1%, under the 95% a complete reading needs. Still open Words at blotted signs: 16 in R9411, including the captain’s name; 27 in R9412, including the second Danube fortress, the bishop, the Nuremberg factor and the signature; 17 scattered words in R9415.

This letter was filed until 15 October 2026 with two letters in other ciphers ( Łaski’s and the Wardein report , each with its own page); it is in this key and is shown here. The signs look like the System A′ set of the dukes’ agents, but the A′ key does not fit, and neither does R9369, Augurelio’s own key of 1531. A gloss over part of line 3 (“incrementum”) gave the first values; a solver (simulated annealing) with a Latin language model and a search over the candidate values gave the rest ( r9415/ ). Six signs after the clear passages are nulls marking the join. … hostis noster una parte tractatum cum […] nobiscum inceperit, ex alia parte Turcarum Caesari pro pace clam supplicaverit, credimus D. vestras illud iam compertum habere. Georgius, the dukes’ servant, came back with their three reasons for urging concord at the diet of Pressburg. Ferdinand, “our enemy”, opened a treaty with King John while secretly suing the Sultan for peace; the Sultan’s own letters revealed it, so John recalled his orators and, at the Sultan’s request, sent his governor to him. Ferdinand boasts of peace but does not know its terms, and the dukes should not believe the rumour. The Turkish envoy in Vienna has made Ferdinand’s orator in Turkey “his” orator. The address on the fourth page, in clear, is to Aurelio Augurelio. Open: 17 scattered words ( r9415/count.txt ).
