From the decipherment ( targets/sperantio1534/r9411/reading_r9411.txt ), in the original Latin, with gaps as […]: Salutem et omne bonum. Illustrissimi principes domini ac fratres carissimi. Accepimus literas Vestre et ea quae […] etiam intelleximus quae […] secretarium suum scripserunt. Vestre ita sibi persuadere velint, quidquid nos in rem commodum et dignitatem earum et fratrum atque amicorum suorum id facere possumus, id semper libentissimo animo facturi sumus. […] videtur tamen esse res communicanda cum illustri domino regni nostri gubernatore, qui propediem hic apud nos futurus est. Videtur enim nobis esse satius de hac re capere consilium ipsius quam si ex abrupto apud potentissimum Turcarum imperatorem rem tentaremus. … Ceterum Vestre medio magnifici […] capitanei et consiliarii nostri … ex parte minerarum auri, argenti et aliorum metallorum, quae res nobis vehementissime fuit cordi, … cum Dei auxilio rem aggredi. … Misimus nunc hunc servitorem nostrum Nicolaum Freeberger ad Vestras … Bude sexta Februarii, anno etc. xxxiiii. In English: King John will do whatever he can for the dukes, whom he addresses as brothers. Their request must first go to the governor of his realm (Lodovico Gritti), who is expected shortly: better to take his counsel than to try the matter abruptly with the Turkish emperor. The news his adversaries spread is false. Through his captain and councillor he has begun on the gold, silver and other mines, a matter very close to his heart. He sends his servant Nicolaus Freiberger to the dukes, invites them to take on the working of such mines, and asks for masters skilled in them. A postscript asks for the Bavarian mining ordinance (“ordinacionem rerum montanarum”) by a sure messenger.

German, no gloss. It opens by repeating what the writer sent on 22 December by an unsure messenger. That date, in line 1, belongs to the earlier letter; this one is dated at its foot, “Datum Ofen, des achten Februarii”. From the decipherment ( targets/sperantio1534/r9411/reading_r9412.txt ; […] not deciphered, braces supplied from sense, capitals in clear on the page): wie erstlich, was der canczler herr Stephan Werbeczi bei dem Turcken hab ausgericht. ET PRIMO: so hat er dem Ungerland mit dem Turcken einen ewigen frid gemacht und angestossen. SECUNDO: das alle stett und flecken … als nemlich Peterwardein und […], mit Titil, Salmaulack {Salankamen} … TERTIO: … die zwitrachten, als von wegen des titels der kunig … QUARTO: … SED TAMEN PER MAXIMOS SUOS CONATUS NIHIL ALIUD IMPETRARE POTUIT QUAM ILLUD QUOD … The chancellor Stephan Werbőczy has obtained at the Porte an everlasting peace between Hungary and the Turk. The Danube places are named: Peterwardein (Petrovaradin), Titel, Salankamen. The dispute over the kings’ titles and the frontier towns is to be settled, and the writer has sent a copy of the Sultan’s letter. Then come plans against Transylvania and the mines. Fridrich Schmalcz has made himself head of the mining business and sends men skilled in mining to Pest; his factor at Nuremberg is named, and “herr Caesar” at Vienna. A bishop sends the duke his greetings in clear Latin. The b/w and d/t pairs share signs, so “beczi” is Werbeczi.

Both letters transcribed sign by sign from full-resolution line crops of the DECODE images (R9411 2,040 signs, R9412 2,725), in four passes on R9411 and three on R9412. R9411: a solver (simulated annealing) with a Latin language model ( la ), started from and held to the values of the interlinear gloss ( r9411/solve.py , run7.txt ); checked by hand against the gloss. R9412: the R9411 key refitted with a language model of sixteenth-century German ( de-1500s ), with pair and digraph signs set from context; then a manual pass on the sense (84% → 89%), a check of every gap, and on 5 October 2026 a further pass on the remaining gaps. Measure ( measure.py , 5 October 2026): cipher words only, leaving out the clear Latin and German passages and the clear date, with every word supplied from sense, whole or in part, counted unread. R9411 340/356 (95.5%), R9412 546/573 (95.3%), together 886/929 (95.4%). The earlier figure of 92% counted clear text and could not be reproduced. Rejected, because each raised its own score while making the German worse: two automated look-alike repairs ( confuse.py ) and two key optimisers driven by a lexicon measure ( lexopt.py , lexopt2.py ). Control: a second, independent transcription of all five pages (4,745 signs) with the R9415 key and a word-level fit ( fit.py ) gives R9411 at 91% without the gloss.

Three letters of the Emperor to his envoy in the private key he sent him in 1720 (DECODE R5021–R5024). The key, on DECODE beside them (R5018: a number and a graphic sign for each letter, codes for names), was transcribed and applied by hand: Orléans and the Barrier, and Beretti Landi’s proposal of a marriage between the Emperor’s children and Philip V’s sons. 29 38 19 69 [E] 37 [C] 24 23 35 [M] 28 [N] der Beretti Landi euch Namen 29 = D · 38 = E · 19 = R · 69 = Beretti Landi · zi = Hof · ab = Anjou Vienna → The Hague, Cambrai · the Emperor’s private key R5018, numbers and signs · 1720–1722 · known key applied Charles VI to Count Windischgrätz in the private key, 1720–1722 from Charles VI Go to the full text ↓ Three letters of the Emperor to his envoy in the private key he sent him in 1720, deciphered with that key, which survives in the family archive: a Spanish marriage for his children, proposed in 1720 and again in 1722. Nos. 2, 3 and 6 of the family’s register. Where Státní oblastní archiv v Plzni, Rodinný archiv Windischgrätzů: autograph inv. 694 karton 5 (R5021), register copies inv. 5 book 5 pp. 404–416 (R5022, R5023, R5024). Catalogue item 69. The cipher The private key R5018: each letter has a number from 10 to 38 and a graphic sign, the vowels a second number; about 300 codes for words and names. How it was deciphered The key, on DECODE and in the same archive, was transcribed and applied by hand, matching the copyist’s signs to the key’s drawings. What it says Orléans and Spain, the burden of the Barrier; Beretti Landi’s proposal of a marriage between the Emperor’s children and Philip V’s sons, “beede so klein”. Still open The cleartext around the cipher is summarised, not edited; Nos. 4, 5 and 7 of the register are not on DECODE. The first letter of the series, of 3 February 1720, is in the Court Chancellery’s nomenclator R5017 and announces this key; it is a different cipher with its own page: Charles VI to Windischgrätz, 3 February 1720 .

R5018 is the new private key, on a single sheet. Each of 24 letters has a number from 10 to 38 and a graphic sign, and the vowels have a second number. About 300 codes follow, as numbers 39–210 or two-letter groups ( ab Anjou, fb Spanien, zi Hof, 69 Beretti Landi, 151 Oesterreich, 159 Orleans), and the nulls are 3 4 5 6 7 9. Several names were added later in paler ink, among them Fleury, Walpole and Windischgrätz himself. The docket on the back reads “Ziffern mit J[hr]: K[ayserlichen] M[ajestät] …”. Mírka noted in 2012 that the later letters are in this key. Key R5018, the top of the sheet: each letter with its number, its sign and, for the vowels, a second number. The nomenclature columns begin below. Image: Státní oblastní archiv v Plzni, Rodinný archiv Windischgrätzů, key sheet, via DECODE R5018.

In R5018 the letters are spelt out one symbol at a time, mixing the number and the sign for the same letter freely, and names are given as codes. Decrypted from the register copy: Register copy, book 5 p. 408 (No. 3): “Was nemblich der Beretti Landi euch Namen seines Hofs über ein Proposition gethan eine Heyrath zwischen ein oder andern meiner Kinder und Anjou Söhne ”. Image: Státní oblastní archiv v Plzni, Rodinný archiv Windischgrätzů inv. 5, book 5 p. 408, via DECODE R5023. No. 2, 13 April 1720. “Das ob und Orleans sich endlich wider miteinander verstehen werden, ist schir zu besorgen”; and a project for how one might free oneself entirely “ von dem onere der Barriere ”, the Emperor’s cost of the Dutch garrisons in the Barrier fortresses. No. 3, 24 July 1720. The Spanish envoy Beretti Landi , in the name of his court, has proposed “ eine Heyrath zwischen ein oder andern meiner Kinder und Anjou Söhne ”. Charles would stay “in guter Verstendnus mit seinen Hof ”, but as for die Heyrath , “wer en beede so klein ” that nothing should yet be made known. His eldest daughter, Maria Theresa, was three. No. 6, 11 April 1722 , to Windischgrätz as plenipotentiary at Cambrai, opening with the Emperor’s grief at the death of his Oberststallmeister. The cipher covers what he writes “ wegen des Beretti ”, especially what he discussed “ mit Beretti wegen einer Heyrath ” between “ Spanien und mir ”. Beretti is “erbittert wider mich und Oesterreich ”, yet it is not bad “sich des Beretti zu gebrauchen ” and to show “ ihm all Convenienz in utili et honorifico”. The marriage theme runs from 1720 to 1722, well before the Ripperda negotiations of 1725 that promised the Emperor’s daughters to Philip V’s sons.

The key sheet was transcribed from tiled crops of the DECODE image, with a confidence mark on each cell. The letters were decoded by hand from the register copies (and the autograph of No. 2), because the copyist’s signs have to be matched to the key’s drawings. The copyist uses one sign for D and N, and one sign for Z and G; the numbered letters around each sign decide which is meant. No. 2, first passage: the cipher opens with a V-sign, giving “und Orleans”. The subject, Spain, is inferred from the context. M. No. 3, “ein Proposition” and “die Heyrath” each contain a copyist’s wrong letter; the words are H. All other passages are H. Letters 4, 5 and 7 of the register (book pp. 409–414, 417 onward) are not on DECODE and were not seen. The cleartext of Nos. 2, 3 and 6 is summarised here, not edited.
